topics.name: An Inspector Calls: plot and characters
An Inspector Calls: themes and context

questions.q: Who says "Fair is foul, and foul is fair"?
ms: The Witches chant it in Act 1 Scene 1, setting up the play's inversion of moral order.
questions.tip: Macbeth echoes it later ("So foul and fair a day"), so don't mix up the two lines.

questions.q: Who says "Out, damned spot!"?
ms: Lady Macbeth says it while sleepwalking in Act 5 Scene 1, showing her guilt.
questions.tip: Know which act: 5.1, the sleepwalking scene, watched by the Doctor and Gentlewoman.

questions.q: In which act does Macbeth murder Duncan?
ms: Duncan is killed offstage in Act 2 Scene 2 at Macbeth's castle at Inverness.
questions.tip: The murder happens offstage; Shakespeare focuses on the before and after.

questions.q: What title is Macbeth given at the start of the play as a reward for his bravery in battle?
ms: Duncan gives him the traitor Cawdor's title in Act 1 Scene 2/3. He is already Thane of Glamis.
questions.tip: Prince of Cumberland is Malcolm's title, the one that blocks Macbeth.

questions.q: Who says "Look like th' innocent flower, / But be the serpent under't"?
ms: Lady Macbeth coaches Macbeth on deception in Act 1 Scene 5; the serpent links to the Fall in Genesis.
questions.tip: Link the serpent to Satan in Eden for AO3 religious context.

questions.q: What do the apparitions in Act 4 Scene 1 tell Macbeth?
options: Beware Macduff; none of woman born can harm him; he is safe until Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane
He will become Thane of Cawdor; Duncan will name him heir; Banquo's sons will not rule
Banquo will kill him; Fleance will be king; Malcolm will flee to England
Lady Macbeth will die; Macduff is loyal; he will rule for ever
ms: The armed head, bloody child and crowned child give the three prophecies, then the show of eight kings.
questions.tip: The prophecies are equivocal: they sound reassuring but come true in unexpected ways.

questions.q: Why is Macduff able to kill Macbeth despite the prophecy?
options: He was born by caesarean ("untimely ripped" from his mother's womb)
He carries a branch from Birnam Wood
He is protected by English soldiers
ms: Macduff "was from his mother's womb / Untimely ripped", so technically not "of woman born".
questions.tip: Use this as an example of equivocation, a key word linked to the Gunpowder Plot trials.

questions.q: Who escapes when Banquo is murdered in Act 3?
ms: Fleance flees, so Banquo's line survives, keeping the prophecy that Banquo's descendants will be kings.
questions.tip: Fleance's escape means the threat from Banquo's line remains, so Macbeth's paranoia continues ("Then comes my fit again").

questions.q: In Act 3 Scene 2, Macbeth tells Lady Macbeth "Be innocent of the knowledge, dearest chuck". What does this show about their relationship?
options: Macbeth now plans murders without her, showing a shift in power and growing distance between them
Macbeth is confessing his guilt to her and seeking forgiveness
Macbeth wants to protect Lady Macbeth because she is pregnant
Lady Macbeth is still controlling all of Macbeth's decisions
ms: He keeps the plan to kill Banquo secret: the partnership has broken down and Macbeth now leads in evil.
questions.tip: Track the relationship as an arc: equal partners, then she leads, then he leads, then isolation.

questions.q: Which character's ghost appears at the banquet in Act 3 Scene 4?
ms: Banquo's ghost sits in Macbeth's seat; only Macbeth sees it.
questions.tip: Only Macbeth sees the ghost, which suggests guilt or the supernatural.

questions.q: Who first suspects Macbeth openly and refuses to attend his coronation?
ms: Macduff goes to Fife instead of Scone (Act 2 Scene 4), showing early distrust.
questions.tip: Macduff's refusal is a small but useful detail for showing Macbeth's isolation.

questions.q: Give two things Lady Macbeth does in Act 2 Scene 2 to make sure the murder of Duncan succeeds.
questions.answer: She drugs the grooms' drinks and returns the daggers to Duncan's chamber, smearing the grooms with blood.
ms: Drugs the grooms / guards (with possets / wine) (1 mark)
Returns the daggers and smears the grooms with blood (1 mark). Allow: takes control of the plan, tells Macbeth to wash his hands.
questions.tip: Give two different actions, not the same idea twice.

questions.q: Explain the effect of the word "scorpions" in the quotation "O, full of scorpions is my mind, dear wife!"
questions.answer: "Scorpions" are poisonous and dangerous, suggesting Macbeth's thoughts are painful, restless and self-destructive. The plural shows many threats at once (Banquo, Fleance), so paranoia infests his mind. The contrast with the tender "dear wife" shows he still loves her but is tortured despite gaining the crown.
ms: Identifies scorpions as dangerous / poisonous / stinging (1 mark)
Links to Macbeth's paranoia, guilt or mental torment (1 mark)
Comments on plural or the idea that his mind is infested / out of control (1 mark)
Develops with context or contrast, e.g. "dear wife" shows tenderness, or link to the cost of ambition (1 mark)
questions.tip: Zoom in on the single word and give more than one layer of meaning.

questions.q: How does Macbeth change between Act 1 Scene 2 and Act 5? Give two points with a reference for each.
questions.answer: At first he is "brave Macbeth", a loyal warrior praised by the Captain. By Act 5 he is a "dead butcher" and tyrant, nihilistic and numb ("Life's but a walking shadow").
ms: Point about early Macbeth: brave, loyal, respected (1 mark)
Supporting reference, e.g. "brave Macbeth", "valour's minion" (1 mark)
Point about later Macbeth: tyrant, isolated, despairing or numb (1 mark)
Supporting reference, e.g. "dead butcher", "Life's but a walking shadow", "I have almost forgot the taste of fears" (1 mark)
questions.tip: Changes need a 'from' and a 'to', each backed with evidence.

questions.q: Explain how Shakespeare presents Banquo as a foil to Macbeth.
questions.answer: Both hear the prophecies, but Banquo distrusts them ("instruments of darkness") and resists temptation, praying to "merciful powers" against "cursed thoughts". Macbeth acts on his ambition. Banquo shows that the Witches do not force evil: Macbeth chooses it. Shakespeare also flatters James I, who claimed descent from Banquo, by making him noble.
ms: Banquo hears the same prophecies but reacts with suspicion (1 mark)
Reference, e.g. "instruments of darkness tell us truths" (1 mark)
Explains the contrast shows Macbeth's free will / responsibility (1 mark)
Context: James I's descent from Banquo, so he is presented positively (1 mark)
questions.tip: A foil is a contrasting character. Say what the contrast reveals about Macbeth.

questions.q:
Starting with the extract in Act 1 Scene 7, where Lady Macbeth persuades Macbeth to go ahead with the murder after he says "We will proceed no further in this business", explore how far Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as being in control of her husband.

Write about:
- how Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth and her influence in this extract
- how Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth and her influence in the play as a whole. [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth's power as real but borrowed: she dominates Macbeth by weaponising Jacobean ideas of masculinity, yet her power depends on rejecting her own nature, so it cannot last and collapses into guilt and madness, warning a Jacobean audience that disrupting the natural order destroys the self.
Plan:
1. Extract: she attacks his manhood ("When you durst do it, then you were a man"), using rhetorical questions and insults to shame him. AO3: masculinity tied to courage and action.
2. Extract: the infanticide image (dashing out the brains of the baby she nursed) shows her willingness to reject motherhood; shocking to an audience valuing women as nurturers.
3. Act 1 Scene 5: "unsex me here" and "take my milk for gall" show she must call on spirits to gain power. AO3: Daemonologie and fear of witchcraft; her soliloquy aligns her with the Witches.
4. Act 3: power shifts. Macbeth excludes her ("Be innocent of the knowledge, dearest chuck"); at the banquet she still covers for him but is losing control.
5. Act 5 Scene 1: sleepwalking, prose not verse, "Out, damned spot!" and a need for light show total collapse; her suicide offstage shows her power was unnatural. AO3: Great Chain of Being, divine punishment.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised response to the task and the whole text; judicious, precisely embedded references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed response to the task and the whole text; apt, integrated references; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.
Below Level 5 (Level 4, 16-20): clear, explained response with effective references and clear understanding of methods and context, but less developed or exploratory.

AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Clear understanding of Lady Macbeth's role; tracks her from dominance to breakdown; well-chosen quotations from extract and whole play; conceptual argument about the nature and limits of her power.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Imperatives and rhetorical questions in Act 1 Scene 7; imagery of babies and milk; soliloquy in 1.5; change from verse to prose in 5.1; dramatic irony of "A little water clears us of this deed" versus 5.1; offstage death.
AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Jacobean patriarchy and expected female roles; witchcraft and James I's Daemonologie (1597); Great Chain of Being; belief in divine order and punishment.

AO4 (4 marks, high performance): consistent accuracy in spelling and punctuation; consistent control of meaning; wide range of vocabulary and sentence structures. 2-3 marks: considerable accuracy; 1 mark: reasonable accuracy.
questions.tip: Do not just retell the extract. Keep moving between the extract and the rest of the play.

questions.q:
Starting with the extract in Act 5 Scene 5, where Macbeth hears of his wife's death and gives the "Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow" speech, explore how Shakespeare presents Macbeth as a tragic hero.

Write about:
- how Shakespeare presents Macbeth in this extract
- how Shakespeare presents Macbeth in the play as a whole. [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: Shakespeare presents Macbeth as a tragic hero whose greatness makes his fall more painful: his hamartia of "vaulting ambition" turns a brave, imaginative man into a nihilistic tyrant, and by Act 5 he understands, too late, that the crown has emptied his life of meaning.
Plan:
1. Extract: "Life's but a walking shadow" and "a tale / Told by an idiot" show nihilism; theatre metaphor ("poor player") suggests life is meaningless performance.
2. Extract: his flat response to his wife's death ("She should have died hereafter") shows emotional numbness; contrast with "dear wife" earlier.
3. Act 1: "brave Macbeth" and "valour's minion" establish his status and heroism, making his fall tragic (Aristotelian tragedy).
4. Act 1 Scene 7: soliloquy shows conscience and awareness ("I have no spur... but only / Vaulting ambition"), so he chooses evil knowingly: hamartia.
5. Act 5 ending: he fights to the end ("Lay on, Macduff"), regaining some warrior courage; Malcolm's label "dead butcher" restores order. AO3: divine right, regicide as sin.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised response to the task and the whole text; judicious, precisely embedded references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed response to the task and the whole text; apt, integrated references; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.
Below Level 5 (Level 4, 16-20): clear, explained response with effective references and clear understanding of methods and context, but less developed or exploratory.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Conceptualised view of Macbeth as a tragic hero; links extract to his journey from hero to tyrant; precise quotations.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Soliloquy form; repetition of "tomorrow" slowing rhythm; light and dark imagery ("brief candle"); metaphor of theatre; structure of tragedy (rise, hamartia, peripeteia, catastrophe).
AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Aristotle's tragic hero; divine right of kings and the Great Chain of Being; regicide as a sin against God; James I and the Gunpowder Plot (1605).

AO4 (4 marks, high performance): consistent accuracy in spelling and punctuation; consistent control of meaning; wide range of vocabulary and sentence structures. 2-3 marks: considerable accuracy; 1 mark: reasonable accuracy.
questions.tip: Name the tragic hero features (hamartia, downfall, catharsis) and tie them to evidence.

questions.q: Give two of the Witches' prophecies to Macbeth in Act 1 Scene 3.
questions.answer: That he will be Thane of Cawdor and that he will be king hereafter.
ms: Thane of Cawdor (1 mark)
King hereafter (1 mark). Do not accept Thane of Glamis alone as a prophecy as he already holds it, but allow if both others are not given.
questions.tip: Glamis is his current title, not a prediction.

questions.q: Explain why Macbeth has Banquo murdered. Give three reasons.
questions.answer: He fears Banquo's "royalty of nature" and wisdom; the Witches said Banquo's children will be kings, so Macbeth's crown is "fruitless"; Banquo suspects him ("Thou hast it now" ... "I fear / Thou play'dst most foully for't").
ms: Fears Banquo's noble nature / wisdom (1 mark)
Prophecy that Banquo's descendants will be kings, making Macbeth's crown "fruitless" / "barren sceptre" (1 mark)
Banquo suspects him of killing Duncan (1 mark)
questions.tip: Three distinct reasons, each linked to the text.

questions.q: Explain how Shakespeare presents Macduff as a model of true masculinity.
questions.answer: When told his family is murdered, Malcolm urges "Dispute it like a man" but Macduff replies he must "also feel it as a man". Shakespeare shows masculinity can include grief and emotion, contrasting Lady Macbeth's idea that manhood means violence. Macduff then channels grief into just action, killing the tyrant and restoring order.
ms: Reference to Macduff's grief scene, e.g. "I must also feel it as a man" (1 mark)
Explains masculinity includes emotion / compassion (1 mark)
Contrasts with Lady Macbeth's or Macbeth's violent definition of manhood (1 mark)
Links to his role restoring order by killing Macbeth (1 mark)
questions.tip: Compare definitions of masculinity across characters for top marks.

questions.q: Which king was on the throne when Macbeth was first performed (around 1606)?
ms: James I (James VI of Scotland) became king of England in 1603.
questions.tip: James was Scottish and believed he descended from Banquo.

questions.q: What was the Gunpowder Plot (1605)?
options: A Catholic plot to blow up Parliament and kill James I
A rebellion by witches in Scotland
A plan by Puritans to close the theatres
ms: Guy Fawkes and conspirators planned regicide; this makes Duncan's murder highly topical.
questions.tip: Link the Plot to regicide and the Porter's "equivocator" joke.

questions.q: What is the Great Chain of Being?
options: A list of Scottish kings descended from Banquo
A law punishing witchcraft with death
The belief that God set a fixed order for everything, with the king directly below God
The chain of murders Macbeth commits
ms: Killing a king breaks the God-given order, causing chaos in nature.
questions.tip: Use it to explain unnatural events after Duncan's death.

questions.q: Which unnatural event is reported after Duncan's murder?
ms: Ross and the Old Man report the horses turning wild and eating each other (Act 2 Scene 4).
questions.tip: Birnam Wood moving is Act 5 and is not supernatural.

questions.q: What book on witchcraft did James I write in 1597?
ms: Daemonologie shows James's belief in witches and their threat to kings.
questions.tip: Holinshed's Chronicles is Shakespeare's source for the plot, not a witchcraft book.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the theme of equivocation in Macbeth?
options: The balance of good and evil shown by the weather
Characters being equal in power, as with Macbeth and Banquo
A rhyme scheme used only by the Witches
Language that is deliberately ambiguous, so it seems true but misleads, as in the apparitions' prophecies
ms: The Porter mentions an "equivocator"; the Witches' half-truths trap Macbeth.
questions.tip: Link to Father Garnet, a Gunpowder Plot priest who defended equivocation at his trial.

questions.q: Which theme is most clearly shown by "Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this blood"?
ms: Macbeth feels his guilt is too great for an ocean to wash away (Act 2 Scene 2).
questions.tip: Compare with Lady Macbeth's "A little water clears us of this deed", ironic by Act 5.

questions.q: Edward the Confessor, King of England, is described as able to cure illness by touch. Why does Shakespeare include this?
options: To contrast a holy, rightful king with Macbeth the tyrant, reflecting the divine right of kings
To explain how Lady Macbeth could be cured
To show England is weaker than Scotland
ms: The healing king (Act 4 Scene 3) shows the "king-becoming graces"; James I also practised touching for the King's Evil.
questions.tip: Mention good kingship as a contrast whenever you write about Macbeth as a tyrant.

questions.q: Give two ways Jacobean context shapes the presentation of the Witches.
questions.answer: James I believed witches were real and dangerous (he wrote Daemonologie and was involved in the North Berwick witch trials), so the Witches are presented as genuinely threatening, and an audience would see them as agents of the devil causing disorder.
ms: James I's belief in / fear of witchcraft, e.g. Daemonologie or North Berwick trials (1 mark)
Audience belief that witches served the devil / caused storms, so they seem truly evil or threatening (1 mark)
questions.tip: Each mark needs a context fact linked to how the Witches appear.

questions.q: Explain the effect of the imagery in "Stars, hide your fires" and "my black and deep desires".
questions.answer: Macbeth uses light and dark imagery. Light represents goodness and God, darkness represents evil. By ordering the stars to hide, he wants his ambition concealed even from heaven, showing he knows it is sinful. The imperative shows his desire for control, and "black and deep" suggests ambition is hidden and growing within him.
ms: Identifies light/dark imagery (1 mark)
Light = goodness/God, dark = evil/sin (1 mark)
Shows Macbeth knows his desire is wrong and wants to hide it (1 mark)
Develops with method, e.g. imperative, aside, "deep" suggests hidden or growing ambition, or link to Lady Macbeth's "Come, thick night" (1 mark)
questions.tip: Say what the image suggests about Macbeth's state of mind, not just what it 'shows'.

questions.q: "Macbeth is a play about the consequences of upsetting the natural order." Explain two ways Shakespeare supports this idea.
questions.answer: After the regicide, nature itself rebels: darkness in day, horses eating each other, showing the Great Chain of Being is broken. Macbeth and Lady Macbeth lose sleep ("Macbeth does murder sleep"), a natural restorative, and she ends sleepwalking. Order only returns when the rightful heir Malcolm is crowned.
ms: First way: unnatural events in nature after regicide (1 mark) with reference (1 mark)
Second way: loss of sleep / madness / Macbeth's downfall, or restoration with Malcolm (1 mark) with reference or context such as Great Chain of Being / divine right (1 mark)
questions.tip: Two developed ways beat four rushed ones.

questions.q:
Starting with the extract in Act 1 Scene 3, where Macbeth and Banquo first meet the Witches on the heath, explore how far Shakespeare presents the Witches as responsible for Macbeth's downfall.

Write about:
- how Shakespeare presents the Witches and their influence in this extract
- how Shakespeare presents the Witches and their influence in the play as a whole. [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: Shakespeare presents the supernatural as a catalyst rather than a cause: the Witches plant suggestion, but the real power of the supernatural lies in how it exposes and feeds desires already in Macbeth, which a Jacobean audience, fearful of witchcraft, would see as the devil exploiting human weakness.
Plan:
1. Extract: the Witches' paradoxical greetings and Macbeth's reaction (he "start[s]" and seems to fear things that "sound so fair") suggest the prophecy touches an existing ambition.
2. Extract: Banquo calls them "instruments of darkness" who "tell us truths" to "betray's"; he is the voice of caution, showing free will.
3. Act 1 Scene 5: Lady Macbeth calls on "spirits" to "unsex me here", linking her to the supernatural and to self-made evil.
4. Act 2 Scene 1: the dagger hallucination ("Is this a dagger which I see before me") shows the supernatural blurring with his guilty mind; Act 3 Scene 4 Banquo's ghost.
5. Act 4 Scene 1: equivocal apparitions give false confidence; Act 5 they come true, showing the Witches' deceit. AO3: Daemonologie, North Berwick trials, equivocation and Father Garnet.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised response to the task and the whole text; judicious, precisely embedded references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed response to the task and the whole text; apt, integrated references; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.
Below Level 5 (Level 4, 16-20): clear, explained response with effective references and clear understanding of methods and context, but less developed or exploratory.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Thoughtful argument on whether the supernatural controls or reveals; clear tracking from extract to whole text.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Trochaic tetrameter and rhyme in the Witches' speech marks them as other; paradox and antithesis; stage directions (thunder); asides revealing Macbeth's thoughts; dramatic irony.
AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Jacobean belief in witchcraft; James I's Daemonologie and the North Berwick trials; Christian idea of the devil tempting humans; equivocation and the Gunpowder Plot.

AO4 (4 marks, high performance): consistent accuracy in spelling and punctuation; consistent control of meaning; wide range of vocabulary and sentence structures. 2-3 marks: considerable accuracy; 1 mark: reasonable accuracy.
questions.tip: Argue a 'how far' view: the strongest essays decide who is really responsible.

questions.q:
Starting with the extract in Act 4 Scene 3, where Malcolm tests Macduff's loyalty and lists the "king-becoming graces", explore how Shakespeare presents ideas about kingship.

Write about:
- how Shakespeare presents kingship in this extract
- how Shakespeare presents kingship in the play as a whole. [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: Shakespeare presents kingship as a sacred duty rather than a prize: through the contrast of Duncan, Edward and Malcolm with the tyrant Macbeth, he shows that a true king serves and nurtures his people, a message that flatters James I and warns against usurpation.
Plan:
1. Extract: Malcolm lists "king-becoming graces" (justice, verity, temperance, mercy), defining ideal kingship; he tests Macduff, showing wisdom.
2. Extract: Edward the Confessor's healing touch links kingship to God (divine right); contrast with Scotland "bleeding" under Macbeth.
3. Duncan: generous and trusting ("I have begun to plant thee", gardening imagery of growth), but too trusting of Cawdor and Macbeth.
4. Macbeth: usurper and tyrant; clothing imagery ("Like a giant's robe / Upon a dwarfish thief") shows the crown does not fit him; "fruitless crown" shows sterility.
5. Ending: Malcolm crowned at Scone, order restored, nature healed. AO3: James I, divine right, Banquo as ancestor, Gunpowder Plot.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised response to the task and the whole text; judicious, precisely embedded references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed response to the task and the whole text; apt, integrated references; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.
Below Level 5 (Level 4, 16-20): clear, explained response with effective references and clear understanding of methods and context, but less developed or exploratory.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Conceptualised comparison of good kings and tyranny; links extract to the wider structure; precise references.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Malcolm's list as a rhetorical device; extended clothing and gardening imagery; contrast/juxtaposition of Scotland and England; cyclical structure ending with a new rightful king.
AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Divine right of kings; Great Chain of Being; James I's views on kingship (Basilikon Doron); regicide and the Gunpowder Plot; English audience attitude to Scotland.

AO4 (4 marks, high performance): consistent accuracy in spelling and punctuation; consistent control of meaning; wide range of vocabulary and sentence structures. 2-3 marks: considerable accuracy; 1 mark: reasonable accuracy.
questions.tip: Kingship essays need at least three kings. Compare them.

questions.q: Explain how the theme of sleep is used in Macbeth. Give one reference.
questions.answer: Sleep represents innocence and peace of mind. After killing Duncan, Macbeth hears a voice cry "Macbeth does murder sleep", so he loses peace. Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking shows guilt invades her unconscious mind.
ms: Sleep symbolises innocence / peace / a clear conscience (1 mark)
Reference, e.g. "Macbeth does murder sleep" or the sleepwalking scene (1 mark)
Explains loss of sleep shows guilt or punishment (1 mark)
questions.tip: Link the symbol to a character's guilt.

questions.q: Give two features of the Witches' language that make them seem unnatural.
questions.answer: They speak in rhyming trochaic tetrameter (four beats, starting stressed), unlike the iambic pentameter of nobles, and use paradoxes such as "Fair is foul, and foul is fair".
ms: Rhyme / chant / trochaic tetrameter, different from other characters' iambic pentameter (1 mark)
Paradox / riddles / equivocal language, with example (1 mark). Allow: incantations, repetition such as "Double, double toil and trouble".
questions.tip: Name the technique and give an example.

questions.q: Who says "Bah! Humbug!"?
ms: Scrooge dismisses Christmas to his nephew Fred in Stave 1.
questions.tip: Know it is Stave 1, before any ghost visits.

questions.q: How many staves are there in A Christmas Carol?
ms: Dickens calls his chapters staves, like verses of a carol; there are five.
questions.tip: Calling them chapters is fine but 'stave' shows awareness of the carol structure.

questions.q: Who visits Scrooge first, in Stave 1?
ms: Jacob Marley, dead seven years, warns Scrooge and announces three spirits.
questions.tip: Marley died seven years ago on Christmas Eve.

questions.q: Who says "I wear the chain I forged in life"?
options: The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come
ms: Marley's chain of cash-boxes and ledgers symbolises the sins of greed.
questions.tip: The chain is self-made: link to personal responsibility.

questions.q: Which spirit reveals the children Ignorance and Want?
options: The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come
ms: They emerge from beneath his robe at the end of Stave 3.
questions.tip: Ignorance is the more dangerous: Dickens wants education for the poor.

questions.q: In which stave does Scrooge see Belle end their engagement?
ms: The Ghost of Christmas Past shows Belle saying a "golden" idol has replaced her.
questions.tip: Stave 2 is the past: school, Fezziwig, Belle.

questions.q: What does Scrooge say about the poor that the Ghost of Christmas Present later throws back at him?
options: "I am as light as a feather"
"I will honour Christmas in my heart"
ms: The Ghost repeats his cruel phrase when Scrooge asks if Tiny Tim will live.
questions.tip: Structural echo: Dickens makes Scrooge face his own words.

questions.q: What job does Bob Cratchit do?
ms: Bob works in Scrooge's counting-house for fifteen shillings a week.
questions.tip: Remember his 15 shillings a week: a useful detail on poverty.

questions.q: Which 1834 law did Dickens criticise, which sent poor people to harsh institutions?
ms: Scrooge asks "Are there no workhouses?" showing support for the system Dickens hated.
questions.tip: Link workhouses to Dickens's own childhood hardship in a blacking factory.

questions.q: Which description best fits the narrator of A Christmas Carol?
options: An intrusive, chatty first-person narrator who addresses the reader directly
Tiny Tim looking back as an adult
A silent third-person narrator with no opinions
ms: The narrator says he is "standing in the spirit at your elbow", creating intimacy and moral guidance.
questions.tip: Comment on how the narrator's warmth guides the reader's response.

questions.q: Who is Fezziwig?
options: Scrooge's kind former employer who throws a Christmas party
ms: Fezziwig shows a good employer; Scrooge realises he has "the power to render us happy or unhappy".
questions.tip: Use Fezziwig as a contrast with Scrooge as an employer.

questions.q: Which statement about Dickens's purpose is most accurate?
options: He wrote it mainly to celebrate the wealth of Victorian businessmen
He wrote it as a ghost story with no moral message
He wrote it to argue that the workhouses were working well
He wrote it to persuade middle-class readers to show social responsibility towards the poor
ms: Dickens planned a pamphlet on child poverty but chose a story to deliver a "sledge-hammer blow".
questions.tip: Every essay should link to Dickens's purpose.

questions.q: Give two ways Scrooge is presented as cold in Stave 1.
questions.answer: Dickens uses cold imagery: "The cold within him froze his old features", and he refuses to heat Bob's office, keeping the fire very small.
ms: Cold / weather imagery, e.g. "solitary as an oyster" or "cold within him" (1 mark)
Action, e.g. tiny fire for Bob, refusing charity, rejecting Fred (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use one description and one action for two clear marks.

questions.q: Explain the effect of the simile in "solitary as an oyster".
questions.answer: An oyster is hard and closed on the outside, suggesting Scrooge is isolated and shut off from others. Yet oysters can hold a pearl, hinting that goodness is hidden inside him and he can be redeemed. "Solitary" emphasises his chosen loneliness.
ms: Identifies simile / comparison to an oyster (1 mark)
Hard shell = closed off, unwelcoming, isolated (1 mark)
Pearl inside suggests hidden goodness / potential for redemption (1 mark)
Comment on "solitary" or link to the transformation by Stave 5 (1 mark)
questions.tip: The pearl reading is what lifts this to top marks.

questions.q: How does Dickens use Tiny Tim to influence the reader? Give three points.
questions.answer: Tiny Tim is disabled, gentle and religious, so he provokes sympathy. His possible death shows the real cost of poverty. His survival in Stave 5 shows what generosity can achieve, and Scrooge becoming "a second father" to him shows Scrooge's change.
ms: Evokes sympathy as innocent, ill, cheerful (1 mark)
Represents the deserving poor / threat of death shows cost of poverty (1 mark)
His survival shows Scrooge's change / impact of charity (1 mark)
questions.tip: Tiny Tim is a symbol: say what he represents.

questions.q: Explain how Dickens uses the structure of the novella to show Scrooge's transformation.
questions.answer: The five staves move from past, to present, to future, so Scrooge learns why he is cold, sees how others suffer now, then faces the consequences. Stave 1 and Stave 5 mirror each other: Fred, the charity collectors and Bob reappear, so the reader sees Scrooge's new behaviour towards the same people.
ms: Chronological past-present-future order of the spirits (1 mark)
Explains how each stage educates Scrooge (1 mark)
Cyclical structure: Stave 1 and 5 mirror each other (1 mark)
Example of mirroring, e.g. charity collectors, Fred's party, Bob's late arrival (1 mark)
questions.tip: Structure answers must discuss whole-text shape, not one moment.

questions.q:
Starting with the extract in Stave 1, where the two charity collectors visit Scrooge's counting-house asking for donations for the poor, explore how Dickens presents attitudes to poverty.

Write about:
- how Dickens presents attitudes to poverty in this extract
- how Dickens presents attitudes to poverty in the novella as a whole. [30 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: Dickens presents attitudes to poverty as a moral test: Scrooge's cold, Malthusian view is shown as the real social disease, and the novella works as a "sledge-hammer blow" to persuade middle-class readers that charity and responsibility are both Christian duty and self-redemption.
Plan:
1. Extract: "Are there no prisons?" and "Are there no workhouses?" Rhetorical questions show Scrooge's reliance on cruel state systems; the collectors represent compassion.
2. Extract: "decrease the surplus population" echoes Malthus; dehumanising language that Dickens later turns against Scrooge in Stave 3.
3. Stave 3: the Cratchits' Christmas shows the "deserving poor": poor but loving; Tiny Tim's fate makes poverty personal.
4. Stave 3: Ignorance and Want, "wretched, abject, frightful" children, an allegory warning society of consequences; "Doom" written on Ignorance's brow.
5. Stave 5: Scrooge donates to the collectors, raises Bob's salary; model for reader. AO3: 1834 Poor Law, workhouses, Ragged Schools, Dickens's childhood.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised response to the task and the whole text; judicious, precisely embedded references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed response to the task and the whole text; apt, integrated references; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.
Below Level 5 (Level 4, 16-20): clear, explained response with effective references and clear understanding of methods and context, but less developed or exploratory.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Thoughtful, conceptualised argument; links extract to the whole text; well-selected quotations.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Rhetorical questions; dialogue; allegory (Ignorance and Want); structural echo of "surplus population"; sympathetic narrator; contrast between Scrooge and collectors.

AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: 1834 Poor Law Amendment Act and workhouses; Malthus's population theory; Dickens's childhood in a blacking factory; the 1843 report on child labour; Victorian Christian charity.
questions.tip: ACC has no SPaG marks, but write accurately anyway.

questions.q:
Starting with the extract in Stave 5, where Scrooge wakes on Christmas morning and says he is "as light as a feather", explore how Dickens presents Scrooge as a changed character.

Write about:
- how Dickens presents Scrooge in this extract
- how Dickens presents Scrooge in the novella as a whole. [30 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: Dickens presents Scrooge's change as a rebirth rather than a reform: the miserly old man who chose isolation is reborn with childlike joy, proving Dickens's message that no one is beyond redemption and that generosity frees the giver as much as the receiver.
Plan:
1. Extract: similes "as light as a feather", "as happy as an angel", "as merry as a schoolboy": a list showing joy and new lightness compared to Marley's heavy chain.
2. Extract: "I don't know what day of the month it is" and "I'm quite a baby": rebirth imagery, linked to Christmas and Christ's birth.
3. Stave 1: "tight-fisted hand at the grindstone", list of verbs ("squeezing, wrenching, grasping") showing greed; cold imagery.
4. Staves 2-4: gradual softening, e.g. weeping at his lonely childhood, asking if Tiny Tim will live, pleading at the gravestone.
5. Stave 5: buys the prize turkey, raises Bob's salary, joins Fred's party; "second father" to Tiny Tim. AO3: Christian redemption, Dickens's purpose.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised response to the task and the whole text; judicious, precisely embedded references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed response to the task and the whole text; apt, integrated references; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.
Below Level 5 (Level 4, 16-20): clear, explained response with effective references and clear understanding of methods and context, but less developed or exploratory.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Conceptualised view of the transformation; tracks change across staves; integrated references.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Similes and listing; exclamatory sentences; contrast with Stave 1 imagery; cyclical structure; narrator's comic tone; symbolism of light and warmth.
AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Christian ideas of redemption and charity; Victorian Christmas revival; Dickens's aim to change middle-class attitudes; social inequality in the 1840s.
questions.tip: Show the change by comparing Stave 5 with Stave 1 evidence.

questions.q: Explain why Dickens includes Fred in the novella.
questions.answer: Fred is Scrooge's cheerful nephew who keeps inviting him despite rejection. He presents the Christmas spirit ("a kind, forgiving, charitable, pleasant time"), acts as a foil to Scrooge, and his persistence shows the family warmth Scrooge can regain in Stave 5.
ms: Foil / contrast to Scrooge (1 mark)
Represents Christmas values, e.g. kindness, forgiveness, with reference (1 mark)
Shows family love and the possibility of Scrooge's redemption when he joins the party (1 mark)
questions.tip: Characters exist for a purpose: say what Dickens uses Fred for.

questions.q: Give two things the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come shows Scrooge.
questions.answer: Businessmen joking about a dead man's funeral, and Scrooge's own neglected gravestone. Also: the Cratchits mourning Tiny Tim; people selling the dead man's belongings.
ms: Any one of: businessmen discussing the death; Old Joe's shop selling belongings; the Cratchits grieving Tiny Tim; the couple relieved by his death (1 mark)
Any second different point, e.g. Scrooge's own grave (1 mark)
questions.tip: Stave 4 only, do not include scenes from Stave 3.

questions.q: Give two ways context shapes Dickens's presentation of the Cratchit family.
questions.answer: Dickens worked in a blacking factory as a child when his father was in debtors' prison, so he shows the poor sympathetically, as loving and hardworking. The 1843 Second Report of the Children's Employment Commission on child labour led him to show Tiny Tim's illness as a result of poverty, to make middle-class readers act.
ms: First context point, e.g. Dickens's childhood poverty / father in Marshalsea (1 mark)
Linked to how the Cratchits are shown, e.g. sympathetic, deserving poor (1 mark)
Second context point, e.g. 1843 report on child labour, Poor Law, high child mortality (1 mark)
Linked to effect, e.g. Tiny Tim's illness used to shock readers into charity (1 mark)
questions.tip: Every context fact must be tied back to the text.

questions.q: In what year is An Inspector Calls set?
ms: Set in spring 1912; written in 1945, first performed 1945-46.
questions.tip: Don't confuse setting (1912) with writing (1945).

questions.q: What is the name of the Inspector?
ms: "Goole" sounds like "ghoul", hinting he may be supernatural.
questions.tip: Comment on the name pun for AO2.

questions.q: Why did Mr Birling sack Eva Smith from his factory?
options: She stole money from the factory
She led a strike for higher wages
ms: Eva asked for 25 shillings a week instead of 22 and six, and Birling sacked the ringleaders.
questions.tip: Know the wage figures: they show how little she wanted.

questions.q: What does Sheila do that gets Eva sacked from Milwards?
options: She complains in a jealous temper after catching Eva smiling at another assistant
She accuses Eva of stealing a dress
She refuses to pay for a hat
ms: Sheila thought Eva was smiling at the assistant about how she looked in a dress, and, jealous and annoyed, threatened to close her account unless Eva was sacked.
questions.tip: Sheila admits jealousy: she thought Eva looked prettier in the dress.

questions.q: Which character refuses Eva help from the charity committee?
ms: Sybil Birling is a prominent member of the Brumley Women's Charity Organisation and uses her influence to persuade the committee to turn Eva down.
questions.tip: Dramatic irony: she blames the father of the child, who is Eric.

questions.q: What name did Eva Smith use when she went to Mrs Birling's charity?
ms: Eva called herself "Mrs Birling", which Sybil called "gross impertinence".
questions.tip: Daisy Renton is the name she used with Gerald.

questions.q: Who says the phrase "a hard-headed, practical man of business" about himself?
ms: Birling repeatedly describes himself this way in Act 1, showing capitalist pride.
questions.tip: Birling's repetition reveals his arrogance and self-interest.

questions.q: Which character steals money from his father's office to support Eva?
ms: Eric took about fifty pounds from the office to give Eva money.
questions.tip: Eric's theft shows irresponsibility but he later accepts blame.

questions.q: How does the play end?
options: A phone call announces that a girl has died and a real police inspector is on his way
ms: The cyclical ending forces the family to face the events again.
questions.tip: Explain why Priestley uses this cliffhanger: second chance for the audience.

questions.q: Which character returns the engagement ring?
options: Sheila gives it back to Gerald
ms: In Act 2 Sheila hands back the ring after Gerald's affair with Daisy is revealed.
questions.tip: The ring symbolises a relationship based on status; she later refuses it again.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the Inspector's dramatic function?
options: He acts as Priestley's mouthpiece, voicing socialist ideas of collective responsibility
He is a comic character who lightens the tension
He represents the views of the upper class
He is an ordinary policeman with no wider purpose
ms: His final speech delivers the play's central message.
questions.tip: Mention 'mouthpiece' and 'catalyst' as terms.

questions.q: Give two ways Mr Birling is presented as arrogant in Act 1.
questions.answer: He makes confident but wrong predictions, such as calling the Titanic "absolutely unsinkable" and saying there will be no war, and he boasts about his possible knighthood.
ms: Wrong predictions e.g. Titanic "unsinkable", no war, labour trouble (1 mark)
Boasts about knighthood / status / being a "hard-headed" businessman, or interrupts others (1 mark)
questions.tip: Dramatic irony: the 1945 audience know he is wrong.

questions.q: Explain how Priestley presents Sheila as changing during the play.
questions.answer: At the start Sheila is childish and materialistic, excited by her ring and calling her mother "mummy". After learning her part in Eva's sacking she feels genuine guilt and promises never to repeat it. By the end she challenges her parents, sees through Gerald and accepts responsibility, representing the younger generation who can change.
ms: Early Sheila: spoilt, childish, materialistic (1 mark)
Turning point: guilt after confessing to Milwards (1 mark)
Later Sheila: perceptive, challenges parents, rejects the ring / Gerald (1 mark)
Purpose: she represents the hope of the young generation (1 mark)
questions.tip: Show change with a beginning, turning point and end.

questions.q: Explain why Gerald's behaviour towards Eva/Daisy is presented as both kind and selfish.
questions.answer: Gerald rescued Daisy from Alderman Meggarty at the Palace bar and gave her money and somewhere to live, which was kind. But he kept her as a mistress, then ended it when it suited him, using his money and power over a vulnerable working-class woman.
ms: Kind: rescued her from Meggarty / gave her rooms and money (1 mark)
Selfish: kept her as a mistress / ended the affair for his convenience (1 mark)
Links to class or gender power, e.g. he exploits his status (1 mark)
questions.tip: A balanced answer covers both sides.

questions.q: Explain how Priestley uses Eric to criticise the older generation.
questions.answer: Eric drinks heavily and his account suggests he forced himself on Eva, so he is far from innocent, yet he accepts responsibility and turns on his parents, telling his mother she killed her own grandchild. Priestley uses his anger to show the older generation's hypocrisy and failure as parents, especially Birling's focus on covering up a scandal.
ms: Eric's wrongdoing acknowledged, e.g. drinking, treatment of Eva, theft (1 mark)
He accepts responsibility unlike his parents (1 mark)
He condemns his parents / attacks Mrs Birling for killing her grandchild (1 mark)
Purpose: shows hypocrisy of older generation / hope for the young (1 mark)
questions.tip: Don't treat Eric as a hero; acknowledge his faults then explain his purpose.

questions.q:
How does Priestley use the character of Sheila to explore the differences between the older and younger generations? [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: Priestley uses Sheila as the clearest sign of hope in the play: her journey from a sheltered, materialistic daughter to a morally aware young woman shows that the younger generation can learn from the Inspector, while her parents stay trapped in the selfish values of 1912 that Priestley wanted his 1945 audience to reject.
Plan:
1. Act 1 opening: childish language ("mummy"), excitement over the ring, shows a sheltered upper middle-class girl shaped by her parents.
2. Act 1 confession: guilt and promise not to repeat it; contrast with Birling's refusal to accept blame for sacking Eva.
3. Act 2: perceptive, warns her mother not to build a wall between herself and the girl; she understands the Inspector's method; dramatic irony as Mrs Birling condemns Eric.
4. Act 3: rejects her parents' relief once the hoax theory appears; refuses the ring; she alone sees the Inspector's message matters whether or not he was real.
5. Context: 1945 Labour landslide, women's changing roles after two wars; Sheila as a model for the audience. Contrast with Mrs Birling as a 'cold woman' and social superior.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised response to the task and the whole text; judicious, precisely embedded references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed response to the task and the whole text; apt, integrated references; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.
Below Level 5 (Level 4, 16-20): clear, explained response with effective references and clear understanding of methods and context, but less developed or exploratory.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Clear argument about generational divide; Sheila's journey tracked across all three acts; references to her parents for contrast.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Stage directions describing her as "pretty" and "pleased with life"; changes in her language; the ring as symbol; dramatic irony; the Inspector's effect on her; final scenes and cyclical structure.
AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: 1912 versus 1945 settings; Edwardian expectations of women; suffrage movement; post-war desire for social change; Priestley's socialism and the welfare state.

AO4 (4 marks, high performance): consistent accuracy in spelling and punctuation; consistent control of meaning; wide range of vocabulary and sentence structures. 2-3 marks: considerable accuracy; 1 mark: reasonable accuracy.
questions.tip: AIC has no extract: plan your whole-text journey before writing.

questions.q:
How does Priestley present Mr Birling as a symbol of capitalism? [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: Priestley presents Mr Birling as a self-satisfied capitalist whose confidence is repeatedly undercut by dramatic irony, so that his values of profit and self-interest are exposed as both morally wrong and foolish, encouraging the 1945 audience to reject the society he represents.
Plan:
1. Act 1 speech: a man must "mind his own business"; mocks "community and all that nonsense"; just before the Inspector's arrival (the doorbell interrupts him).
2. Dramatic irony: Titanic "absolutely unsinkable", no war; the audience in 1945 had lived through two world wars, so he is discredited.
3. Treatment of Eva: sacked her for asking for higher wages; worries about his knighthood and the scandal rather than her death.
4. Act 3: refuses to change; relieved when the Inspector may be a hoax; mocks the younger generation, showing he learns nothing.
5. Context: Priestley's socialism, 1945 Labour victory, class system, capitalist factory owners in 1912; Birling as the 'old order'.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised response to the task and the whole text; judicious, precisely embedded references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed response to the task and the whole text; apt, integrated references; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.
Below Level 5 (Level 4, 16-20): clear, explained response with effective references and clear understanding of methods and context, but less developed or exploratory.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Clear understanding of Birling's symbolic role; tracks his refusal to change; links to Priestley's purpose.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Stage directions ("heavy-looking, rather portentous man"); dramatic irony; interruption by the doorbell; repetition of "hard-headed"; lighting change from pink and intimate to brighter and harder; cyclical ending.
AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Capitalism versus socialism; 1912 industrial England; workers' strikes; Priestley's experiences in WW1 and his Postscripts broadcasts; post-war welfare state.

AO4 (4 marks, high performance): consistent accuracy in spelling and punctuation; consistent control of meaning; wide range of vocabulary and sentence structures. 2-3 marks: considerable accuracy; 1 mark: reasonable accuracy.
questions.tip: Each paragraph should end with what Priestley wants the audience to think.

questions.q: Name two characters the Inspector questions in Act 2.
questions.answer: Gerald and Mrs Birling (Sheila is present and involved too).
ms: Gerald (1 mark)
Mrs Birling (1 mark). Allow Sheila as she is questioned about Gerald.
questions.tip: Act 1 is Birling and Sheila; Act 2 is Gerald and Mrs Birling; Act 3 is Eric.

questions.q: When was An Inspector Calls first performed?
ms: First performed in Moscow in 1945 and London in 1946.
questions.tip: Know that 1945 also saw the Labour landslide.

questions.q: Which political idea did Priestley support?
ms: Priestley helped found the Common Wealth Party and believed in collective responsibility.
questions.tip: Link socialism to the Inspector's final speech.

questions.q: Which theme is central to the Inspector's line about us being "members of one body"?
ms: The Inspector argues that we are all responsible for each other.
questions.tip: This is the play's key message: learn the phrase.

questions.q: What does the Inspector warn will happen if people do not learn responsibility?
options: They will be taught it in "fire and blood and anguish"
ms: This prophecy refers to the two world wars the 1945 audience had lived through.
questions.tip: Link to WW1 and WW2 for AO3.

questions.q: How does the lighting change when the Inspector arrives?
options: It changes from pink and intimate to brighter and harder
ms: Priestley's stage directions show the comfortable rosy view of life is replaced by harsh truth.
questions.tip: Rose-tinted glasses: the family saw life too comfortably.

questions.q: What genre does An Inspector Calls belong to, which makes the audience expect a solution?
ms: Priestley uses the crime-drama form but subverts it: everyone is guilty.
questions.tip: Explain how the 'whodunnit' becomes a 'we-all-did-it'.

questions.q: Which statement about the play's dramatic unities is correct?
options: Each act is set in a different house
It moves between the factory, Milwards and the Palace bar
It covers two years of Eva's life on stage
It takes place in one room, on one evening, in continuous time
ms: Unity of time, place and action creates a claustrophobic, intense atmosphere.
questions.tip: Tie the single setting to the family being trapped with their guilt.

questions.q: What does Eva Smith's surname suggest?
options: She is related to the Inspector
She is from a wealthy family
She represents ordinary working-class people (Smith is a very common name)
ms: "Eva" links to Eve, the first woman; "Smith" is common, so she stands for all the working class.
questions.tip: Priestley's Inspector mentions millions of Eva Smiths.

questions.q: Give two ways context shapes Priestley's presentation of Mr Birling.
questions.answer: Writing in 1945, Priestley gives Birling predictions the audience knew were wrong (no war, Titanic unsinkable), and as a socialist Priestley presents him as a selfish capitalist factory owner to criticise that class.
ms: Hindsight of 1945 audience after two world wars / Titanic, making Birling foolish (1 mark)
Priestley's socialism / criticism of capitalism and the class system shaping Birling as a negative figure (1 mark)
questions.tip: Two different contexts, each linked to Birling.

questions.q: Explain how Priestley presents the theme of gender in An Inspector Calls.
questions.answer: Women are judged by appearance and expected to accept a lesser role: Mrs Birling tells Sheila she must get used to men spending their time on business, Birling says clothes mean more to women, and Gerald is attracted to Daisy's looks. Eva is vulnerable because she is a working-class woman with no protection. Sheila grows to challenge male authority, reflecting changing women's roles by 1945, while Mrs Birling shows that women could also enforce class prejudice.
ms: Women seen as decorative / subordinate, with example (1 mark)
Eva as a victim of male power and class (1 mark)
Sheila's growing independence (1 mark)
Context: women's changing roles after the wars / suffrage, or Mrs Birling enforcing class values (1 mark)
questions.tip: Include both male attitudes and the female characters' own roles.

questions.q: Explain the purpose of the cyclical structure at the end of the play.
questions.answer: The final phone call repeats the start of the investigation, so the family must face judgement again. It punishes the Birlings and Gerald for returning to complacency, shows Sheila and Eric were right to change, and warns the audience that if society does not learn, history (the wars) will repeat. It also leaves the Inspector's identity mysterious, supporting the moral message.
ms: Identifies the cyclical structure / final phone call (1 mark)
Older characters have not learned so must face it again (1 mark)
Validates the younger generation's change (1 mark)
Warning to audience / history repeating or mystery of the Inspector (1 mark)
questions.tip: Always link structure to Priestley's purpose.

questions.q:
How does Priestley use the Inspector to present ideas about social responsibility? [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: Priestley uses the Inspector as both a catalyst and a moral voice: he exposes the Birlings' guilt one by one, then states directly that society is "one body", turning a crime drama into a socialist warning that a 1945 audience, who had seen two wars, should build a fairer society.
Plan:
1. Entrance: interrupts Birling's selfish speech; stage directions on his "massiveness, solidity and purposefulness" show authority.
2. Method: one line of enquiry at a time; shows each character the photograph; controls the pace, revealing a chain of events.
3. Language: graphic reminders of Eva's death; challenges class prejudice; tells Birling public men have responsibilities as well as privileges.
4. Final speech: "We are members of one body" and "fire and blood and anguish": biblical and prophetic tone; millions of Eva Smiths.
5. Mystery: "Goole"/ghoul, possibly a supernatural figure or Priestley's mouthpiece; cyclical ending. AO3: welfare state, 1945 Labour victory, wars.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised response to the task and the whole text; judicious, precisely embedded references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed response to the task and the whole text; apt, integrated references; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.
Below Level 5 (Level 4, 16-20): clear, explained response with effective references and clear understanding of methods and context, but less developed or exploratory.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Clear and conceptual argument about the Inspector's methods and message; references across all three acts.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Stage directions; dramatic irony; lighting changes; short, imperative sentences; rhetoric of final speech (repetition, tricolon, biblical allusion); exit and phone call.
AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Priestley's socialism; 1912 class divide; 1945 Labour victory and the Beveridge Report; WW1 and WW2; morality plays and the Inspector as a moral figure.

AO4 (4 marks, high performance): consistent accuracy in spelling and punctuation; consistent control of meaning; wide range of vocabulary and sentence structures. 2-3 marks: considerable accuracy; 1 mark: reasonable accuracy.
questions.tip: Name his methods (questioning, photograph, timing) not just what he says.

questions.q:
How does Priestley show the ways characters use their social position against those below them in An Inspector Calls? [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: Priestley presents class as a system that protects the powerful and destroys the powerless: every Birling uses their status against Eva, and by showing the upper class refusing to accept blame, he argues that the class divide of 1912 must be swept away in post-war Britain.
Plan:
1. Birling's social climbing: worries about his knighthood and Gerald's family being socially superior (Lady Croft).
2. Eva's exploitation at each stage: factory wages, Milwards, Gerald, Eric, the charity committee; she has no power.
3. Mrs Birling: "girls of that class" shows prejudice; uses her charity to judge the deserving and undeserving poor.
4. Gerald: rescues and then drops Daisy; reflects upper-class entitlement; returns to complacency in Act 3.
5. The Inspector's warning and the young characters' change. AO3: Edwardian class rigidity, 1945 welfare state, Priestley's socialism.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised response to the task and the whole text; judicious, precisely embedded references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed response to the task and the whole text; apt, integrated references; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.
Below Level 5 (Level 4, 16-20): clear, explained response with effective references and clear understanding of methods and context, but less developed or exploratory.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Thoughtful argument on class as a system; uses all characters; precise short references.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Stage directions on the setting ("heavily comfortable house"); dramatic irony; contrasts between Eva (offstage, voiceless) and the family; the Inspector's language.
AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Edwardian class structure; poor working conditions in 1912; 1945 Labour landslide; creation of NHS and welfare state; Priestley's beliefs.

AO4 (4 marks, high performance): consistent accuracy in spelling and punctuation; consistent control of meaning; wide range of vocabulary and sentence structures. 2-3 marks: considerable accuracy; 1 mark: reasonable accuracy.
questions.tip: Show how every character contributes, then explain the system.

questions.q: Explain why Eva Smith never appears on stage.
questions.answer: Eva remains offstage so she can represent all working-class people rather than one individual. Her absence also means she has no voice, mirroring how the poor were ignored. The audience have to imagine her, which makes the family's guilt the focus.
ms: She can represent all working-class people / universal victim (1 mark)
Shows the powerless have no voice (1 mark)
Focuses attention on the Birlings' responsibility, or adds mystery as to whether she was one person (1 mark)
questions.tip: Absence is a choice: explain what it achieves.

questions.q: Who wrote "Ozymandias"?
ms: Shelley, a Romantic poet, published it in 1818.
questions.tip: Shelley was a radical who opposed tyranny and monarchy.

questions.q: Which poem contains the phrase "mind-forg'd manacles"?
ms: Blake's London (1794) suggests people are mentally imprisoned by society.
questions.tip: Manacles = handcuffs; 'mind-forg'd' means self-made or society-made.

questions.q: Which poem is about a Kamikaze pilot who turns back from his mission?
ms: Beatrice Garland's poem tells how the pilot returns and is shunned by his family.
questions.tip: A narrator reports the daughter's account to her children, so the pilot never speaks for himself; the final stanzas shift into the daughter's voice.

questions.q: Which poem is a dramatic monologue spoken by the Duke of Ferrara?
ms: Browning's 1842 poem has the Duke show a portrait of his late wife to an envoy.
questions.tip: The listener is an envoy arranging his next marriage.

questions.q: Which poem was written about the Battle of Balaclava in the Crimean War?
options: The Charge of the Light Brigade
ms: Tennyson, Poet Laureate, wrote it in 1854 after reading a report in The Times.
questions.tip: A military blunder sent around 600 cavalry into the valley.

questions.q: Which poem uses the refrain "But nothing happens"?
options: The Charge of the Light Brigade
ms: Owen repeats it to show the boredom and futility of waiting in the trenches.
questions.tip: The enemy in Exposure is the weather, not the Germans.

questions.q: Who wrote "Remains"?
ms: Armitage based it on a soldier's account of a shooting in Iraq, from The Not Dead (2008).
questions.tip: Remains is about PTSD and guilt.

questions.q: Which poet wrote "War Photographer"?
ms: Duffy was inspired by her friendship with war photographers.
questions.tip: Duffy later became Poet Laureate (2009).

questions.q: In which poem does a mother pin a poppy on her son's lapel before he leaves?
ms: Jane Weir's Poppies is written from a mother's perspective as her son leaves for war.
questions.tip: Weir was a textile designer: note the fabric imagery.

questions.q: Which poem contrasts the history taught in British schools with Black and Caribbean history?
ms: Agard contrasts figures like Dick Whittington with Toussaint L'Ouverture and Mary Seacole.
questions.tip: Agard was born in Guyana; the poem uses Caribbean dialect.

questions.q: Which poem's form is described correctly?
options: London is written in free verse
Exposure is written in rhyming couplets
Ozymandias is a sonnet that breaks conventional rhyme, mirroring broken power
ms: Ozymandias mixes Petrarchan and Shakespearean features with an unusual rhyme scheme.
questions.tip: London is regular quatrains; Exposure uses pararhyme; Remains is free-flowing quatrains with a final couplet.

questions.q: In "Storm on the Island", what is the effect of the oxymoron "exploding comfortably"?
options: It shows the islanders enjoy the storm
It proves the storm has ended
It describes a fire in the cottage
It suggests the sea's violence seems safe from a distance but is actually dangerous
ms: The contradiction shows the power of nature is deceptive and unsettling.
questions.tip: Name the device (oxymoron) and explain the tension.

questions.q: Which poem features a boy who steals a boat and is frightened by a huge mountain peak?
ms: Wordsworth's autobiographical extract shows nature's power over human pride.
questions.tip: The volta is the moment the 'huge peak' appears.

questions.q: Which technique is Owen using in pairs such as "knive us" and "nervous"?
ms: Pararhyme gives an unsettled, incomplete feel that matches the soldiers' discomfort.
questions.tip: Pararhyme matches consonants but changes the vowel.

questions.q: Which poem uses the image of a "yellow hare" that "rolled like a flame"?
ms: Hughes uses the hare to show the suffering of nature and the soldier's sudden awareness.
questions.tip: The hare mirrors the soldier: both are trapped.

questions.q: In "Tissue", what does paper represent?
options: The strength of buildings and governments
The fragility of human-made power and the things people use to control lives, like maps and money
ms: Dharker suggests borders, deeds and money are thin, yet humanity should be like tissue that "lets the light" through.
questions.tip: Tissue also means human skin: note the double meaning.

questions.q: Give two ways Blake presents suffering in "London".
questions.answer: He describes "marks of weakness, marks of woe" on every face and the "youthful Harlot's curse" which blights the newborn infant.
ms: Reference to suffering of ordinary people, e.g. "marks of weakness, marks of woe" / "cry of fear" (1 mark)
Second, different reference, e.g. chimney-sweeper, "hapless Soldier", "youthful Harlot" (1 mark)
questions.tip: Two different groups of sufferers make the strongest pair.

questions.q: Explain the effect of the phrase "sneer of cold command" in "Ozymandias".
questions.answer: "Sneer" shows Ozymandias's arrogance and contempt for his people, while "cold" suggests he was cruel and unfeeling. The harsh alliteration of the 'c' sounds mimics his aggression. Ironically the sculptor has captured and mocked these qualities, which survive only as broken stone: art outlasts power.
ms: "sneer" suggests arrogance / contempt (1 mark)
"cold" suggests cruelty / lack of compassion (1 mark)
Comment on method, e.g. alliteration of hard c sound (1 mark)
Wider point: the sculptor mocks him / art outlasts power / Shelley's anti-tyranny views (1 mark)
questions.tip: Pick out individual words and comment on the sound too.

questions.q: Explain how Armitage presents the effects of conflict on the speaker in "Remains".
questions.answer: The casual opening "On another occasion" shows violence has become routine. The speaker is haunted: the dead man is "dug in behind enemy lines" inside his head, a metaphor turning his mind into a battlefield. The final image of the "bloody life in my bloody hands" alludes to Macbeth's guilt and shows trauma is permanent: PTSD.
ms: Casual / colloquial tone at the start showing violence normalised (1 mark)
Speaker haunted / flashbacks, e.g. "dug in behind enemy lines" (1 mark)
Guilt shown through final lines, e.g. "bloody hands" (1 mark)
Context: PTSD, Iraq, real soldier's testimony, or shift from "we" to "I" (1 mark)
questions.tip: Track the shift from 'we' to 'I'.

questions.q: Explain how Wordsworth presents the power of nature in "The Prelude".
questions.answer: At first nature is gentle and maternal ("led by her"), and the boy is confident, rowing "lustily". At the volta a "huge peak, black and huge" rises, personified as a threatening giant, and the boy flees. Repetition of "huge" stresses scale. Afterwards he is haunted by "huge and mighty forms", showing nature's power is spiritual and changes how he sees the world. As a Romantic, Wordsworth shows nature as a teacher.
ms: Nature initially calm / maternal (1 mark)
Shift at volta: personified peak becomes threatening (1 mark)
Effect on speaker: fear, lasting psychological effect (1 mark)
Context: Romanticism / nature as moral teacher / autobiographical (1 mark)
questions.tip: The volta is the key structural point to name.

questions.q: Explain how Duffy presents the photographer's feelings in "War Photographer".
questions.answer: He is calm in his darkroom, comparing himself to a priest preparing for mass, but as images develop his hands tremble, showing trauma. He feels anger and bitterness that readers in "Rural England" are briefly moved, but "they do not care" for long.
ms: Calm / ritual detachment, e.g. priest simile or "ordered rows" (1 mark)
Haunted / traumatised as memories return (1 mark)
Bitterness at public indifference, e.g. "they do not care" (1 mark)
questions.tip: Show more than one feeling.

questions.q: Explain how Weir uses textile imagery in "Poppies".
questions.answer: Weir, a textile designer, uses words like "felt", "tucks" and "blazer" to show the mother's domestic, caring role. In "flattened, rolled, turned into felt" her words become fabric, showing she cannot express her grief. The texture makes her loss tangible and intimate.
ms: Identifies textile language with an example (1 mark)
Links to the mother's care / domestic role (1 mark)
Explains how it shows suppressed emotion or grief (1 mark)
questions.tip: Mention Weir's background only if you tie it to effect.

questions.q: Explain how Agard uses language and structure in "Checking Out Me History" to show his anger.
questions.answer: The repeated "Dem tell me" attacks the education system for imposing a white British history. Phonetic dialect and lack of standard punctuation reject imposed rules. Lines about British figures are short and mocking, while stanzas about Black heroes are set apart in italics with lyrical natural imagery, such as Mary Seacole as a "healing star". The final line "I carving out me identity" shows his determination to reclaim his identity.
ms: Repetition of "Dem tell me" showing anger / blame (1 mark)
Dialect / non-standard grammar as rebellion (1 mark)
Structural contrast between British figures and Black heroes (1 mark)
Ending: "carving out me identity" showing reclaiming power (1 mark)
questions.tip: Comment on both language and structure for the full marks.

questions.q: Explain how the ending of "Kamikaze" presents the consequences of the pilot's decision.
questions.answer: The pilot is shunned: his wife never spoke again in his presence and his children stop playing with him, so he is treated as though dead. The final line wonders which kind of death was preferable, suggesting this social death was as painful as dying in the mission. The narrative distance (the daughter telling her children) shows how shame passes through generations.
ms: Family rejection / silence (1 mark)
Treated as if dead / social death (1 mark)
Final line questions which death was better (1 mark)
Context of Japanese honour / shame, or narrative perspective (1 mark)
questions.tip: The pilot never speaks; mention whose voice we hear.

questions.q: Give two ways "The Emigree" presents the speaker's memories of her city.
questions.answer: She remembers it as bright and full of light, "sunlight-clear", and she personifies it as a living companion she takes care of and loves.
ms: Bright / positive / light imagery, e.g. "sunlight-clear" (1 mark)
Personification of the city as a person or child she loves / takes care of (1 mark). Allow: memories are fixed from childhood and cannot be changed by war or tyrants.
questions.tip: Light imagery is the key pattern in this poem.

questions.q: Explain how Heaney presents the power of nature in "Storm on the Island".
questions.answer: The poem opens confidently, "We are prepared", but the islanders are trapped as the storm strikes. Military language ("strafes", "salvo", "bombarded") presents nature as an army. The sea "spits like a tame cat" that turns savage, showing something familiar becoming dangerous. The final line admits it is "a huge nothing that we fear", showing the power of the invisible wind. Some read it as a metaphor for the Troubles in Northern Ireland.
ms: Initial confidence undermined (1 mark)
Military / violent language for the storm (1 mark)
Simile of the cat or 'exploding comfortably' showing deceptive danger (1 mark)
Final line / Troubles context or the invisible power of wind (1 mark)
questions.tip: The title can be read as 'Stormont', Northern Ireland's parliament.

questions.q: Which pair would work best for comparing the power of nature?
options: Checking Out Me History and London
Storm on the Island and The Prelude
ms: Both show nature overwhelming humans; Exposure is another good choice.
questions.tip: Choose a pair with a strong shared idea and clear differences.

questions.q: Which two poems both present abuse of power by a ruler?
ms: Both feature arrogant, controlling men whose power is shown through art (a statue and a portrait).
questions.tip: Art as a link: both rulers are judged through art.

questions.q: Which pair best compares the psychological effects of conflict on individuals?
options: Tissue and Checking Out Me History
The Prelude and Storm on the Island
ms: Both explore trauma and memory that cannot be escaped.
questions.tip: Also strong: Kamikaze or Poppies for loss and memory.

questions.q: Which pair both explore identity and the influence of the past?
options: Ozymandias and Storm on the Island
Checking Out Me History and The Emigree
The Charge of the Light Brigade and Exposure
ms: Both speakers hold on to a sense of self linked to a history or homeland.
questions.tip: Tissue and Kamikaze also work for identity.

questions.q: Compare how poets present the power of nature in "Storm on the Island" and in one other poem from "Power and conflict". [30 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: Both Heaney and Wordsworth (The Prelude) show nature as a force that humbles human confidence, but while Heaney's islanders face a physical, invisible threat they can only endure, Wordsworth's boy experiences nature's power as a spiritual lesson that permanently reshapes his mind.
Plan:
1. Openings: "We are prepared" (confident, collective) versus the boy's solitary pride in rowing; both confidence is undermined.
2. Shift: Heaney's military lexis and 'exploding comfortably'; Wordsworth's volta and personified peak that "Upreared its head".
3. Form: Heaney's single block of blank verse (a fortress-like stanza, but enjambment lets the storm flood through); Wordsworth's blank verse autobiographical narrative.
4. Endings: "a huge nothing that we fear" versus "huge and mighty forms" troubling his dreams: both end in lingering fear, but Wordsworth's is internalised.
5. Context: Heaney's rural Northern Ireland and possible Troubles reading; Wordsworth's Romanticism and nature as teacher.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised comparison of both poems in response to the task and the whole text; judicious, precisely embedded references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed comparison of both poems in response to the task and the whole text; apt, integrated references; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.
Below Level 5 (Level 4, 16-20): clear, explained response with effective references and clear understanding of methods and context, but less developed or exploratory.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Critical comparison of ideas throughout, with comparative connectives; judicious references from both poems.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Comparison of language (military lexis, personification), structure (volta, single stanza), form (blank verse) and their effects.
AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Romantic movement; Heaney's upbringing in rural Northern Ireland; the Troubles; the sublime.
questions.tip: Compare in every paragraph, not one poem then the other.

questions.q: Compare how poets present the effects of war on soldiers in "Exposure" and in one other poem from "Power and conflict". [30 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: Owen and Armitage (Remains) both reveal war's hidden suffering beyond heroic myths, but where Owen's soldiers are slowly destroyed by the indifference of nature and futile waiting, Armitage's soldier is destroyed by what he did, carrying an inescapable guilt home.
Plan:
1. Openings: "Our brains ache" collective present tense; "On another occasion" casual anecdote; both voices of ordinary soldiers.
2. Enemy: in Exposure the weather ("merciless iced east winds", personified) and boredom ("But nothing happens"); in Remains, the looter and then memory itself.
3. Death and guilt: frozen bodies, "All their eyes are ice"; versus the looter's "blood-shadow" and "bloody hands".
4. Structure: refrain and pararhyme showing endless waiting; Remains shifts from 'we' to 'I' and ends with enjambment into a disrupted final couplet, showing trauma has no end.
5. Context: Owen in WW1 trenches, died 1918, anti-war poems; Armitage's Iraq testimony and PTSD.
