ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised comparison of both poems in response to the task and the whole text; judicious, precisely embedded references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed comparison of both poems in response to the task and the whole text; apt, integrated references; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.
Below Level 5 (Level 4, 16-20): clear, explained response with effective references and clear understanding of methods and context, but less developed or exploratory.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Sustained comparison of effects of war; precise references; conceptual understanding of each poet's purpose.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Personification, pararhyme, refrain, half lines; colloquial language, enjambment, repetition, allusion to Macbeth.
AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: WW1 trench conditions and Owen's experience; Iraq War and The Not Dead documentary; PTSD awareness.
questions.tip: Use comparative connectives (whereas, similarly, in contrast) in every paragraph.

questions.q: Compare how poets present arrogant rulers in "My Last Duchess" and in one other poem from "Power and conflict". [30 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: Browning and Shelley (Ozymandias) both expose arrogant rulers through works of art, but the Duke's power is chilling because it is still active and controlling, while Ozymandias's power has been ironically reduced to ruins by time.
Plan:
1. Voice: Duke's dramatic monologue reveals his jealousy and control ("since none puts by / The curtain"); Ozymandias reported through a traveller, distancing.
2. Control: "I gave commands; / Then all smiles stopped together" implies murder; Ozymandias's "sneer of cold command".
3. Art: the Duke owns his wife only in a portrait; the sculptor's mockery of Ozymandias survives.
4. Structure: rhyming couplets with enjambment show control masking emotion; Ozymandias's broken sonnet form mirrors fallen power.
5. Context: Renaissance Duke of Ferrara, patriarchal ownership of women; Shelley's opposition to tyranny and monarchy, Rameses II.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised comparison of both poems in response to the task and the whole text; judicious, precisely embedded references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed comparison of both poems in response to the task and the whole text; apt, integrated references; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.
Below Level 5 (Level 4, 16-20): clear, explained response with effective references and clear understanding of methods and context, but less developed or exploratory.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Perceptive comparison of how power is shown and judged; judicious quotations.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Dramatic monologue, caesura, enjambment, rhyming couplets; sonnet form, irony, alliteration, contrasts of scale.
AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Victorian views of the Renaissance; patriarchy; Romanticism and Shelley's politics; ancient Egypt.
questions.tip: Keep the question's focus (arrogant rulers) in every paragraph's topic sentence.

questions.q: Compare how poets present memory in "Poppies" and in one other poem from "Power and conflict". [30 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: Weir and Rumens (The Emigree) both show memory as a way of holding on to something loved and lost, but the mother's memories of her son are tactile and painful, while the emigree's memories of her city are idealised, glowing with light, and defiantly protected.
Plan:
1. Openings: "Three days before Armistice Sunday" sets a time of remembrance; "There once was a country" fairy-tale opening.
2. Childhood: mother remembers playing "at being Eskimos"; emigree's city is fixed in childhood memory.
3. Emotion: "steeled the softening of my face" shows suppressed grief; emigree's "sunlight" imagery shows love and longing.
4. Structure: Poppies' free verse and enjambment flow like memory and grief; Emigree's recurring light imagery across all three stanzas, ending on "sunlight", shows persistence.
5. Context: modern wars in Iraq/Afghanistan and mothers' grief; exile from oppressive regimes.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised comparison of both poems in response to the task and the whole text; judicious, precisely embedded references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed comparison of both poems in response to the task and the whole text; apt, integrated references; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.
Below Level 5 (Level 4, 16-20): clear, explained response with effective references and clear understanding of methods and context, but less developed or exploratory.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Critical comparison of memory in both poems; perceptive interpretation.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Sensory and textile imagery, metaphor, symbolism (dove, poppy); light imagery, personification, fairy-tale form.
AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Remembrance traditions; refugees and exile; Weir's textile background; Rumens's interest in place.
questions.tip: Memory poems need you to explore what is being remembered and why.

questions.q: Explain one similarity and one difference in how war is presented in "The Charge of the Light Brigade" and "Bayonet Charge".
questions.answer: Similarity: both show soldiers charging into danger, and both suggest the soldiers have no control, obeying orders or being swept along. Difference: Tennyson glorifies the soldiers' heroism ("Honour the Light Brigade"), while Hughes strips away patriotism, as "King, honour, human dignity, etcetera" are dropped "like luxuries".
ms: Similarity identified, e.g. lack of control / charge into danger (1 mark)
Supported with references from both poems (1 mark)
Difference identified: glorification versus disillusionment (1 mark)
Supported with references from both poems (1 mark)
questions.tip: Similarity and difference both need evidence from BOTH poems.

questions.q: Explain how "Tissue" and "Ozymandias" both present human power as temporary.
questions.answer: Shelley shows a ruler's statue reduced to "colossal Wreck" in "lone and level sands": nature and time destroy his power. Dharker shows that buildings, maps and money are as fragile as paper: buildings could "fall away on a sigh". Shelley's tone is ironic and mocking; Dharker's is hopeful, imagining a world built of something lighter and more humane.
ms: Ozymandias: power destroyed by time, with reference (1 mark)
Tissue: human systems fragile, with reference (1 mark)
Comparison of tone or method, e.g. irony versus hope (1 mark)
Context or purpose, e.g. Shelley's anti-tyranny, Dharker's view of borders and identity (1 mark)
questions.tip: Explicitly compare, using 'whereas' or 'similarly'.

questions.q: Explain how both "London" and "Checking Out Me History" criticise those in authority.
questions.answer: Blake attacks the Church ("black'ning Church") and Palace for causing suffering; Agard attacks the education system ("Dem tell me") for hiding Black history. Both use repetition to build anger.
ms: London: criticism of Church / monarchy / institutions with reference (1 mark)
Checking Out Me History: criticism of education / those who control history with reference (1 mark)
Shared method, e.g. repetition or angry tone (1 mark)
questions.tip: Find a shared method as well as shared ideas.

questions.q: Compare how "Kamikaze" and "Remains" present the long-term consequences of a single moment in conflict.
questions.answer: In Remains, one shooting haunts the soldier forever: his life becomes a cycle of flashbacks. In Kamikaze, one decision to turn back leads to lifelong shunning by his family. Remains uses a first-person voice to show internal guilt, whereas Kamikaze uses a distant narrative voice, showing external social judgement.
ms: Remains: one moment causing lasting trauma (1 mark)
Kamikaze: one decision causing lifelong rejection (1 mark)
Comparison of perspective / voice (1 mark)
Comparison of cause: guilt for killing versus shame for surviving (1 mark)
questions.tip: Contrast internal guilt with external shame: that's the grade 8 insight.

questions.q:
Q27.1 style. Read Poem A.

Poem A: "Night Shift" (original poem)
My mother leaves the house as streetlights wake,
her coat a darker shadow on the stairs.
She hums the songs her mother used to make
and folds the evening in among her cares.

All night the ward breathes slowly round her hands;
she counts the pulses, smooths the paper sheets.
The city sleeps. She is the one who stands
between the dark and every heart that beats.

At six she comes home grey as morning rain,
and kisses us, and sleeps, and starts again.

In "Night Shift", how does the poet present the speaker's feelings about her mother? [24 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: The speaker presents her mother with quiet awe, seeing her as an ordinary, tired woman who is also a protective, almost heroic guardian of the sleeping city, so admiration and concern mix throughout.
Plan:
1. Opening: personified "streetlights wake" shows the mother's life runs opposite to everyone else's; "darker shadow" hints at the speaker's sense of absence and worry.
2. Inherited love: humming her own mother's songs shows tradition and comfort; the metaphor of folding the evening "among her cares" suggests she tidies away her own life for others.
3. Heroic image: the ward "breathes" (personification) round her hands; the climactic lines where she "stands / between the dark and every heart" present her as a protector, with enjambment emphasising her steadiness.
4. Cost: simile "grey as morning rain" shows exhaustion; the polysyndeton in the final line ("and kisses us, and sleeps, and starts again") creates a relentless cycle.
5. Form: regular rhyme and iambic rhythm mirror her routine and reliability; the final rhyming couplet works like a sonnet ending, summing up love and sacrifice.
ms: Level 6 (21-24 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised response to the task and text; judicious references; analysis of the poet's methods with judicious subject terminology; exploration of effects on the reader.
Level 5 (17-20 marks): thoughtful, developed response; apt references integrated into interpretation; examination of methods with effective terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects.
Level 4 (13-16 marks): clear, explained response; effective references; clear explanation of methods with appropriate terminology.
AO1 indicative content: admiration, pride, worry, love; mother as both ordinary and heroic; awareness of her sacrifice.

AO2 indicative content: personification (streetlights, ward), metaphor of folding the evening, simile "grey as morning rain", enjambment, polysyndeton, rhyme scheme and couplet, cyclical day structure.
Note: AO3 is not assessed in unseen poetry. Do not reward guesses about the poet's biography.
questions.tip: No context marks here. Spend all your time on methods and effects.

questions.q:
Q27.2 style. Read Poem B alongside Poem A.

Poem A: "Night Shift" (original poem)
My mother leaves the house as streetlights wake,
her coat a darker shadow on the stairs.
She hums the songs her mother used to make
and folds the evening in among her cares.

All night the ward breathes slowly round her hands;
she counts the pulses, smooths the paper sheets.
The city sleeps. She is the one who stands
between the dark and every heart that beats.

At six she comes home grey as morning rain,
and kisses us, and sleeps, and starts again.

Poem B: "Saturday Market" (original poem)
Dad is up before the gulls,
stacking oranges like small suns
into pyramids that never fall.
He shouts the prices,
loud as a brass band,
and every customer is 'darling', 'boss', 'my friend'.
By noon his hands are cracked and sticky,
his voice a frayed rope.
But he winks at me over the scales
as if the whole street
were a joke we share.

In both "Night Shift" and "Saturday Market" the speakers describe a parent at work. What are the similarities and/or differences between the methods the poets use to present these feelings? [8 marks]
questions.answer: Both poets use imagery to show the cost of work: "grey as morning rain" and "hands are cracked and sticky". However, Poem A uses a quiet, reverent tone and regular rhyme to suggest the mother's solemn, steady duty, whereas Poem B uses free verse, loud sound imagery ("loud as a brass band") and dialogue to show the father's noisy, joyful energy. Both end on a turn: Poem A's couplet stresses relentless sacrifice, while Poem B's final wink turns tiredness into shared humour, so the child feels included rather than left behind.
ms: Level 4 (7-8 marks): exploratory comparison of the writers' use of language, structure and form, with subject terminology used judiciously; convincing comparison of effects on the reader.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): thoughtful comparison of methods with effective terminology; clear comparison of effects.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): relevant comparison of methods with some terminology; some comparison of effects.

Indicative: similes (grey as rain / oranges like suns / loud as a brass band), sound and tone (hushed vs loud), form (rhymed regular stanzas vs free verse), endings (couplet vs wink), perspective of child narrator in both.
Only methods are credited (AO2). Do not reward discussion of content without methods.
questions.tip: Q27.2 rewards METHODS only. Comparing what happens earns little.

questions.q:
Q27.1 style. Read the poem.

"The Old Bridge" (original poem)
They built it out of stone and pride,
each arch a promise to the tide.
Now moss has crept along its spine;
the river does not read the sign.
It wears the stone the way a tongue
wears down a sweet. The workmen, young
when they first laid the keystone, lie
beneath the hill. The bridge stays. Why?

In "The Old Bridge", how does the poet present ideas about time and human achievement? [24 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: The poet presents human achievement as proud but fragile: the bridge outlasts its builders, yet time and nature slowly erode it, leaving the reader with an uneasy question about what really lasts.
Plan:
1. "stone and pride": pairing a concrete and an abstract noun shows the bridge is a symbol of human confidence; "promise to the tide" personifies nature as something humans try to bargain with.
2. Decay: "moss has crept along its spine" personifies the bridge as an ageing body; "crept" suggests slow, sly change. "The river does not read the sign" shows nature ignores human rules.
3. Simile: the river wears stone "the way a tongue / wears down a sweet": an oddly gentle, everyday image making erosion seem patient and inevitable.
4. Mortality: enjambment across "young / when" and "lie / beneath the hill" mirrors time passing; the builders are dead but their work stays.
5. Ending: short sentences and caesura ("The bridge stays. Why?") halt the rhythm; the rhetorical question leaves ambiguity about whether lasting achievement has meaning. Regular rhyming couplets suggest order, which the final broken line disrupts.
ms: Level 6 (21-24 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised response; judicious references; analysis of methods with judicious terminology; exploration of effects.
Level 5 (17-20 marks): thoughtful, developed response; apt integrated references; examination of methods; thoughtful effects.
Level 4 (13-16 marks): clear, explained response; effective references; clear explanation of methods.
AO1 indicative: pride, decay, mortality, nature's indifference, paradox that the bridge outlives its builders.
AO2 indicative: personification, simile of tongue and sweet, rhyming couplets, enjambment, caesura, final rhetorical question, contrast of permanence and erosion.
AO3 not assessed for unseen poetry.
questions.tip: Track how the poem moves from start to end: structure is often underused.

questions.q:
Q27.2 style. Read "The Old Bridge" and "Tide Clock".

"The Old Bridge" (original poem)
They built it out of stone and pride,
each arch a promise to the tide.
Now moss has crept along its spine;
the river does not read the sign.
It wears the stone the way a tongue
wears down a sweet. The workmen, young
when they first laid the keystone, lie
beneath the hill. The bridge stays. Why?

"Tide Clock" (original poem)
Grandad never wore a watch.
He told the hour by water: low,
the mudflats shining like a plate;
high, the boats lifted, patient, proud.
Now his kitchen clock ticks on
above a chair that no one sits in,
counting time he does not need.

In both poems the poets describe the passing of time. What are the similarities and/or differences between the methods the poets use to present time? [8 marks]
questions.answer: Both poets link time to water: the river erodes the bridge and Grandad tells time by the tide, presenting nature as a truer measure than human inventions. However, "The Old Bridge" uses regular rhyming couplets that are broken by the final question, suggesting order giving way to doubt, while "Tide Clock" uses unrhymed free verse with a quiet, elegiac tone. Both end by contrasting objects with absent people: the bridge outlives the workmen, and the clock "ticks on" over an empty chair, a poignant image of grief. The final line of "Tide Clock" is a calm statement, whereas "The Old Bridge" ends with an unsettling question.
ms: Level 4 (7-8 marks): exploratory comparison of methods with judicious terminology; convincing comparison of effects.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): thoughtful comparison of methods; clear comparison of effects.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): relevant comparison of methods; some comparison of effects.

Indicative: water imagery in both; similes (shining like a plate / tongue and sweet); rhyme versus free verse; empty chair and dead workmen; question versus statement endings; personification of the clock and river.
questions.tip: Aim for two or three developed comparisons, not a list of techniques.

questions.q: In AQA Paper 2 Section C, how many marks is question 27.1 worth?
ms: 27.1 is 24 marks, 27.2 is 8 marks, total 32 for Section C.
questions.tip: Spend about 30-35 minutes on 27.1 and 10-15 minutes on 27.2.

questions.q: Which Assessment Objective is NOT assessed in the unseen poetry questions?
ms: You cannot be expected to know the context of an unseen poem, so AO3 is not assessed.
questions.tip: Don't waste time guessing a poet's life.

questions.q: Question 27.2 only rewards comparison of what?
options: Your personal opinion of each poem
ms: 27.2 is assessed on AO2 alone: comparing language, structure and form.
questions.tip: If you compare only content, you cap your mark.

questions.q: Read: "stacking oranges like small suns". What technique is used?
ms: "like" signals a simile comparing oranges to suns.
questions.tip: Then explain the effect: brightness, warmth, the father's cheerfulness.

questions.q: Read: "the ward breathes slowly round her hands". What technique is used and what is its effect?
options: Alliteration, making the line sound harsh
Personification, making the hospital seem alive and dependent on her
Hyperbole, exaggerating how big the ward is
Simile, comparing the ward to a person
ms: A ward cannot breathe: giving it a human action personifies it.
questions.tip: Always pair the technique with its effect.

questions.q: A poem written in regular rhyming couplets ends with a line broken up by full stops: "The bridge stays. Why?" What is the most likely effect?
options: It makes the ending more cheerful and resolved
The disruption creates uncertainty, undermining the sense of order built up by the regular form
It shows the speaker is angry with the builders
It shows the poet ran out of rhymes
ms: Structural disruption at the end of a regular poem often signals doubt or a shift in tone.
questions.tip: Comment on endings: examiners reward structural awareness.

questions.q:
Read these original lines:
"The rain applauds the empty street,
then leaves without a bow."
Explain how the poet uses language to create mood in these lines.
questions.answer: The rain is personified as an audience that "applauds", which suggests the sound of rain on the ground like clapping. But the street is "empty", so the applause is for nobody, creating a lonely, ironic mood. The rain "leaves without a bow", continuing the theatre metaphor and suggesting things end abruptly, leaving emptiness.
ms: Identifies personification (1 mark)
Explains the sound / clapping effect of "applauds" (1 mark)
Explains irony / loneliness of the "empty street" (1 mark)
Develops the extended theatre metaphor and abrupt ending (1 mark)
questions.tip: Look for extended metaphors across lines.

questions.q: What does AO2 assess in English Literature?
options: Analysis of the writer's methods (language, form, structure) and their effects, using subject terminology
ms: AO2 is about how the writer creates meaning.
questions.tip: Techniques alone earn little: explain the effect.

questions.q: What does AO3 assess?
options: Understanding of the relationships between texts and the contexts in which they were written
ms: AO3 is context: social, historical, literary.
questions.tip: Context should be woven in, not a separate paragraph of facts.

questions.q: Which texts carry the 4 AO4 SPaG marks in AQA English Literature?
options: A Christmas Carol and the poetry anthology
Shakespeare (Macbeth) and the modern text (An Inspector Calls)
ms: AO4 is assessed on Shakespeare (Paper 1 Section A) and Modern text (Paper 2 Section A).
questions.tip: Leave 3 minutes to proofread these two essays.

questions.q: How long is AQA English Literature Paper 1 and what does it cover?
options: 2 hours 15 minutes: modern text and poetry
1 hour 45 minutes: Shakespeare and the 19th-century novel
ms: Paper 1 is 1h 45m, 64 marks (34 Shakespeare including SPaG, 30 for the 19th-century novel).
questions.tip: Split about 50 minutes per essay.

questions.q: How long is AQA English Literature Paper 2?
ms: Paper 2: 2h 15m, 96 marks (modern text 34, anthology 30, unseen 32).
questions.tip: Roughly 45 minutes each for AIC, the anthology and unseen.

questions.q: Which is the best example of an embedded quotation?
options: "solitary as an oyster" is a quote that shows he is lonely.
Scrooge is lonely. Quote: "solitary as an oyster".
Scrooge is "solitary as an oyster", suggesting he shuts himself away
Dickens writes a lot about Scrooge being lonely in Stave 1.
ms: Embedding weaves the quotation into your own sentence.
questions.tip: Short embedded quotes beat long dropped-in ones.

questions.q: Which thesis statement would score most highly for 'How does Priestley present Mrs Birling?'
options: Priestley presents Mrs Birling as the embodiment of upper-class prejudice whose refusal to change makes her the play's clearest warning against complacency
Mrs Birling is the mother of Sheila and Eric and the wife of Arthur.
Mrs Birling is a character in An Inspector Calls who is quite mean.
In this essay I will talk about Mrs Birling and what she does.
ms: A strong thesis is an arguable, conceptual answer to the question linked to the writer's purpose.
questions.tip: Answer the question in your first sentence.

questions.q: In the poetry anthology question, how is the first poem provided?
options: One named poem is printed; you choose the second from memory
You choose both poems from memory
ms: AQA prints one poem; you compare with another poem from the cluster that you have learned.
questions.tip: Learn key quotes for every poem so any pairing works.

questions.q: What does 'conceptualised' mean in the Level 6 mark scheme descriptor?
options: The response is driven by a clear overarching argument about the writer's ideas and purpose
The response uses lots of technical terms
The response retells the plot in order
ms: A conceptualised essay has a big idea that shapes every paragraph.
questions.tip: Plan the thesis first; every paragraph should prove it.

questions.q: What does 'judicious' mean when describing use of references?
options: Carefully and precisely chosen to support the argument
ms: Judicious means chosen with good judgement.
questions.tip: One short, well-chosen quote analysed deeply beats three long ones.

questions.q: Give two things you should do in the first five minutes of a 30-mark literature essay.
questions.answer: Read and annotate the question and extract to identify key words; write a quick plan with a thesis and 4-5 points from across the text.
ms: Underline / identify key words of the question or annotate the extract (1 mark)
Plan: thesis and paragraph order / quotes from whole text (1 mark)
questions.tip: Planning time is never wasted on a 30-mark essay.

questions.q: Explain what a strong analytical paragraph should include. Give three features.
questions.answer: A topic sentence that links to the question and thesis; an embedded quotation with zoomed-in analysis of a method and its effect (using terminology); a link to context and the writer's purpose.
ms: Topic sentence answering the question / linked to thesis (1 mark)
Embedded evidence with analysis of method and effect, terminology (1 mark)
Context / writer's purpose / alternative interpretation (1 mark)
questions.tip: Avoid PEE that stops at 'this shows'. Keep exploring.

questions.q: Rewrite this weak sentence into a grade 8-9 sentence of analysis: "Shakespeare uses a metaphor to show Macbeth is bad." Explain what you improved.
questions.answer: Improved: "Shakespeare's metaphor 'full of scorpions is my mind' exposes how Macbeth's ambition has poisoned him from within, suggesting that the crown he murdered for has become a source of torment rather than power." Improvements: an embedded quotation, precise vocabulary instead of 'bad', explanation of the effect, and a link to the wider idea of ambition's cost.
ms: Embeds a relevant quotation (1 mark)
Replaces vague words ('bad', 'show') with precise vocabulary (1 mark)
Explains the effect / connotations in detail (1 mark)
Links to a wider theme or the writer's purpose (1 mark)
questions.tip: Swap 'shows' for verbs like 'suggests', 'exposes', 'reveals', 'implies'.

questions.q: Explain how to use context effectively in an essay on A Christmas Carol.
questions.answer: Context should be linked directly to a point about the text, e.g. Scrooge's "Are there no workhouses?" reflects the 1834 Poor Law, which Dickens criticised. Keep it brief, use it to explain the writer's purpose, and avoid a separate paragraph of history.
ms: Context integrated into analysis rather than bolted on (1 mark)
Linked to the writer's purpose / intended effect on readers (1 mark)
Relevant example, e.g. Poor Law, workhouses, Malthus, Dickens's childhood (1 mark)
questions.tip: Context earns marks only when it explains the text.

questions.q: Explain two differences between how you approach the Macbeth question and the An Inspector Calls question.
questions.answer: Macbeth has a printed extract: start with close analysis of it, then move to the whole play. AIC has no extract and gives a choice of two questions, so you must rely on memorised quotations from across the play. Both carry 4 SPaG marks.
ms: Macbeth includes an extract (1 mark)
Must cover extract and whole play (1 mark)
AIC has no extract / choice of two questions (1 mark)
Must use memorised references from the whole play (1 mark)
questions.tip: Practise AIC quotes so you are not stuck without an extract.

questions.q: What is meant by an 'alternative interpretation' and why does it help?
questions.answer: It is a second plausible reading of a quotation or character, e.g. Lady Macbeth could be seen as evil, or as a victim of a patriarchal society that gives her power only through her husband. It shows critical, exploratory thinking for Level 6.
ms: Definition: more than one valid reading (1 mark)
Example from a set text (1 mark)
Explains why it helps: exploratory / critical / Level 6 (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use 'perhaps' and 'alternatively' to signal interpretations.

questions.q: Give two things that happen at the banquet in Act 3 Scene 4.
questions.answer: Macbeth learns Banquo is dead but Fleance escaped, and Banquo's ghost appears in Macbeth's seat, causing Macbeth to rave so Lady Macbeth sends the guests away.
ms: Murderer reports Banquo dead / Fleance escaped (1 mark)
Banquo's ghost appears / Macbeth's outburst / Lady Macbeth dismisses the guests (1 mark)
questions.tip: Keep plot answers precise and brief.

questions.q: Explain the effect of the dramatic irony in Lady Macbeth's line "A little water clears us of this deed".
questions.answer: In Act 2 she dismisses the murder as easily washed away, contrasting Macbeth's fear that an ocean could not clean his hands. The audience later sees her in Act 5 desperately trying to wash invisible blood, so the line becomes ironic: guilt cannot be cleaned away and her confidence was false. Shakespeare suggests sin leaves a permanent stain, a Christian idea the audience would recognise.
ms: Identifies the line's dismissive / confident tone (1 mark)
Contrast with Macbeth's Neptune's ocean line (1 mark)
Explains irony with Act 5 sleepwalking / handwashing (1 mark)
Wider meaning: guilt is permanent / Christian sin / divine punishment (1 mark)
questions.tip: Dramatic irony means the audience knows more than the character. Say what they know.

questions.q: Explain how Dickens presents the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come.
questions.answer: It is silent and "shrouded in a deep black garment", like the Grim Reaper, which creates fear and links it to death. It only points, forcing Scrooge to interpret what he sees himself. Its silence makes Scrooge more frightened than any other spirit, showing that his future is uncertain and depends on his choices now.
ms: Description links to death / Grim Reaper, with reference (1 mark)
Silence / only points (1 mark)
Effect on Scrooge: fear, he must interpret (1 mark)
Purpose: future can be changed / climax of his transformation (1 mark)
questions.tip: Contrast it with the jolly Ghost of Christmas Present for development.

questions.q: Explain how Priestley presents Mrs Birling as refusing to accept responsibility.
questions.answer: Mrs Birling admits she used her influence to refuse Eva help but insists she did her duty. She blames the father of the child, unaware it is Eric, creating dramatic irony. Even at the end she is relieved the Inspector may be a hoax, showing she has learned nothing. Priestley uses her to represent the older generation's stubborn class prejudice.
ms: Admits refusing Eva but feels justified (1 mark)
Blames the father / dramatic irony with Eric (1 mark)
No change by end of play (1 mark)
Purpose: represents older generation / upper-class prejudice (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use the dramatic irony moment: it's the best evidence.

questions.q: Explain why Priestley sets the play in 1912 but wrote it in 1945.
questions.answer: In 1912, rigid class divisions and capitalism dominated; by 1945 two world wars had shaken society. Using dramatic irony, the audience knows Birling's predictions are wrong, which discredits his views. Priestley uses the gap to warn that society must change after the war rather than return to pre-war selfishness.
ms: 1912: rigid class system / before WW1 / Titanic (1 mark)
Dramatic irony discredits Birling (1 mark)
Message to 1945 audience: build a fairer society / avoid repeating mistakes (1 mark)
questions.tip: Always mention both dates and why the gap matters.

questions.q: Explain how Tennyson presents the soldiers in "The Charge of the Light Brigade".
questions.answer: Tennyson presents them as heroic and obedient: "Theirs not to reason why, / Theirs but to do and die" shows unquestioning duty. The dactylic rhythm imitates galloping horses, creating momentum. The "valley of Death" alludes to Psalm 23, making their sacrifice almost sacred. Although he admits "Some one had blunder'd", the ending commands readers to "Honour the Light Brigade", glorifying them.
ms: Heroism / obedience with reference (1 mark)
Rhythm / repetition creates galloping effect (1 mark)
Biblical allusion or "jaws of Death" personification (1 mark)
Ending glorifies them despite the blunder; context of Poet Laureate (1 mark)
questions.tip: Tennyson criticises the leaders but celebrates the soldiers. Keep both.

questions.q: Explain how Browning uses form and structure in "My Last Duchess" to present the Duke.
questions.answer: It is a dramatic monologue, so we only hear the Duke, who reveals more than he intends. Rhyming couplets (iambic pentameter) suggest control, but enjambment makes the speech run on, hinting that his jealousy is barely contained. Caesura in lines like "I gave commands; / Then all smiles stopped together" creates a chilling pause. The ending returns to his possessions (Neptune taming a sea-horse), showing he sees women as objects.
ms: Dramatic monologue: Duke reveals his character unintentionally (1 mark)
Rhyming couplets show control (1 mark)
Enjambment / caesura suggesting hidden emotion or menace (1 mark)
Ending with Neptune statue: possession and control (1 mark)
questions.tip: Form questions: name the form, then say why it suits the speaker.

questions.q: Explain one similarity and one difference in how "Poppies" and "War Photographer" present the impact of conflict on those at home.
questions.answer: Similarity: both show people at home affected by distant war, the mother through her son's departure and the photographer through images that the public sees. Difference: Poppies shows deep personal grief, while War Photographer criticises the public's brief, shallow reaction as readers' eyes "prick" with tears only briefly.
ms: Similarity identified (1 mark) with evidence from both poems (1 mark)
Difference identified (1 mark) with evidence from both poems (1 mark)
questions.tip: Point, evidence from poem 1, evidence from poem 2, then comment.

questions.q: Explain how "Bayonet Charge" and "Exposure" both challenge the idea of war as glorious.
questions.answer: Hughes's soldier is suddenly woken from patriotism; ideals like honour become "luxuries" he drops as he runs in terror. Owen's soldiers suffer pointless waiting in freezing cold, repeating "But nothing happens". Both remove glory: Hughes through sudden, physical panic in one moment; Owen through slow, endless misery. Both poets show nature suffering or hostile: the yellow hare and the merciless wind.
ms: Bayonet Charge challenge to glory with reference (1 mark)
Exposure challenge to glory with reference (1 mark)
Comparison of method, e.g. single moment versus repetition / time (1 mark)
Shared or contrasting use of nature or context (Hughes imagining WW1, Owen's experience) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Hughes did not fight; Owen did. That difference is worth a sentence.

questions.q: Give two ways to show AO1 in a literature essay.
questions.answer: Write a clear, relevant argument that answers the question, and support it with well-chosen, embedded quotations or references.
ms: Informed personal response / argument addressing the question (1 mark)
Use of references / embedded quotations to support interpretations (1 mark)
questions.tip: AO1 is your argument plus evidence.

questions.q:
Read these original lines:
"My brother's laughter rattles down the hall,
loose change thrown at a quiet afternoon."
Explain how the poet presents the brother.
questions.answer: The verb "rattles" gives the laughter a noisy, lively sound. The metaphor of "loose change thrown" suggests his laughter is careless, scattered and generous, spending joy freely. It contrasts with the "quiet afternoon", so he brings energy and disruption to a still household. The speaker seems fond of him.
ms: Comment on "rattles" as sound / energy (1 mark)
Identifies metaphor of loose change (1 mark)
Explains connotations: careless, generous, scattered (1 mark)
Contrast with "quiet afternoon" / speaker's affectionate attitude (1 mark)
questions.tip: Find the verb and the image, then the contrast.

questions.q:
Starting with the extract from Act 2 Scene 1, where Macbeth is alone at night just before murdering Duncan and sees a dagger floating in front of him, explore how Shakespeare presents Macbeth's state of mind.

Write about:
- how Shakespeare presents Macbeth's state of mind in this extract
- how Shakespeare presents Macbeth's state of mind in the play as a whole. [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Shakespeare presents Macbeth's mind as a battlefield between conscience and ambition, where his imagination works faster than his morality; the dagger is the first sign that a mind which can picture murder so vividly will never be at peace once it acts, turning the play into a study of a man who destroys himself from the inside.
Plan:
1. Extract: the hallucination ('a dagger of the mind, a false creation') blurs the line between the supernatural and psychological. Rhetorical questions show he cannot trust his own senses. AO3: Jacobean audiences might read the dagger as demonic temptation, which links him to the Witches.
2. Extract: the dagger turns to 'gouts of blood', foreshadowing guilt. His dark catalogue ('witchcraft', 'wither'd murder') and the personified night show him summoning evil to drown out conscience. Iambic pentameter here is tense and broken by caesura.
3. Earlier: 'Present fears / Are less than horrible imaginings' (1.3) shows his imagination was always his weakness; 'Stars, hide your fires' shows he already wants to hide from himself.
4. Later: 'full of scorpions is my mind' (3.2) and Banquo's ghost (3.4) show the same visionary mind now punishing him. The dagger and the ghost are structural echoes: one leads him to murder, the other shows its cost.
5. Ending: by 5.5 his mind is numb ('I have almost forgot the taste of fears'). Alternative reading: the loss of fear is a darker punishment than the dagger, because a mind that once felt too much now feels nothing. AO3: tragedy shows sin corrupting the soul.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised argument that answers the task across the whole text; judicious, precisely embedded references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience, including alternative readings; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task woven into the argument.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed argument across the whole text; apt references integrated into the interpretation; examination of methods with effective terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.

Level 4 and below (16-20 marks): clear, explained response with effective references and clear explanation of methods and context, but not yet developed or exploratory. A response that only retells the plot or only covers the extract cannot move past the lower levels.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Tracks Macbeth's psychology across the play; links the dagger to later hallucinations; conceptual argument about imagination, conscience and self-destruction.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Soliloquy giving direct access to his mind; rhetorical questions; personification of night and murder; blood imagery; caesura and broken rhythm; structural echo between the dagger and the ghost; the bell as a dramatic sound cue.

AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Jacobean belief in the divine right of kings and the Great Chain of Being; James I's interest in witchcraft (Daemonologie, 1597); the Gunpowder Plot (1605) and fear of regicide; Jacobean ideas about masculinity and female roles; tragedy as a moral warning.

AO4 (4 marks, high performance): consistently accurate spelling and punctuation, consistent control of meaning, wide range of vocabulary and sentence structures. 2-3 marks: considerable accuracy; 1 mark: reasonable accuracy.
questions.tip: Treat the dagger as evidence of his conscience, not just a spooky moment. Link it forward to the ghost.

questions.q:
Starting with the extract from Act 3 Scene 1, where Macbeth, now king, speaks alone about his fear of Banquo and then persuades two murderers to kill him, explore how Shakespeare presents the consequences of ambition.

Write about:
- how Shakespeare presents the consequences of ambition in this extract
- how Shakespeare presents the consequences of ambition in the play as a whole. [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Shakespeare presents ambition as a hunger that grows the more it is fed: having the crown is never enough for Macbeth because it brings no security, so ambition turns from a desire for power into a desperate need to protect it, and this shift from aspiration to paranoia is the real punishment the play gives him.
Plan:
1. Extract: 'To be thus is nothing, / But to be safely thus' uses antithesis to show the crown is worthless without safety. His fear of Banquo's 'royalty of nature' shows he knows Banquo is the better man.
2. Extract: 'fruitless crown' and 'barren sceptre' create a semantic field of infertility: ambition has given him power without a future. AO3: James I traced his line to Banquo, so the audience sees Macbeth fighting God's chosen line.
3. Extract: with the murderers he manipulates manhood ('Ay, in the catalogue ye go for men'), echoing Lady Macbeth in 1.7. He has become the manipulator, showing how ambition spreads corruption.
4. Earlier: 'Vaulting ambition' in 1.7 shows he knew the danger; the horse metaphor predicted the fall that now begins. Banquo, who shares the prophecy, resists it, which shows ambition is a choice.
5. Later: the murder of Macduff's family (4.2) shows ambition now has no purpose but terror. By 5.3 'fall'n into the sere, the yellow leaf': natural imagery shows ambition has stripped his life of 'honour, love, obedience'. AO3: tragedy as a warning to subjects tempted by regicide.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised argument that answers the task across the whole text; judicious, precisely embedded references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience, including alternative readings; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task woven into the argument.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed argument across the whole text; apt references integrated into the interpretation; examination of methods with effective terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.

Level 4 and below (16-20 marks): clear, explained response with effective references and clear explanation of methods and context, but not yet developed or exploratory. A response that only retells the plot or only covers the extract cannot move past the lower levels.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Clear concept of ambition changing from aspiration to paranoia; links extract to 1.7, 4.2 and 5.3; considers Banquo as a contrast showing free will.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Soliloquy; antithesis ('thus'/'safely thus'); infertility imagery; manipulation through rhetorical questions and the dog 'catalogue'; horse metaphor in 1.7; seasonal imagery in 5.3; structure of escalating murders.

AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Jacobean belief in the divine right of kings and the Great Chain of Being; James I's interest in witchcraft (Daemonologie, 1597); the Gunpowder Plot (1605) and fear of regicide; Jacobean ideas about masculinity and female roles; tragedy as a moral warning.

AO4 (4 marks, high performance): consistently accurate spelling and punctuation, consistent control of meaning, wide range of vocabulary and sentence structures. 2-3 marks: considerable accuracy; 1 mark: reasonable accuracy.
questions.tip: Do not just say 'ambition is bad'. Explain HOW ambition changes as the play goes on.

questions.q:
Starting with the extract from Act 1 Scene 2, where a wounded Captain reports to Duncan how Macbeth fought the rebels and the Norwegian army, explore how Shakespeare presents violence.

Write about:
- how Shakespeare presents violence in this extract
- how Shakespeare presents violence in the play as a whole. [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Shakespeare presents violence as morally neutral until it is aimed at the right or wrong target: the same brutality that makes Macbeth a hero on the battlefield makes him a monster once he turns it on his king, suggesting that a society which praises violence creates the very men who threaten it.
Plan:
1. Extract: the graphic image of Macbeth unseaming a rebel 'from the nave to th' chaps' is celebrated, and Duncan replies 'O valiant cousin!'. The audience is invited to admire butchery when it serves the king. AO3: loyal violence upheld the divine right of kings.
2. Later in 1.2: Ross's report calls Macbeth 'Bellona's bridegroom' (the Roman goddess of war) makes Macbeth almost godlike and married to war. Irony: the traitor Cawdor's title passes to a man who will be a worse traitor.
3. Turning point: Duncan's murder happens offstage, which makes it more horrifying because the audience must imagine it, and 'Macbeth does murder sleep' shows violence against the king breaking the natural order.
4. Escalation: Banquo's murder by hired killers and the slaughter of Lady Macduff's son ('He has killed me, mother') show violence becoming cowardly and aimed at the innocent. Violence is now a tool of tyranny.
5. Ending: Macduff kills Macbeth and brings his head on stage, so the play ends with violence again, but legitimate violence that restores order. Alternative reading: the play cannot fully escape its own cycle of blood. AO3: Jacobean audiences would accept the violence as justice against a tyrant.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised argument that answers the task across the whole text; judicious, precisely embedded references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience, including alternative readings; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task woven into the argument.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed argument across the whole text; apt references integrated into the interpretation; examination of methods with effective terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.

Level 4 and below (16-20 marks): clear, explained response with effective references and clear explanation of methods and context, but not yet developed or exploratory. A response that only retells the plot or only covers the extract cannot move past the lower levels.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Concept of 'right' and 'wrong' violence; whole-play journey from battlefield to tyranny to restoration; evaluates whether Scottish society encourages violence.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Reported action and graphic imagery in 1.2; classical allusion to Bellona; dramatic irony of Cawdor; offstage murder; structural echo of beheadings (Macdonwald and Macbeth); blood motif.

AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Jacobean belief in the divine right of kings and the Great Chain of Being; James I's interest in witchcraft (Daemonologie, 1597); the Gunpowder Plot (1605) and fear of regicide; Jacobean ideas about masculinity and female roles; tragedy as a moral warning.

AO4 (4 marks, high performance): consistently accurate spelling and punctuation, consistent control of meaning, wide range of vocabulary and sentence structures. 2-3 marks: considerable accuracy; 1 mark: reasonable accuracy.
questions.tip: The opening and ending mirror each other: a severed head. Use that structural link for a top-band point.

questions.q:
Starting with the extract from Act 5 Scene 1, where a Doctor and a Gentlewoman watch Lady Macbeth sleepwalking and trying to wash her hands, explore how Shakespeare presents guilt.

Write about:
- how Shakespeare presents guilt in this extract
- how Shakespeare presents guilt in the play as a whole. [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Shakespeare presents guilt as something that cannot be commanded or washed away: Lady Macbeth, who once controlled language and others, is finally controlled by her own unconscious, showing that guilt is the natural order reasserting itself inside a mind that tried to deny it.
Plan:
1. Extract: she speaks in fragmented prose rather than the commanding verse of Act 1, showing loss of control. Repetition and exclamations ('Out, damned spot') reveal a mind looping on one memory.
2. Extract: 'Hell is murky' shows she now fears damnation; 'all the perfumes of Arabia' shows guilt is permanent. The watchers provide dramatic irony: the Doctor says she needs 'the divine' not 'the physician'. AO3: guilt as a sign of the soul, sin needing confession.
3. Earlier contrast: 'A little water clears us of this deed' (2.2) is directly reversed, a structural echo that shows guilt was buried, not removed. Her need for light now reverses 'Come, thick night'.
4. Macbeth's guilt: 'Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this blood' (2.2) shows he felt guilt immediately; later he tries to bury it in more murders, so guilt is expressed differently for each.
5. Ending: her offstage suicide, reported coldly by Malcolm ('fiend-like queen'), contrasts with the audience's pity. Alternative reading: her guilt makes her more human than Macbeth, who loses the ability to feel. AO3: Jacobean belief that suicide was a mortal sin, completing her damnation.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised argument that answers the task across the whole text; judicious, precisely embedded references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience, including alternative readings; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task woven into the argument.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed argument across the whole text; apt references integrated into the interpretation; examination of methods with effective terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.

Level 4 and below (16-20 marks): clear, explained response with effective references and clear explanation of methods and context, but not yet developed or exploratory. A response that only retells the plot or only covers the extract cannot move past the lower levels.

AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Contrasts how both Macbeths experience guilt; links 5.1 to 2.2 and 1.5; conceptual idea of guilt as the natural order fighting back; considers sympathy for Lady Macbeth.

questions.q:
Starting with the extract from Act 4 Scene 2, where Lady Macduff talks with her young son about his absent father before murderers arrive and kill them, explore how Shakespeare presents innocence.

Write about:
- how Shakespeare presents innocence in this extract
- how Shakespeare presents innocence in the play as a whole. [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Shakespeare presents innocence as the true victim of tyranny: by placing a witty, loving child on stage moments before his murder, he forces the audience to see Macbeth's crimes from the receiving end, so innocence becomes the measure by which Macbeth's moral collapse is judged.
Plan:
1. Extract: the playful dialogue between mother and son (he argues that liars outnumber honest men) is tender and darkly ironic, because his childish logic describes Macbeth's Scotland. Innocence speaks truth.
2. Extract: Lady Macduff's 'I have done no harm' shows the world has turned upside down, where doing harm is praised. The son's 'He has killed me, mother' is shockingly simple, monosyllabic and on stage.
3. Wider: Duncan as an innocent king ('his virtues / Will plead like angels'), and the babe imagery in 1.7 ('pity, like a naked new-born babe') show innocence as heavenly. Lady Macbeth's infanticide image destroys this symbol.
4. Wider: the apparitions include a bloody child and a crowned child (4.1), showing innocent children (Macduff, Malcolm/Fleance) will defeat Macbeth. Innocence is wounded but ultimately triumphs.
5. Macduff's grief in 4.3 ('all my pretty ones') and his line about Macbeth having no children show innocence also stirs justice. AO3: Jacobean audiences saw children as the future of a lineage; killing them is an attack on God's order.

questions.q:
Starting with the extract from Act 2 Scene 4, where Ross and an Old Man describe the strange events in nature since Duncan's murder, explore how Shakespeare presents order and disorder.

Write about:
- how Shakespeare presents order and disorder in this extract
- how Shakespeare presents order and disorder in the play as a whole. [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Shakespeare presents order as a God-given chain that links king, nature and the human soul, so that Macbeth's regicide does not just remove a man but breaks the whole universe; the play's structure moves from order to chaos and back again, reassuring a Jacobean audience that disorder is always temporary.
Plan:
1. Extract: darkness in daytime ('dark night strangles the travelling lamp') uses personification to show nature itself being murdered. The owl killing a falcon reverses the natural hierarchy, mirroring a subject killing a king.
2. Extract: Duncan's horses eating each other is grotesque, showing the chaos spreads to animals. The Old Man as a chorus figure gives the audience a voice of tradition: nothing like this in seventy years.
3. Earlier: the Witches' paradoxes ('Fair is foul') and trochaic rhythm set up a world where order is already threatened; Duncan's murder is the moment the threat becomes real ('Confusion now hath made his masterpiece').
4. Macbeth's reign: the banquet's broken seating ('You know your own degrees') collapses when the ghost appears, so social order falls apart in his court.
5. Restoration: Malcolm's final speech uses 'by the grace of Grace' and the language of time and place, restoring hierarchy; Birnam Wood moving shows nature itself rising against Macbeth. AO3: Great Chain of Being; James I and the Gunpowder Plot.

questions.q:
Starting with the extract from Stave 1, where Marley's Ghost appears in Scrooge's room, wrapped in a chain, and warns him about his future, explore how Dickens uses the supernatural to present ideas about change.

Write about:
- how Dickens presents the supernatural and change in this extract
- how Dickens presents the supernatural and change in the novel as a whole. [30 marks]
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Dickens uses the supernatural not as horror but as a teaching method: the ghosts force Scrooge, and the reader, to see what greed hides, so the supernatural becomes the moral engine of the novella, proving that change is possible but only if a person is made to face the consequences of their choices.
Plan:
1. Extract: Marley's chain made of 'cash-boxes, keys, padlocks' is a symbol of how greed traps the soul. The objects he forged show that sin is self-made, built link by link through ordinary business choices. Scrooge's rationalism ('a blot of mustard') shows his resistance to change.
2. Extract: Marley's regret for not helping the poor ('Mankind was my business') and the wailing phantoms outside show what happens if change comes too late. Gothic conventions (clanking, wailing) are used to frighten Scrooge into listening.
3. Ghost of Christmas Past: the light from its head and Scrooge's attempt to crush it with the cap show he resists painful memory. Seeing his lonely child self makes him weep, the first sign of change.
4. Ghost of Christmas Present: abundance and the children Ignorance and Want show social consequences. The spirit throws Scrooge's words back at him, so the supernatural makes him hear himself.
5. Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come: silent and faceless, it forces Scrooge to interpret, so change becomes his own work. His plea at the grave in Stave 4, 'I am not the man I was', and his joy in Stave 5 complete the arc. AO3: Christian ideas of repentance and Dickens's aim to change readers' attitudes to the poor.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Gothic conventions; symbolism of the chain; light imagery of the Ghost of Christmas Past; personification of Ignorance and Want; silence of the final ghost; structure of five staves and three ghosts in time order; narrator's direct address.

questions.tip: Each ghost teaches a different lesson. Name the lesson and the method in each paragraph.

questions.q:
Starting with the extract from Stave 2, where the Ghost of Christmas Past shows Scrooge the Christmas Eve party thrown by his old employer Fezziwig, explore how Dickens presents the responsibilities of employers.

Write about:
- how Dickens presents the responsibilities of employers in this extract
- how Dickens presents the responsibilities of employers in the novel as a whole. [30 marks]
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Dickens presents employers as having power over far more than wages: Fezziwig shows that a boss shapes the happiness of everyone who depends on him, and by placing this memory against Scrooge's treatment of Bob, Dickens argues that kindness from employers is not charity but a moral duty owed to workers.
Plan:
1. Extract: listing and energetic verbs make the ball lively and inclusive; servants, the cook and the milkman are all welcome, so Fezziwig removes class barriers for a night. The fiddler 'tuned like fifty stomach-aches' adds comic warmth.
2. Extract: Scrooge's own line that Fezziwig has 'the power to render us happy or unhappy' and that happiness he gives is as great as if it 'cost a fortune' is a turning point: Scrooge argues against his own beliefs. The Ghost's prompting shows change through self-recognition.
3. Contrast: Stave 1, Bob's 'dismal little cell' and tiny fire, and Scrooge's resentment of a paid holiday show the opposite employer. Cold imagery links meanness to lack of humanity.
4. Stave 3: the Cratchits toast Scrooge as 'the Founder of the Feast' with bitterness, showing how a mean employer poisons his worker's family life.
5. Stave 5: Scrooge raises Bob's salary and offers 'a bowl of smoking bishop', becoming a new Fezziwig, so the structure turns memory into model. AO3: Victorian factory owners and clerks' long hours; Dickens's anger at exploitation.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Listing and lively syntax; comic similes; contrast between Fezziwig's warehouse and Scrooge's office; cold/warm imagery; dialogue revealing change; cyclical structure with Bob at the start and end.

questions.tip: Compare Fezziwig and Scrooge directly. Contrast is Dickens's main method here.

questions.q:
Starting with the extract from Stave 3, where the Ghost of Christmas Present takes Scrooge to watch the Cratchit family's Christmas dinner, explore how Dickens presents the importance of family.

Write about:
- how Dickens presents the importance of family in this extract
- how Dickens presents the importance of family in the novel as a whole. [30 marks]
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Dickens presents family as a kind of wealth that poverty cannot destroy: the Cratchits have almost nothing but each other, and by making their love vivid while Scrooge watches from outside, Dickens shows that a life cut off from family is the true poverty.
Plan:
1. Extract: the excitement over a small goose and pudding, described with hyperbole by the narrator, shows love making little seem like plenty. Collective action (everyone helps) shows family as teamwork.
2. Extract: Tiny Tim is carried on Bob's shoulder and hopes people see him in church; pathos makes him a symbol of the vulnerable poor. Scrooge's question about whether Tim will live shows family stirring his sympathy.
3. Wider: Fan rescuing young Scrooge from school ('to bring you home') shows family as rescue; her death links to Scrooge's isolation, and her son Fred is the family Scrooge rejects.
4. Wider: Fred's party and his refusal to give up on his uncle show family as forgiveness. Belle's later family (Stave 2) shows the life Scrooge lost through greed.
5. Stave 4 and 5: the 'vacant seat' foreseen in Stave 3 and Bob's grief in Stave 4 make the family's love painful; Scrooge's return to Fred's party ('Will you let me in?') shows he rejoins family. AO3: Victorian ideal of the family Christmas, popularised in the 1840s; Dickens's own experience of family debt.

AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Concept of family as wealth; links Cratchits, Fan, Fred and Belle; Scrooge as outsider who becomes insider.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Narrator's hyperbole and humour; pathos around Tiny Tim; symbolism of the vacant seat and the crutch without an owner; contrast between warm interiors and Scrooge's cold house; structure of observation then participation.

AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: 1840s 'Hungry Forties'; the 1834 Poor Law Amendment Act and workhouses; Malthus and the 'surplus population'; child labour and the 1843 report on children's employment that shocked Dickens; Dickens's childhood in Warren's Blacking Factory; Christian values of charity; the novella as a moral fable.

questions.q:
Starting with the extract from Stave 3, where the Ghost of Christmas Present reveals two starving children hidden under its robe, explore how Dickens presents the treatment of children.

Write about:
- how Dickens presents the treatment of children in this extract
- how Dickens presents the treatment of children in the novel as a whole. [30 marks]
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Dickens presents the treatment of children as the test of a society's morality: the neglected children of the novella, from young Scrooge to Ignorance and Want, show that cruelty to the young does not just harm them but creates the future 'doom' of the nation, so caring for children is presented as both a moral and a practical necessity.
Plan:
1. Extract: the adjectives 'yellow, meagre, ragged, scowling, wolfish' dehumanise the children, showing what poverty turns them into. The allegorical names show they represent social problems, not individuals.
2. Extract: 'Beware them both' and the word 'Doom' written on the boy's brow give a prophetic, almost biblical warning. The Ghost repeats Scrooge's 'Are there no workhouses?' to show his attitudes create these children.
3. Wider: young Scrooge 'a solitary child, neglected by his friends' at school shows emotional neglect, explaining (not excusing) the adult he became.
4. Wider: Tiny Tim and Martha (who works at a milliner's) and Peter's collar show the working poor's children. Tim's possible death makes the reader feel the cost of low wages.
5. Ending: Scrooge becomes 'a second father' to Tiny Tim, showing adults must take responsibility. AO3: the 1843 Children's Employment Commission report, Ragged Schools, child labour, and Dickens's own time in the blacking factory aged 12.

AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Concept of children as a test of society; links Ignorance and Want, young Scrooge, Tiny Tim and Martha; considers how Dickens moves from symbol to individual.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Allegory; listing of adjectives; prophetic/biblical language; repetition of Scrooge's own words; pathos; structure of past, present and future children.

AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: 1840s 'Hungry Forties'; the 1834 Poor Law Amendment Act and workhouses; Malthus and the 'surplus population'; child labour and the 1843 report on children's employment that shocked Dickens; Dickens's childhood in Warren's Blacking Factory; Christian values of charity; the novella as a moral fable.
questions.tip: Ignorance and Want are allegory. Say what each represents, then what Dickens wanted readers to do about it.

questions.q:
Starting with the extract from Stave 2, where the Ghost of Christmas Past shows Scrooge as a young man and his fiancee Belle releases him from their engagement, explore how Dickens presents the effects of greed.

Write about:
- how Dickens presents the effects of greed in this extract
- how Dickens presents the effects of greed in the novel as a whole. [30 marks]
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Dickens presents greed as a slow replacement of the heart: Belle's speech shows greed does not arrive as a single sin but as a gradual idolatry that pushes out love, so the novella shows greed's real cost as loneliness rather than lack of money.
Plan:
1. Extract: 'Another idol has displaced me' uses religious language: money has become a false god. The verb 'displaced' shows love being pushed out gradually.
2. Extract: Belle's 'You fear the world too much' suggests greed grows from fear of poverty, a sympathetic reading that links to Dickens's own childhood. Her calm, measured speech contrasts with Scrooge's silence, showing he has no defence.
3. Wider: Stave 1 descriptions ('Hard and sharp as flint', the cold within him) show the final result: greed has frozen him physically and emotionally.
4. Wider: Belle's later happy family, with children everywhere, shows the life greed cost him; Scrooge's 'Remove me!' shows the pain of this realisation.
5. Stave 4: the thieves selling his bed-curtains to Old Joe show that greed breeds greed; nobody mourns him. Stave 5: giving money away becomes joyful. AO3: Victorian capitalism and the rising middle class; Christian teaching on the love of money.

AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Concept of greed as idolatry that replaces love; links Belle to Stave 1 and Stave 4; considers the cause of greed (fear) as well as its effects.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Religious lexis ('idol'); dialogue and silence; simile 'Hard and sharp as flint'; contrast between Belle's family and Scrooge's isolation; structure showing cause (Stave 2) and consequence (Stave 4).

AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: 1840s 'Hungry Forties'; the 1834 Poor Law Amendment Act and workhouses; Malthus and the 'surplus population'; child labour and the 1843 report on children's employment that shocked Dickens; Dickens's childhood in Warren's Blacking Factory; Christian values of charity; the novella as a moral fable.
questions.tip: Explore WHY Scrooge became greedy, not just that he was. 'You fear the world too much' is the key.

questions.q:
Starting with the extract from Stave 4, where the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come shows Scrooge a group of people selling a dead man's belongings to Old Joe, explore how Dickens presents death and isolation.

Write about:
- how Dickens presents death and isolation in this extract
- how Dickens presents death and isolation in the novel as a whole. [30 marks]
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Dickens presents an isolated death as the logical end of a selfish life: the man who refused to share his wealth has it stripped from him by strangers, so Stave 4 turns Scrooge's own values against him and shows that a life without connection ends without meaning.
Plan:
1. Extract: the dark, filthy setting of Old Joe's shop and the 'unseemly rags' create a Gothic underworld. The charwoman laughs as she sells the bed-curtains, showing nobody grieves him.
2. Extract: the thieves echo Scrooge's own business values (taking what they can). Dramatic irony: the reader suspects the dead man is Scrooge before he does, which builds tension and dread.
3. Wider: the businessmen on the Exchange joke that they will attend only if lunch is provided, showing his social world is cold and transactional.
4. Contrast: Tiny Tim's death is mourned with love, showing that a poor life rich in family has value, while Scrooge's rich, lonely life does not. Juxtaposition makes the moral clear.
5. Ending: Scrooge reads his own name on the neglected grave and begs 'Why show me this, if I am past all hope?', leading to his vow. Stave 5 shows connection replacing isolation. AO3: Victorian rituals of mourning and respect for the dead; Christian ideas of judgement.

AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Concept of isolated death as the consequence of a selfish life; covers Old Joe, the businessmen, Tim and the grave; links to Scrooge's change.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Gothic setting; the silent, shrouded Ghost; dramatic irony; juxtaposition of two deaths; dialogue of the thieves; delayed reveal of the name on the grave; structure of fear before redemption.

AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: 1840s 'Hungry Forties'; the 1834 Poor Law Amendment Act and workhouses; Malthus and the 'surplus population'; child labour and the 1843 report on children's employment that shocked Dickens; Dickens's childhood in Warren's Blacking Factory; Christian values of charity; the novella as a moral fable.
questions.tip: Juxtapose Tiny Tim's death with Scrooge's. That contrast is the core of Stave 4.

questions.q:
Character option. How does Priestley present Mrs Birling in An Inspector Calls?

Write about:
- what Mrs Birling says and does
- how Priestley presents Mrs Birling by the ways he writes. [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
(On the real paper you choose one of two questions: this one or a theme question.)
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Priestley presents Mrs Birling as the embodiment of upper-class moral blindness: she uses respectability as armour against responsibility, and because she is the only character whose cruelty directly condemns her own grandchild, Priestley turns her into a warning that class prejudice destroys the very families it claims to protect.
Plan:
1. Opening stage directions: 'a rather cold woman' and 'her husband's social superior' establish her through status, not warmth. Her correction of Birling's manners shows she polices class rules.
2. Act 2: her dismissive phrase 'girls of that class' and claim that Eva gave herself 'ridiculous airs' show prejudice disguised as judgement. Priestley uses her formal, clipped language to show emotional distance.
3. Act 2 climax: she insists the blame lies with 'the father of the child', unaware it is Eric. Priestley builds dramatic irony as Sheila begs her to stop, so the audience watches her condemn her own son.
4. Act 3: she refuses to change, praising herself for being the only one who 'didn't give in'. She becomes an obstacle in the morality play, standing for pride.
5. Writer's purpose: Mrs Birling represents the charitable organisations that judged the 'deserving poor'. AO3: 1945 audience voting for a welfare state that replaced judgemental charity with universal support. Alternative reading: her coldness hides fear of losing status, making her a product of the system she defends.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised argument that answers the task across the whole text; judicious, precisely embedded references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience, including alternative readings; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task woven into the argument.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed argument across the whole text; apt references integrated into the interpretation; examination of methods with effective terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.

Level 4 and below (16-20 marks): clear, explained response with effective references and clear explanation of methods and context, but not yet developed or exploratory. A response that only retells the plot or only covers the extract cannot move past the lower levels.

AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Clear concept of Mrs Birling as respectability without morality; covers her stage directions, interrogation, dramatic irony and refusal to change; links to the charity system.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Stage directions; dramatic irony at the end of Act 2; curtain line; formal register; contrast with Sheila; her role in a morality play (pride); structure of the interrogations.

AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Written in 1945 (first performed 1945/46) but set in 1912; Priestley's socialism and the 1945 Labour landslide; the welfare state; two world wars the Birlings cannot foresee; rigid Edwardian class and gender hierarchies; women's suffrage campaigns before 1918; the Titanic (1912) and dramatic irony; the play as a morality play / well-made play.

AO4 (4 marks, high performance): consistently accurate spelling and punctuation, consistent control of meaning, wide range of vocabulary and sentence structures. 2-3 marks: considerable accuracy; 1 mark: reasonable accuracy.
questions.tip: Focus on the end of Act 2. The dramatic irony there is the strongest evidence in the play for Mrs Birling.

questions.q:
Character option. How does Priestley present Eric in An Inspector Calls?

Write about:
- what Eric says and does
- how Priestley presents Eric by the ways he writes. [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
(On the real paper you choose one of two questions: this one or a theme question.)
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Priestley presents Eric as the most damaged product of the Birling household: his drinking, violence and theft are symptoms of a father who offers money instead of guidance, yet by giving Eric the clearest acceptance of guilt, Priestley suggests that even the most flawed young person can be redeemed if they face the truth.
Plan:
1. Opening: 'half shy, half assertive' and his laughter at the dinner hint at hidden guilt. Sheila's teasing remark that Eric is 'squiffy' shows his drinking is known but ignored.
2. Act 3 confession: Eric admits that 'a chap easily turns nasty' when drunk, an evasive phrase showing his attempt to minimise his assault on Eva. Priestley does not excuse him; his behaviour shows privilege and sexual exploitation.
3. Stealing from the office shows the Birling values of money passed down: he tries to fix things with cash, like his father, but it is stolen money.
4. Generational conflict: 'You're not the kind of father' shows he blames Birling for emotional neglect; his anger at his mother ('you killed her') shows he now sees through their respectability.
5. Ending: Eric, with Sheila, refuses to pretend nothing happened. AO3: the young generation in 1945 who voted for change; Priestley's hope for the future. Alternative reading: Eric's change may be emotional rather than political, so Priestley leaves the audience to decide.

questions.q:
Character option. How does Priestley present Gerald in An Inspector Calls?

Write about:
- what Gerald says and does
- how Priestley presents Gerald by the ways he writes. [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
(On the real paper you choose one of two questions: this one or a theme question.)
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Priestley presents Gerald as the most dangerous kind of upper-class man because he is the most likeable: his genuine moments of kindness to Eva make his final return to complacency more disturbing, showing that charm and good manners can disguise the same exploitation the Inspector exposes.
Plan:
1. Opening: 'an attractive chap about thirty' and his easy agreement with Birling show he belongs to the capitalist upper class; his marriage to Sheila is partly a business merger with Crofts Limited.
2. Act 2: he meets Daisy Renton at the Palace bar and rescues her from 'Alderman Meggarty', which makes him seem heroic. But he chose when the affair ended, showing power over her life.
3. Emotion: Gerald's distress at her death is real, and Sheila respects his honesty, which complicates the audience's judgement.
4. Act 3: he returns having learned from a police sergeant that there is no Inspector Goole on the force, investigates the infirmary story, and offers Sheila the ring again. He leads the older generation's attempt to escape guilt.
5. Purpose: Gerald sits between the generations and chooses the old. AO3: the aristocracy's power in 1912; Priestley's warning that charming elites would resist the 1945 reforms. Alternative reading: Gerald as a 'fairy prince' figure exposes the romantic stories the upper class tells itself.

questions.q:
Character option. How does Priestley present Eva Smith in An Inspector Calls?

Write about:
- what Eva Smith says and does
- how Priestley presents Eva Smith by the ways he writes. [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
(On the real paper you choose one of two questions: this one or a theme question.)
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Priestley presents Eva Smith as an absence at the centre of the play: by never letting her appear, he turns her into a symbol for every powerless worker, so the audience must judge the Birlings only by what they did to her, and her silence becomes the loudest argument for social responsibility.
Plan:
1. Absence: she never appears on stage and her story is told by those who harmed her, so the audience sees how the powerful control the narrative. Her body in the infirmary is described but not shown.
2. Names: 'Smith' is the most common surname, suggesting she is everyone; 'Daisy Renton' and 'Mrs Birling' show her identity changing to survive, and she even takes on the family's own name.
3. Each stage of her life shows a different form of exploitation: wages (Birling), jealousy and power (Sheila), sexual and romantic power (Gerald), sexual violence (Eric), judgement (Mrs Birling).
4. Her dignity: she refuses stolen money and refuses to marry Eric, showing moral strength the Birlings lack. Priestley gives the poorest character the strongest values.
5. The Inspector's speech about 'millions and millions of Eva Smiths' makes her a symbol. AO3: unprotected female workers in 1912, no welfare state, no vote for women. Alternative reading: the uncertainty about whether she is one girl or several strengthens the symbolism.
