questions.q:
Theme option. How does Priestley explore ideas about gender in An Inspector Calls?

Write about:
- the ways men and women are treated and behave in the play
- how Priestley presents these ideas by the ways he writes. [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
(On the real paper you choose one of two questions: this one or a character question.)
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Priestley explores gender as a second hierarchy alongside class: the men treat women as decorations or commodities and the women are trained to accept it, but by letting Sheila break free of these expectations, Priestley suggests that gender roles, like class, are learned and can be changed.
Plan:
1. Birling's comment that clothes are a 'token of their self-respect' for women and the men's jokes show women are seen as concerned with appearance, not ideas.
2. Eva is exploited as a worker and as a woman: her sacking, Gerald's 'rescue' and Eric's assault show male power over working-class women at every level.
3. Mrs Birling enforces gender rules, telling Sheila she will have to get used to men spending time on business; she accepts male power because it protects her status.
4. Sheila's change from 'mummy' to 'mother' and her ironic 'the wonderful Fairy Prince' show her rejecting the role of passive fiancee. Returning the ring shows independence.
5. Ending: Sheila is not sure she will take the ring back. AO3: 1912 women had no vote; the war gave women work and some the vote in 1918; by 1945 women's roles had changed. Alternative reading: Priestley still gives most power to male voices, especially the Inspector.

questions.q:
Theme option. How does Priestley explore ideas about guilt and blame in An Inspector Calls?

Write about:
- how the characters respond to their guilt
- how Priestley presents these ideas by the ways he writes. [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
(On the real paper you choose one of two questions: this one or a character question.)
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Priestley explores guilt as a test that divides the characters: the young accept guilt and are changed by it, while the old seek someone else to blame, and because the final phone call removes any escape, Priestley argues that guilt is not something to be avoided but the starting point of moral responsibility.
Plan:
1. Birling's refusal ('I can't accept any responsibility') sets up blame-shifting from the start; he sees guilt only as public scandal.
2. Sheila feels guilt immediately and deeply ('I'll never, never do it again'); her guilt is moral, not social, which makes her the model response.
3. Mrs Birling blames Eva and then 'the father of the child', showing how far some will go to avoid guilt; dramatic irony punishes her.
4. The Inspector's line 'helped to kill her' distributes guilt collectively, so no one can hide behind someone else. Priestley's structure (one confession per character) makes each share visible.
5. Ending: the elders celebrate when the Inspector seems fake, but Sheila and Eric insist that what they did still matters. The phone call proves guilt cannot be dodged. AO3: post-war collective guilt and responsibility; Christian ideas of confession; the 1945 vote.

questions.q:
Theme option. How does Priestley explore ideas about change in An Inspector Calls?

Write about:
- which characters change and which do not
- how Priestley presents these ideas by the ways he writes. [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
(On the real paper you choose one of two questions: this one or a character question.)
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Priestley explores change as a choice, not something forced on people: the Inspector gives every Birling the same evidence, yet only the young choose to change, so the play becomes a direct appeal to its 1945 audience to choose change for society rather than return to 1912.
Plan:
1. Birling's opening speeches ('absolutely unsinkable', no war) show a man who believes nothing needs to change; dramatic irony shows the audience he is wrong about the future.
2. Sheila changes most: from childish and jealous to perceptive, warning others that the Inspector knows everything. Her language becomes sharper and more ironic.
3. Eric changes from drunk and evasive to angry and honest, turning on his parents.
4. Gerald and the older Birlings briefly shaken, then return to normal ('Everything's all right now, Sheila'), showing change can be rejected.
5. Ending: the phone call gives them a second chance, mirroring the 1945 audience's chance to build a better society. AO3: 1945 Labour election, welfare state, the 'younger generation' who had fought in the war. The lighting change from 'pink and intimate' to 'brighter and harder' shows change in how the family is seen.

questions.q:
Theme option. How does Priestley explore ideas about power in An Inspector Calls?

Write about:
- the different kinds of power characters have and how they use it
- how Priestley presents these ideas by the ways he writes. [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
(On the real paper you choose one of two questions: this one or a character question.)
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Priestley explores power as something the Birlings take for granted and the Inspector exposes: every character uses a form of power, economic, social, sexual or moral, over Eva, and by giving the Inspector a different kind of power, based on truth rather than status, Priestley imagines a society where power is used to protect rather than exploit.
Plan:
1. Economic power: Birling sacks Eva to keep 'lower costs and higher prices'; his status as a former mayor and hopes for a knighthood show economic power buying social power.
2. Social power: Sheila uses her status as a customer to get Eva sacked; Mrs Birling uses her position on the charity committee to refuse help.
3. Sexual power: Gerald and Eric use their wealth and gender over Eva; Alderman Meggarty shows this is common among powerful men.
4. The Inspector's power: he 'cuts through' interruptions, controls the pace and refuses to be intimidated by Birling's connections. His power comes from moral authority.
5. Final speech: the warning of 'fire and blood and anguish' threatens the powerful. AO3: 1912 class structure, the strikes of 1912, the post-1945 welfare state. Alternative reading: the Inspector is godlike or ghostly, suggesting moral power must come from outside the system.

questions.q:
Compare how poets present pride in "Ozymandias" and in one other poem from "Power and conflict". [30 marks]
("Ozymandias" is printed on the paper; you choose the second poem from memory.)
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Shelley and Browning (My Last Duchess) both present pride as a form of blindness, but Shelley shows pride defeated by time, so the ruler becomes a ruin, while Browning shows pride that is still alive and dangerous in the speaker's own voice; together they suggest pride is most frightening when it does not know it is being judged.
Plan:
1. Openings and voice: Shelley's sonnet is told at a double distance (the speaker hears it from a 'traveller'), which shrinks Ozymandias; Browning's dramatic monologue lets the Duke speak directly, so his pride condemns itself.
2. Language of control: 'sneer of cold command' (sibilance, harsh consonants) versus the Duke's possessive 'my' and his refusal to 'stoop'. Both men need others to obey them.
3. Art as power: the sculptor 'mocked' the king's passions, so art outlives and judges the ruler; the Duke controls the Duchess's portrait behind a curtain, so art becomes a tool of ownership. Contrast: art defeats Ozymandias but serves the Duke.
4. Form: Shelley's sonnet breaks its rhyme scheme, mirroring the broken statue; Browning's rhyming couplets are hidden by enjambment, mirroring the Duke's controlled surface hiding violence.
5. Endings and context: 'lone and level sands' stretch away (time wins); the Duke points to a statue of Neptune taming a sea-horse (he still wants control). AO3: Shelley's Romantic hatred of tyranny and George III; Renaissance Italian aristocracy and Victorian interest in psychology.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised comparison of both poems in every paragraph; judicious, precisely embedded references from both; analysis of both poets' methods with judicious terminology; exploration of effects on the reader; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed comparison; apt references from both poems integrated into the argument; examination of methods with effective terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.
Level 4 and below (16-20 marks): clear, explained comparison with effective references, but the comparison is uneven (one poem then the other) or not developed. No AO4 marks on this question.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Judicious comparison of how pride is presented and judged; references from both poems throughout; conceptual idea about pride's blindness.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Sonnet vs dramatic monologue; framing narrator vs direct speech; sibilance; possessive pronouns; enjambment hiding rhyme; endings with art objects (statue, bronze Neptune); broken rhyme scheme.

AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Shelley's Romanticism and political radicalism; Ozymandias as Rameses II; Browning's Renaissance setting based on Alfonso II of Ferrara; Victorian interest in the psychology of power.
questions.tip: Both poems end with a work of art. Compare those endings for a top-band final paragraph.

questions.q:
Compare how poets present the suffering caused by those in authority in "London" and in one other poem from "Power and conflict". [30 marks]
("London" is printed on the paper; you choose the second poem from memory.)
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Blake and Agard (Checking Out Me History) both expose institutions that damage people while claiming authority over them, but Blake presents power as an inescapable system that brands everyone, whereas Agard shows that people can take power back by rewriting the story they were given.
Plan:
1. Openings: Blake's 'chartered' streets and river show even nature is owned; Agard's 'Dem tell me' shows authority imposing a version of history. Both begin with institutions controlling space or knowledge.
2. Language: Blake's 'mind-forg'd manacles' suggests people are trapped by thought as well as law; Agard's repeated 'Bandage up me eye' shows education as a wound that blinds. Both present control of the mind.
3. Institutions: Blake attacks the Church ('blackning Church') and the monarchy ('Palace walls' running with blood); Agard attacks the school curriculum. Both show institutions failing those below them.
4. Form: Blake's regular quatrains and ABAB rhyme mirror the relentless, mechanical system; Agard's shifts between italic stanzas about Black heroes and blunt stanzas about British history mirror two competing histories, and his non-standard phonetic spelling rejects authority.
5. Endings: Blake ends with the 'Marriage hearse', a bleak oxymoron of hope destroyed; Agard ends with 'carving out me identity', a hopeful act of rebellion. AO3: Blake and the French Revolution, child labour, Romantic protest; Agard's Guyanese heritage and the colonial curriculum.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised comparison of both poems in every paragraph; judicious, precisely embedded references from both; analysis of both poets' methods with judicious terminology; exploration of effects on the reader; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed comparison; apt references from both poems integrated into the argument; examination of methods with effective terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.
Level 4 and below (16-20 marks): clear, explained comparison with effective references, but the comparison is uneven (one poem then the other) or not developed. No AO4 marks on this question.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Comparison of how institutions abuse power and whether people can resist; references from both; contrasting endings.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Repetition ('chartered', 'Dem tell me'); metaphor ('manacles', 'bandage'); oxymoron; regular vs disrupted form; dialect and phonetic spelling; italics; contrasting endings.
AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Blake's Romantic radicalism and the Industrial Revolution; French Revolution fears; Agard born in Guyana, British colonial education, Caribbean history.
questions.tip: Show the contrast in endings: Blake is trapped, Agard breaks free.

questions.q:
Compare how poets present the effects of fear in "The Prelude (Stealing the Boat)" and in one other poem from "Power and conflict". [30 marks]
("The Prelude (Stealing the Boat)" is printed on the paper; you choose the second poem from memory.)
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Wordsworth and Hughes (Bayonet Charge) both show fear arriving suddenly and stripping away a young man's confidence, but Wordsworth presents fear as a lasting spiritual education from nature, whereas Hughes presents fear as an animal instinct that reduces a soldier to survival, so one poem grows the mind while the other empties it.
Plan:
1. Openings: Wordsworth begins calmly with 'one summer evening (led by her)', personifying nature as a guide; Hughes begins mid-action ('Suddenly he awoke'). Both show a confident or unthinking young man.
2. Moment of fear: the 'huge peak, black and huge' (repetition, personification) suddenly 'Upreared its head'; Hughes's soldier stops in 'bewilderment', and the 'yellow hare' rolls 'like a flame'. Both turn on a sudden, shocking image.
3. Structure: Wordsworth's volta shifts from pleasure to terror; Hughes freezes time in the second stanza, slowing the poem as the soldier questions why he is running. Both use structure to mirror the moment fear takes over.
4. Effect: Wordsworth's boy returns 'with trembling oars' and is haunted by 'huge and mighty forms'; Hughes's soldier drops 'King, honour, human dignity' and runs on pure fear. One is reflective, the other stripped of ideals.
5. Context: Romantic belief that nature shapes the mind and the sublime; Hughes writing about WW1 soldiers he never fought beside, and his father's experience. Both are about young men learning a hard truth.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised comparison of both poems in every paragraph; judicious, precisely embedded references from both; analysis of both poets' methods with judicious terminology; exploration of effects on the reader; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed comparison; apt references from both poems integrated into the argument; examination of methods with effective terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.
Level 4 and below (16-20 marks): clear, explained comparison with effective references, but the comparison is uneven (one poem then the other) or not developed. No AO4 marks on this question.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Comparison of how fear changes the young men; references from both throughout; conceptual contrast between fear as education and fear as survival.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Personification of nature; repetition; volta; time freezing; enjambment and caesura; listing ('King, honour, human dignity'); blank verse vs free verse; first-person reflection vs third-person immediacy.
AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Romanticism and the sublime; Wordsworth's autobiographical Prelude; WW1; Hughes's father fought at Gallipoli.
questions.tip: Compare the shift in each poem (volta vs frozen time). Structure points push you into Level 6.

questions.q:
Compare how poets present heroism in "The Charge of the Light Brigade" and in one other poem from "Power and conflict". [30 marks]
("The Charge of the Light Brigade" is printed on the paper; you choose the second poem from memory.)
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Tennyson and Owen (Exposure) both write about soldiers dying because of decisions made above them, but Tennyson turns their deaths into public, glorious heroism to be honoured, while Owen strips heroism away entirely, showing soldiers dying slowly and pointlessly; the contrast reflects the shift from Victorian patriotism to the disillusion of WW1.
Plan:
1. Openings: Tennyson's dactylic rhythm ('Half a league, half a league') gallops forward, creating excitement; Owen's 'Our brains ache' opens with stillness and pain. One poem moves, the other is frozen.
2. Language: Tennyson's 'Valley of Death' and 'jaws of Death' are dramatic, almost biblical; Owen's personified weather ('merciless iced east winds that knive us') is the real enemy. Tennyson's danger is glorious; Owen's is dull and cruel.
3. Authority: Tennyson admits 'Some one had blunder'd' but insists 'Theirs not to reason why', praising obedience; Owen's repeated 'But nothing happens' quietly blames the pointlessness of war.
4. Form: Tennyson's refrain 'the six hundred' and anaphora ('Cannon to right of them') build a ballad of public memory; Owen's half-rhymes and short final lines create unease and an unresolved ending.
5. Endings: Tennyson commands 'Honour the Light Brigade'; Owen's soldiers' eyes are 'ice', with the final 'But nothing happens'. AO3: Tennyson as Poet Laureate in 1854 writing from newspaper reports; Owen as a soldier writing from the trenches in 1917, killed in 1918.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised comparison of both poems in every paragraph; judicious, precisely embedded references from both; analysis of both poets' methods with judicious terminology; exploration of effects on the reader; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed comparison; apt references from both poems integrated into the argument; examination of methods with effective terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.
Level 4 and below (16-20 marks): clear, explained comparison with effective references, but the comparison is uneven (one poem then the other) or not developed. No AO4 marks on this question.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Comparison of glorified vs denied heroism; references from both; links to purpose and audience.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Dactylic metre; refrain and anaphora; personification of weather; half-rhyme (pararhyme); rhetorical questions; imperative ending vs anticlimactic refrain.

AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Crimean War 1854, the Battle of Balaclava, newspaper report in The Times; Tennyson's role as Poet Laureate; Owen's frontline experience, 1917 winter, death a week before the Armistice.
questions.tip: Explain why the two poets see heroism so differently. Context IS the answer here.

questions.q:
Compare how poets present guilt in "Remains" and in one other poem from "Power and conflict". [30 marks]
("Remains" is printed on the paper; you choose the second poem from memory.)
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Armitage and Duffy (War Photographer) both show guilt that follows a man home from conflict, but Armitage's soldier is haunted by a single act he committed, turning guilt into a psychological wound, whereas Duffy's photographer feels guilt for witnessing and profiting from suffering while his audience feels almost nothing.
Plan:
1. Openings: Armitage's casual 'On another occasion' and slang ('legs it') show the soldier trying to make the killing seem ordinary; Duffy's photographer is alone in a darkroom 'finally alone', a quiet, almost religious space. Both begin with distance from the trauma.
2. Central image: the looter's body ('blood-shadow' on the street) and the photographer's developing image of a man's face 'twist before his eyes'. Both images refuse to stay fixed and return to haunt them.
3. Guilt and responsibility: 'probably armed, possibly not' shows the soldier's uncertainty; Duffy's photographer remembers seeking a grieving wife's approval 'without words'. Both feel complicit.
4. Form: Armitage's shift from casual storytelling to present-tense haunting ('he's here in my head') mirrors PTSD; Duffy's regular stanzas and rhyme mirror the photographer's ordered rows of film, a control that his memories break.
5. Endings: 'bloody life in my bloody hands' (pun on 'bloody') shows guilt that will not leave; Duffy's 'they do not care' turns guilt outwards onto readers. AO3: Remains from 'The Not Dead', interviews with soldiers in Iraq; Duffy's friendship with war photographers; Sunday supplements.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised comparison of both poems in every paragraph; judicious, precisely embedded references from both; analysis of both poets' methods with judicious terminology; exploration of effects on the reader; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed comparison; apt references from both poems integrated into the argument; examination of methods with effective terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.
Level 4 and below (16-20 marks): clear, explained comparison with effective references, but the comparison is uneven (one poem then the other) or not developed. No AO4 marks on this question.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Comparison of personal vs observer guilt; references from both throughout; includes the reader's response in Duffy.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Colloquial language vs formal, religious lexis; shift in tense; repetition; pun; regular form vs breakdown of time; imagery of blood and developing images.

AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Armitage's 'The Not Dead' documentary and PTSD among veterans; Duffy's friendship with photographers covering Northern Ireland, Beirut and Cambodia; public indifference to war images.
questions.tip: Use the short phrases precisely. Both poems' endings make a strong final comparison.

questions.q:
Compare how poets present conflict between duty and the individual in "Kamikaze" and in one other poem from "Power and conflict". [30 marks]
("Kamikaze" is printed on the paper; you choose the second poem from memory.)
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Garland and Tennyson (The Charge of the Light Brigade) both show men facing an order to die, but Tennyson praises the soldiers for obeying without question, while Garland's pilot chooses life over duty and is punished by his own family, so one poem honours obedience and the other exposes its human cost.
Plan:
1. Duty: Tennyson's 'Theirs not to reason why' praises unquestioning obedience; Garland's pilot was sent on a mission he 'must have' turned back from, showing the narrator piecing his choice together.
2. What changes them: Tennyson's soldiers never doubt; Garland's pilot sees the sea and fishing boats, memories of childhood, and the natural beauty pulls him back to life. Nature and memory challenge duty.
3. Consequences: the Light Brigade are honoured; the pilot's family treat him 'as though he no longer existed', a social death.
4. Form and voice: Tennyson's collective, ballad-like voice speaks for a nation; Garland uses a daughter's reported speech in italics and an outer narrator, layering voices to show a family story. Garland's regular six-line stanzas feel quiet and reflective, while Tennyson's stanzas vary in length like a surging charge.
5. Endings: 'Honour the Light Brigade' versus the pilot left wondering which way to die had been better. AO3: Japanese Bushido code and the shame of failing a kamikaze mission in WW2; Victorian patriotism and the Crimean War.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised comparison of both poems in every paragraph; judicious, precisely embedded references from both; analysis of both poets' methods with judicious terminology; exploration of effects on the reader; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed comparison; apt references from both poems integrated into the argument; examination of methods with effective terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.
Level 4 and below (16-20 marks): clear, explained comparison with effective references, but the comparison is uneven (one poem then the other) or not developed. No AO4 marks on this question.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Comparison of duty versus individual choice; considers how each society responds; references from both throughout.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Imperatives; refrain; multiple narrative voices and italics; natural imagery; dramatic irony; contrasting endings.
AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Kamikaze pilots in WW2 and the shame of returning; Bushido and loyalty to the Emperor; Crimean War 1854, the Times report, Tennyson as Poet Laureate.
questions.tip: Ask who is speaking in Kamikaze. The layers of voice are your best AO2 point.

questions.q:
Compare how poets present the reality of conflict in "War Photographer" and in one other poem from "Power and conflict". [30 marks]
("War Photographer" is printed on the paper; you choose the second poem from memory.)
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Duffy and Owen (Exposure) both insist on showing a reality that people at home would rather ignore, but Duffy places the reality inside a photograph that readers flick past, while Owen places it in the bodies of soldiers who are dying of cold; both suggest that the truth of war is not dramatic but ignored.
Plan:
1. Openings: Duffy's darkroom with 'spools of suffering' (sibilance, alliteration) presents suffering as ordered and stored; Owen's 'Our brains ache' and silence present war as waiting and pain.
2. Reality vs expectation: Duffy contrasts 'Rural England' with fields that 'explode beneath the feet'; Owen's soldiers dream of home fires but find the doors 'closed'. Both contrast home and war.
3. Audience: Duffy's readers' 'eyeballs prick / with tears' only briefly, between 'the bath and pre-lunch beers'; Owen's 'We only know war lasts' blames no one directly but implies that the leaders do not know.
4. Form: Duffy's controlled rhyme and four regular stanzas mirror the ordered rows of film; Owen's half-rhyme and short final refrain create unease and anticlimax.
5. Endings: the photographer stares 'impassively' at readers who 'do not care'; Owen's soldiers die and 'nothing happens'. AO3: Duffy's friendships with war photographers and Sunday newspaper culture; Owen's frontline letters and the winter of 1917.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised comparison of both poems in every paragraph; judicious, precisely embedded references from both; analysis of both poets' methods with judicious terminology; exploration of effects on the reader; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed comparison; apt references from both poems integrated into the argument; examination of methods with effective terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.
Level 4 and below (16-20 marks): clear, explained comparison with effective references, but the comparison is uneven (one poem then the other) or not developed. No AO4 marks on this question.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Comparison of hidden reality and indifference at home; references from both; considers each poet's purpose.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Sibilance and alliteration; religious imagery (priest, Mass); contrast of home and conflict; half-rhyme; refrain; regular form vs disrupted rhythm.
AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Duffy's 1985 poem, photographers in Northern Ireland, Beirut and Cambodia; Owen's WW1 service and death in 1918; the pressure on home audiences.
questions.tip: Both poems blame people at home. Compare how gently or harshly each does it.

questions.q:
Compare how poets present the importance of place in "The Emigree" and in one other poem from "Power and conflict". [30 marks]
("The Emigree" is printed on the paper; you choose the second poem from memory.)
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: Rumens and Wordsworth (The Prelude) both show a place that shapes the speaker's identity, but Rumens's speaker holds on to a city she can no longer reach, keeping it alive through memory and love, while Wordsworth's speaker is changed by a real landscape that he cannot forget; one place is idealised, the other is overwhelming.
Plan:
1. Openings: Rumens's fairy-tale 'There once was a country' sets up a lost, idealised past; Wordsworth's 'One summer evening' also begins with a gentle, nostalgic tone. Both look back.
2. Light and memory: Rumens's city is full of 'sunlight' and is 'my city' (possessive), showing love and loyalty; Wordsworth's lake and stars are beautiful until the mountain appears.
3. Threat: Rumens's city is 'sick with tyrants', yet her memory stays bright, showing defiance; Wordsworth's mountain is threatening because it is real and sublime.
4. Form: Rumens uses free verse with a repeated refrain about sunlight at the end of each stanza, mirroring the memory she returns to; Wordsworth uses a single stanza of blank verse, an unbroken flow of memory with a dramatic volta.
5. Endings: Rumens's city 'takes me dancing' while she is under threat, a paradox of joy and danger; Wordsworth ends troubled, with 'huge and mighty forms' in his mind. AO3: refugees, exile and political oppression in the late 20th century; Romanticism and nature as a teacher.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised comparison of both poems in every paragraph; judicious, precisely embedded references from both; analysis of both poets' methods with judicious terminology; exploration of effects on the reader; detailed, perceptive links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed comparison; apt references from both poems integrated into the argument; examination of methods with effective terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.
Level 4 and below (16-20 marks): clear, explained comparison with effective references, but the comparison is uneven (one poem then the other) or not developed. No AO4 marks on this question.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Comparison of idealised vs real place; references from both; considers how place shapes identity.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Fairy-tale opening; light imagery; possessive pronouns; personification of the city and mountain; refrain; free verse vs blank verse; volta.
AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Rumens's 1993 poem and the experience of exiles and refugees; Wordsworth's Lake District childhood; the Romantic sublime.
questions.tip: Rumens never names the city. Discuss why: it lets the poem stand for every exile.

questions.q:
Q27.1 style. Read the poem.

"Allotment" (original poem)
My grandmother kneels as if the soil were church,
her knuckles brown as the potatoes she lifts.
She talks to the beans, scolds the slugs,
forgives the rain for being late again.

Each row is a sentence she has written
for forty years, and I am still
learning the alphabet: onion, leek,
the patient vowels of the marrow.

When she stands, her back unfolds
slow as a deckchair, and she laughs,
and the whole plot leans towards her
the way flowers lean towards the light.

In "Allotment", how does the poet present the speaker's feelings about her grandmother? [24 marks]
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: The speaker presents her grandmother with reverent affection, seeing her as a figure whose quiet, physical work is a kind of wisdom; the poem moves from observation to awe, suggesting the speaker sees her as a source of life she can learn from but not yet match.
Plan:
1. Religious simile: kneeling 'as if the soil were church' presents gardening as worship and the grandmother as devoted; the speaker's tone is respectful, almost sacred.
2. Connection to the earth: the simile 'knuckles brown as the potatoes' merges her body with the land, suggesting she belongs to it. Personification in stanza 1 (she talks to beans, 'forgives the rain') shows warmth and humour: she treats nature as family.
3. Extended metaphor of language: each row is 'a sentence' and the speaker is 'still / learning the alphabet'. Enjambment across 'still / learning' stretches the line, showing the long distance between them. 'patient vowels of the marrow' is playful, rounded imagery, showing admiration.
4. Final stanza: the simile 'slow as a deckchair' is affectionate and gently comic, showing age without pity. Polysyndeton ('and she laughs, / and the whole plot') builds joy.
5. Ending: the closing simile of flowers leaning 'towards the light' presents her as a sun-like source of life. Structure: three regular quatrains move from her work, to the speaker's learning, to celebration, so feelings grow from respect to wonder. Alternative reading: the 'forty years' and her slowness hint at mortality, adding tenderness.
ms: Level 6 (21-24 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised response to the task and the poem; judicious references; analysis of the poet's methods with judicious terminology; exploration of effects on the reader, including more than one interpretation.
Level 5 (17-20 marks): thoughtful, developed response; apt references integrated into the interpretation; examination of methods with effective terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects.
Level 4 (13-16 marks): clear, explained response; effective references; clear explanation of methods with appropriate terminology.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Admiration, reverence, affection and humility; the grandmother as wise, warm and life-giving; awareness of age and inheritance.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Religious and natural similes; personification; extended metaphor of language and writing; enjambment; polysyndeton; regular quatrains; final image of light; gentle humour in tone.
AO3 is not assessed on the unseen poem and there is no AO4. Do not reward guesses about the poet's life.
questions.tip: Track how the feelings change from stanza to stanza. Structure is half of AO2.

questions.q:
Q27.2 style. Read "Allotment" and "Inheritance".

"Allotment" (original poem)
My grandmother kneels as if the soil were church,
her knuckles brown as the potatoes she lifts.
She talks to the beans, scolds the slugs,
forgives the rain for being late again.

Each row is a sentence she has written
for forty years, and I am still
learning the alphabet: onion, leek,
the patient vowels of the marrow.

When she stands, her back unfolds
slow as a deckchair, and she laughs,
and the whole plot leans towards her
the way flowers lean towards the light.

"Inheritance" (original poem)
Dad left me his toolbox.
Rust has chewed the hinges.
Inside: a spirit level, its bubble
still trying to find the centre,
a hammer worn smooth
where his palm used to be,
nails in a jam jar, sorted
by a logic I will never know.
I lift the hammer.
It is heavier than I remember,
or I am lighter.

In both "Allotment" and "Inheritance" the speakers describe an older relative. What are the similarities and/or differences between the methods the poets use to present these relationships? [8 marks]
questions.answer: Both poets present the relationship through physical objects linked to work: the grandmother's vegetables and the father's tools. However, "Allotment" uses warm similes and personification to present a living, joyful relationship, while "Inheritance" uses short, plain sentences and personification of decay ('Rust has chewed') to present grief and absence. Both use an object to symbolise the gap between generations: the speaker in "Allotment" is 'still / learning the alphabet', and in "Inheritance" the nails are sorted 'by a logic I will never know'. Structurally, "Allotment" builds to a celebratory final image of light, while "Inheritance" ends with a turn, 'or I am lighter', which shifts the focus from the hammer to the speaker's own grief, making the ending more painful.
ms: Level 4 (7-8 marks): exploratory comparison of both poets' use of language, structure and form, with judicious terminology; convincing comparison of effects on the reader.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): thoughtful comparison of methods with effective terminology; clear comparison of effects.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): relevant comparison of methods with some terminology; some comparison of effects. Level 1 (1-2): simple comments on methods.

Indicative content: Objects as symbols in both (vegetables/tools, hammer worn by the palm); warm similes vs plain declaratives; personification of nature (forgiving rain) vs of decay (rust chewing); regular quatrains vs a single block of free verse; endings: light and celebration vs the ambiguous 'lighter' (weight of grief, loss of self); present living relative vs absent dead one.
Only AO2 (methods) is credited. Comparing what the poems are about without methods cannot reach Level 3.
questions.tip: Compare effects, not just techniques. Say what each method makes the reader feel about the relationship.

questions.q:
Q27.1 style. Read the poem.

"Exam Hall" (original poem)
Two hundred chairs face one clock
like sunflowers that have given up on the sun.
The silence is a held breath
nobody is allowed to let go.

I write my name. It looks like someone else's.
The invigilator's shoes
squeak their slow patrol,
a metronome for worry.

Outside, a blackbird
does not know it is June,
does not know about grade boundaries,
sings anyway.

In "Exam Hall", how does the poet present the experience of taking an exam? [24 marks]
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: The poet presents the exam as an experience that shrinks the individual: the hall is rigid, timed and silent, and the speaker almost loses her own identity, but the blackbird at the end offers a quiet rebellion, suggesting that life and freedom continue outside the pressure of results.
Plan:
1. Opening simile: chairs 'like sunflowers that have given up on the sun' presents the students as drooping and defeated; the single clock replaces the sun, suggesting time has replaced hope.
2. Metaphor: silence as 'a held breath' creates tension and physical discomfort; 'nobody is allowed' shows rules controlling even breathing.
3. Identity: 'It looks like someone else's' shows alienation; the short, end-stopped sentence mimics a nervous pause. The invigilator's squeaking shoes are 'a metronome for worry', turning anxiety into a rhythm.
4. Volta: 'Outside' shifts the poem from the hall to nature. The blackbird's repeated 'does not know' (anaphora) contrasts its freedom with the students' pressure.
5. Ending: the final short line 'sings anyway' is defiant and hopeful. Structure: three quatrains moving from the room to the self to the world outside, widening the perspective. Alternative reading: the blackbird may also be ironic, showing how small the exam is in the scale of nature.
ms: Level 6 (21-24 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised response to the task and the poem; judicious references; analysis of the poet's methods with judicious terminology; exploration of effects on the reader, including more than one interpretation.
Level 5 (17-20 marks): thoughtful, developed response; apt references integrated into the interpretation; examination of methods with effective terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects.
Level 4 (13-16 marks): clear, explained response; effective references; clear explanation of methods with appropriate terminology.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Pressure, alienation and anxiety; loss of identity; contrast with natural freedom; possibility of hope.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Simile of sunflowers; metaphor of the held breath; sound imagery (squeak, metronome); short end-stopped sentences; volta; anaphora; one-line ending; free verse in regular quatrains.
AO3 is not assessed on the unseen poem and there is no AO4. Do not reward guesses about the poet's life.
questions.tip: Find the volta. Writing about where the poem turns is an easy way to show structural understanding.

questions.q:
Q27.2 style. Read "Exam Hall" and "Results Day".

"Exam Hall" (original poem)
Two hundred chairs face one clock
like sunflowers that have given up on the sun.
The silence is a held breath
nobody is allowed to let go.

I write my name. It looks like someone else's.
The invigilator's shoes
squeak their slow patrol,
a metronome for worry.

Outside, a blackbird
does not know it is June,
does not know about grade boundaries,
sings anyway.

"Results Day" (original poem)
The envelope is thin as an excuse.
Mum stands behind me
pretending to read the fridge.
I peel it open like a plaster -
quick, they say, it hurts less.
Numbers. Just numbers.
And then the kitchen
fills with her shout,
and the dog barks,
and the kettle, for once, is not the loudest thing in the house.

In both poems the speakers describe a stressful experience. What are the similarities and/or differences between the methods the poets use to present these experiences? [8 marks]
questions.answer: Both poets use similes to show anxiety: the chairs 'like sunflowers that have given up' and the envelope 'thin as an excuse', which suggests the speaker expects bad news. Both use sound to build tension: the squeaking shoes in "Exam Hall" and the silence before the mother's shout in "Results Day". However, "Exam Hall" is set in a public, controlled space, while "Results Day" is domestic and intimate, with the mother 'pretending to read the fridge', a gently comic detail showing shared nerves. The endings differ: "Exam Hall" ends quietly with the blackbird singing, while "Results Day" builds through polysyndeton ('and the dog barks, / and the kettle') to a loud, joyful climax. Both endings turn tension into release, but one is reflective and the other celebratory.
ms: Level 4 (7-8 marks): exploratory comparison of both poets' use of language, structure and form, with judicious terminology; convincing comparison of effects on the reader.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): thoughtful comparison of methods with effective terminology; clear comparison of effects.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): relevant comparison of methods with some terminology; some comparison of effects. Level 1 (1-2): simple comments on methods.

Indicative content: Similes (sunflowers, 'thin as an excuse', 'like a plaster'); sound imagery (silence, squeak, shout, kettle); short sentences ('Numbers. Just numbers.'); public vs domestic setting; volta in both; quiet vs loud ending; polysyndeton; humour.
Only AO2 (methods) is credited. Comparing what the poems are about without methods cannot reach Level 3.
questions.tip: Pick two or three methods and compare their effects in depth rather than listing many.

questions.q:
Q27.1 style. Read the poem.

"The Last Bus" (original poem)
It comes round the corner lit up like a lantern,
half empty, half asleep,
its windows full of strangers
who have each been somewhere.

A nurse with her shoes in a bag.
A boy with music leaking from his hood.
An old man holding flowers
as if they might escape.

Nobody speaks. The engine hums
a lullaby in a language
we all understand,
and the city slides past like a dream we share.

In "The Last Bus", how does the poet present a sense of community? [24 marks]
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: The poet presents community as something quiet and unspoken: the passengers are strangers who never talk, yet the shared space and gentle rhythm of the bus join them, suggesting that community can exist in small moments of shared tiredness rather than in conversation.
Plan:
1. Opening simile: 'lit up like a lantern' presents the bus as warm and guiding in the dark city, a symbol of safety. 'half empty, half asleep' (parallelism and personification) gives the bus human tiredness, mirroring the passengers.
2. Individuals: 'who have each been somewhere' suggests every stranger has a story, encouraging empathy. Stanza 2 is a list of three snapshot sentences, like portraits, each with a telling detail (shoes in a bag, music 'leaking').
3. Gentle humour: the old man holding flowers 'as if they might escape' is tender and playful, showing the speaker's affectionate observation.
4. Volta: 'Nobody speaks' could suggest isolation, but the engine's 'lullaby in a language / we all understand' turns silence into connection. The shift to 'we' shows the speaker joining the group.
5. Ending: the simile 'like a dream we share' completes the movement from strangers to a shared experience. Structure: three quatrains move from the outside of the bus, to individuals, to unity. Alternative reading: the community is fragile and temporary, existing only for the length of a journey.
ms: Level 6 (21-24 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised response to the task and the poem; judicious references; analysis of the poet's methods with judicious terminology; exploration of effects on the reader, including more than one interpretation.
Level 5 (17-20 marks): thoughtful, developed response; apt references integrated into the interpretation; examination of methods with effective terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects.
Level 4 (13-16 marks): clear, explained response; effective references; clear explanation of methods with appropriate terminology.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Community, empathy, warmth, shared tiredness; strangers becoming 'we'; fragility of the connection.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Similes (lantern, dream); personification of the bus and engine; listing of portraits; minor sentences; pronoun shift to 'we'; volta at 'Nobody speaks'; sound imagery; regular quatrains.
AO3 is not assessed on the unseen poem and there is no AO4. Do not reward guesses about the poet's life.
questions.tip: Pronoun shifts (I to we) are a precise, high-level structural point. Always look for them.

questions.q:
Q27.2 style. Read "The Last Bus" and "Rush Hour".

"The Last Bus" (original poem)
It comes round the corner lit up like a lantern,
half empty, half asleep,
its windows full of strangers
who have each been somewhere.

A nurse with her shoes in a bag.
A boy with music leaking from his hood.
An old man holding flowers
as if they might escape.

Nobody speaks. The engine hums
a lullaby in a language
we all understand,
and the city slides past like a dream we share.

"Rush Hour" (original poem)
Elbows. Umbrellas. Somebody's coffee
breathing on my neck.
The train is a tin of tired fish
and we are packed in our own oil.
Nobody looks up.
A hundred phones glow like a hundred tiny fires
and none of them is warm.

In both poems the speakers describe travelling with strangers. What are the similarities and/or differences between the methods the poets use to present these experiences? [8 marks]
questions.answer: Both poets use the silence of strangers ('Nobody speaks' / 'Nobody looks up'), but to opposite effects: in "The Last Bus" silence becomes a shared 'lullaby', while in "Rush Hour" it shows isolation. "Rush Hour" opens with blunt minor sentences ('Elbows. Umbrellas.') that create a crowded, aggressive rhythm, whereas "The Last Bus" uses long, flowing lines and gentle sound. The extended metaphor of the 'tin of tired fish' dehumanises commuters, while the portraits in "The Last Bus" individualise them. Both end on a simile: the bus is a shared 'dream', but the phones glow 'like a hundred tiny fires' that are not 'warm', an ironic image of technology giving light without human connection.
ms: Level 4 (7-8 marks): exploratory comparison of both poets' use of language, structure and form, with judicious terminology; convincing comparison of effects on the reader.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): thoughtful comparison of methods with effective terminology; clear comparison of effects.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): relevant comparison of methods with some terminology; some comparison of effects. Level 1 (1-2): simple comments on methods.

Indicative content: Silence used for unity vs isolation; minor sentences vs flowing lines; dehumanising metaphor (tinned fish) vs individual portraits; light imagery (lantern, phones as fires); irony of the final line; pronouns ('we' sharing a dream vs 'we' packed like tinned fish); regular quatrains vs a single short stanza.
Only AO2 (methods) is credited. Comparing what the poems are about without methods cannot reach Level 3.
questions.tip: Notice when both poems use the same device for opposite effects. That is the best kind of comparison.

questions.q:
Q27.1 style. Read the poem.

"Moving Day" (original poem)
The house is a mouth with all its teeth pulled out:
the walls show pale squares where pictures were.
My voice comes back to me from every room
as if the house is learning how to speak.

I find a pencil line inside the cupboard door,
my height at six, my brother's at four,
our names in Mum's slanted hand.
I cannot take the door.

The van is full. The key is in my palm,
small and cold as a coin for the ferryman.
I lock the door. I do not look back.
I look back.

In "Moving Day", how does the poet present the speaker's feelings about leaving home? [24 marks]
questions.answer:
Grade 9 thesis: The poet presents leaving home as a kind of bereavement: the house becomes a body emptied of life and the speaker treats the move almost as a death, but the final contradiction shows the speaker cannot fully let go, so the poem is about the impossibility of leaving the past behind.
Plan:
1. Opening metaphor: the house as 'a mouth with all its teeth pulled out' is violent and uncomfortable, suggesting the emptying of the house is painful. The 'pale squares' are visual traces of absence, like ghosts of memories.
2. Echo: the voice coming back 'as if the house is learning how to speak' is eerie; personification makes the house almost alive, but its only words are the speaker's own, emphasising loneliness.
3. Memory: the pencil height marks are a precise, domestic detail; the full rhyme 'door/four' and the list of names show family history. The short line 'I cannot take the door' is bluntly emotional, showing that what matters cannot be packed.
4. Death imagery: the simile 'cold as a coin for the ferryman' alludes to Greek myth (paying Charon to cross into the underworld), so leaving becomes like dying.
5. Ending: the contradiction 'I do not look back. / I look back.' uses repetition and a final one-line sentence to show that the speaker's resolve collapses; it may also allude to Orpheus or Lot's wife, figures who look back. Structure: three regular quatrains move from the empty house, to memory, to departure, and the final line breaks the pattern.
ms: Level 6 (21-24 marks): critical, exploratory, conceptualised response to the task and the poem; judicious references; analysis of the poet's methods with judicious terminology; exploration of effects on the reader, including more than one interpretation.
Level 5 (17-20 marks): thoughtful, developed response; apt references integrated into the interpretation; examination of methods with effective terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects.
Level 4 (13-16 marks): clear, explained response; effective references; clear explanation of methods with appropriate terminology.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Grief, nostalgia, loss, attachment to family memory, attempted resolve and failure to let go.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Metaphor of the mouth; personification of the house; domestic detail; rhyme; short declaratives; classical allusion; contradiction and repetition in the ending; quatrain structure and final one-line sentence.
AO3 is not assessed on the unseen poem and there is no AO4. Do not reward guesses about the poet's life.
questions.tip: Allusions are worth naming, but always explain how they change the meaning of the line.

questions.q:
Q27.2 style. Read "Moving Day" and "New Flat".

"Moving Day" (original poem)
The house is a mouth with all its teeth pulled out:
the walls show pale squares where pictures were.
My voice comes back to me from every room
as if the house is learning how to speak.

I find a pencil line inside the cupboard door,
my height at six, my brother's at four,
our names in Mum's slanted hand.
I cannot take the door.

The van is full. The key is in my palm,
small and cold as a coin for the ferryman.
I lock the door. I do not look back.
I look back.

"New Flat" (original poem)
Boxes stacked like a city skyline.
I eat cereal from a saucepan,
sit on the floor because the floor is mine.
The radiator clanks its welcome,
the window hands me a slice of sky.
Nothing here remembers me yet.
That is the point.
That is the whole bright point.

In both poems the speakers describe moving home. What are the similarities and/or differences between the methods the poets use to present these feelings? [8 marks]
questions.answer: Both poets personify their homes, but in opposite ways: in "Moving Day" the house is a damaged 'mouth' that only echoes the speaker, while in "New Flat" the radiator 'clanks its welcome' and the window 'hands me a slice of sky', making the new home kind and generous. Both use memory as a key idea: "Moving Day" is weighed down by the pencil marks of the past, while "New Flat" celebrates that 'Nothing here remembers me yet'. Structurally, both end with repetition, but "Moving Day" uses it to show a contradiction and failed resolve ('I look back.'), whereas "New Flat" uses it to build confidence, with the final line expanding into 'the whole bright point'. The regular quatrains of "Moving Day" feel formal and mournful, while the single stanza and casual details (cereal from a saucepan) in "New Flat" feel free and improvised.
ms: Level 4 (7-8 marks): exploratory comparison of both poets' use of language, structure and form, with judicious terminology; convincing comparison of effects on the reader.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): thoughtful comparison of methods with effective terminology; clear comparison of effects.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): relevant comparison of methods with some terminology; some comparison of effects. Level 1 (1-2): simple comments on methods.

Indicative content: Personification in both (hostile/echoing vs welcoming); memory as weight vs freedom; similes (coin for the ferryman vs city skyline); repetition at both endings with opposite effects; form: regular quatrains vs a single loose stanza; tone: elegiac vs hopeful.
Only AO2 (methods) is credited. Comparing what the poems are about without methods cannot reach Level 3.
questions.tip: Both poems use repetition at the end. Compare HOW it works differently - that is a Level 4 point.

questions.q: Paragraph drill. Write one top-band analytical paragraph on the quotation "Come, thick night" (Lady Macbeth, Act 1 Scene 5), focusing on how Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth's relationship with evil. [6 marks]
questions.answer: Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as actively summoning evil rather than simply being tempted by it. The imperative "Come" shows her commanding the darkness as if it were a servant, which reverses the Jacobean expectation that women should be obedient. The adjective "thick" suggests a darkness so dense that it can hide the murder from heaven itself, implying she knows the act is sinful and wants to block God's view. This echoes the Witches' fog and aligns her with the supernatural, which a Jacobean audience, influenced by James I's Daemonologie, would find deeply threatening. Ironically, by Act 5 she needs a light beside her constantly, so the darkness she summoned becomes the thing she fears most.
ms: Topic sentence that answers the focus with a clear idea, not a retelling (1 mark)
Identifies the imperative and explains the power/command it suggests (1 mark)
Zooms in on "thick" (or "night") with connotations, e.g. hiding sin from heaven (1 mark)
Links to the Witches / supernatural (1 mark)
Relevant Jacobean context integrated, e.g. gender roles or witchcraft (1 mark)
Whole-text link or structural echo, e.g. her need for light in 5.1 (1 mark)
questions.tip: Link the quote forward in the play. A structural echo is what lifts a paragraph to Level 6.

questions.q: Paragraph drill. Write one top-band analytical paragraph on the quotation "I have no spur / To prick the sides of my intent" (Macbeth, Act 1 Scene 7), focusing on how Shakespeare presents Macbeth's doubts before the murder. [6 marks]
questions.answer: In his soliloquy, Shakespeare presents Macbeth as a man who understands exactly why murder is wrong yet still cannot let go of the desire. The extended horse-riding metaphor casts his "intent" as a horse with no "spur" to drive it on, suggesting his ambition lacks any moral reason. Since Macbeth is a soldier and a rider, the image sounds natural to him, but it also hints that ambition is an animal force that needs pushing. Because he admits that only "vaulting ambition" remains, the audience sees that the murder will be a free choice, not fate, which makes him more culpable and more tragic. At that very moment Lady Macbeth enters, as if she is the spur he lacked, so Shakespeare's structure answers his doubt with temptation.
ms: Clear argument about Macbeth's doubt or self-awareness (1 mark)
Identifies the extended metaphor of horse riding (1 mark)
Explores "spur" and/or "prick": lack of motive, ambition needing force (1 mark)
Comments on soliloquy revealing his private thoughts (1 mark)
Links to free will vs fate / tragic hero (1 mark)
Perceptive structural point: Lady Macbeth enters as the 'spur' (1 mark)
questions.tip: Notice who enters straight after a soliloquy. Shakespeare's timing is a method.

questions.q: Zoom drill. In the quotation "my dearest partner of greatness" (Macbeth's letter, Act 1 Scene 5), zoom in on the word "partner". Explain its connotations and effect. [3 marks]
questions.answer: "Partner" suggests equality, which was unusual in a Jacobean marriage where the wife was expected to obey. It implies Macbeth sees her as a co-owner of his ambition, so the murder becomes a shared project. Ironically, by Act 3 he shuts her out, so the word marks the high point of a relationship that later breaks apart.
ms: Connotation of equality or shared business (1 mark)
Contrast with Jacobean expectations of marriage (1 mark)
Development: shared ambition, or irony of their later separation (1 mark)
questions.tip: Always give a second layer: how the word's meaning changes later in the play.

questions.q: Zoom drill. In the quotation "There's daggers in men's smiles" (Donalbain, Act 2 Scene 3), zoom in on the word "daggers". Explain its connotations and effect. [3 marks]
questions.answer: "Daggers" connotes hidden, close-range violence, the weapon used to kill Duncan. Placing daggers "in" smiles shows that friendliness can hide murder, linking to the theme of appearance versus reality. It explains why Donalbain flees: in Macbeth's court nobody can be trusted.
ms: Connotation of hidden or treacherous violence (1 mark)
Link to appearance vs reality / deception (1 mark)
Development: link to Duncan's murder or Donalbain's flight (1 mark)
questions.tip: Short quotes from minor characters are great for showing whole-text knowledge.

questions.q: Context drill. Explain how context shapes the way Macbeth describes Duncan's virtues pleading "like angels" in Act 1 Scene 7. [4 marks]
questions.answer: Jacobean audiences believed in the divine right of kings: a king was appointed by God. By comparing Duncan's virtues to angels, Macbeth admits that killing him is an attack on heaven itself, not just a crime. James I, Shakespeare's patron, had survived the Gunpowder Plot in 1605, so the idea of regicide as sacrilege would feel urgent. This context makes Macbeth's later choice more shocking because he fully understands the religious consequences.
ms: Identifies divine right of kings (1 mark)
Explains how the angel simile reflects it (1 mark)
Links to James I / Gunpowder Plot or the Great Chain of Being (1 mark)
Explains the effect on the audience's judgement of Macbeth (1 mark)
questions.tip: Context must explain the quote, not sit next to it. Use 'because' to link them.

questions.q: Context drill. Explain how context shapes the Witches' chant "Double, double toil and trouble" in Act 4 Scene 1. [4 marks]
questions.answer: James I wrote Daemonologie (1597) and believed witches had tried to kill him with storms, so a Jacobean audience saw witches as real agents of the devil. The chant's trochaic rhythm and rhyme sound like a spell, which separates the Witches from the iambic speech of human characters and makes them unnatural. The grotesque ingredients they add to the cauldron would horrify an audience who believed in witchcraft. Shakespeare plays on these fears to make the Witches a genuine threat.
ms: States James I's interest in witchcraft / Daemonologie (1 mark)
Explains witches seen as real and evil by a Jacobean audience (1 mark)
Links the rhythm/chant to unnatural or spell-like effect (1 mark)
Explains effect on the audience (fear, threat) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Do not just say 'people believed in witches'. Say why that changes how this line feels.

questions.q: Paragraph drill. Write one top-band analytical paragraph on the quotation "It will have blood, they say; blood will have blood" (Macbeth, Act 3 Scene 4), focusing on how Shakespeare presents the consequences of violence. [6 marks]
questions.answer: After the ghost leaves the banquet, Macbeth sounds fatalistic, as if violence has a will of its own. The vague pronoun "It" and the hearsay "they say" make the murder seem like a force beyond him, an attempt to escape blame. The repetition of "blood" turns the line into a cycle, where each killing demands another, which foreshadows the murders of Macduff's family. Blood imagery has followed him since 2.2, but here it moves from guilt on his hands to an unstoppable chain of revenge. For a Jacobean audience, this reflects the belief that murdered blood cries out for justice, as Abel's blood does in Genesis, so Macbeth's own words predict his downfall.
ms: Argument that violence becomes cyclical or self-perpetuating (1 mark)
Comments on repetition of "blood" and its effect (1 mark)
Comments on "It" / "they say" as evasion or fatalism (1 mark)
Tracks the blood motif across the play (1 mark)
Foreshadowing of later murders / his downfall (1 mark)
Relevant context, e.g. biblical idea of blood crying out, divine justice (1 mark)
questions.tip: Analyse the small words too ('It', 'they say'). Examiners reward close reading of grammar.

questions.q: Zoom drill. In the quotation "fall'n into the sere, the yellow leaf" (Macbeth, Act 5 Scene 3), zoom in on the word "sere". Explain its connotations and effect. [3 marks]
questions.answer: "Sere" means withered and dried up, like a dead autumn leaf. It shows Macbeth sees his life as having aged and lost its vitality, with no future growth, which links to his "fruitless crown". The natural, seasonal image suggests his decline is as inevitable as winter, presenting a tired, self-aware tragic hero.
ms: Meaning: withered / dried up / dead (1 mark)
Effect: Macbeth's sense of emptiness, aging or loss of purpose (1 mark)
Development: link to seasons and inevitability, or 'fruitless crown' and lack of heirs (1 mark)
questions.tip: If you know an archaic word's meaning, use it. It is precise AO2.

questions.q: Zoom drill. In the quotation "why do you dress me / In borrow'd robes?" (Macbeth, Act 1 Scene 3), zoom in on the word "borrow'd". Explain its connotations and effect. [3 marks]
questions.answer: "Borrow'd" suggests the title of Thane of Cawdor does not really belong to Macbeth and must one day be returned. It starts the clothing imagery that runs through the play: later his kingship hangs on him like a giant's robe on a dwarfish thief. The word foreshadows that his power will always feel stolen and temporary.
ms: Connotation of not owning / temporary / not rightfully his (1 mark)
Links to the clothing imagery motif (1 mark)
Development: foreshadows his illegitimate kingship (1 mark)
questions.tip: Name the motif. 'Clothing imagery' shows you are tracking patterns across the play.

questions.q: Paragraph drill. Write one top-band analytical paragraph on the quotation "He has no children" (Macduff, Act 4 Scene 3), focusing on how Shakespeare presents Macduff's grief. [5 marks]
questions.answer: Macduff's short, blunt sentence shows grief so deep that elaborate language fails him. The line is ambiguous: he may mean that Malcolm, who has no children, cannot understand his loss, or that Macbeth, who has no children, can never be repaid in kind. Either way, Shakespeare presents grief as a natural, human response that contrasts with Macbeth's numbness. Malcolm urges him to "dispute it like a man" but Macduff insists he must "feel it as a man", redefining masculinity as including emotion.
ms: Clear idea about Macduff's grief (1 mark)
Comments on the short, simple sentence (1 mark)
Explores the ambiguity of who 'He' refers to (1 mark)
Contrast with Macbeth or Malcolm (1 mark)
Link to the theme of masculinity (1 mark)
questions.tip: Ambiguity is a gift. Give two readings and say why both are possible.

questions.q: Context drill. Explain how context shapes the Porter's joke about an "equivocator" knocking at hell's gate in Act 2 Scene 3. [4 marks]
questions.answer: In 1606 the Jesuit priest Henry Garnet was tried for his part in the Gunpowder Plot and defended lying under oath as 'equivocation'. A Jacobean audience would recognise the Porter's equivocator as a direct reference to him and to the traitors who tried to kill James I. Placing this joke straight after Duncan's murder links Macbeth to real-life traitors and suggests that, like Garnet, he will be damned. The comedy also releases tension but makes the castle seem like hell, deepening the horror.
ms: Identifies Henry Garnet / the Gunpowder Plot trial (1 mark)
Explains what equivocation means (1 mark)
Links Macbeth to treason and damnation (1 mark)
Comments on the timing / comic relief / castle as hell (1 mark)
questions.tip: Specific context (a name, a date) beats vague context every time.

questions.q: Context drill. Explain how context shapes Lady Macbeth's question "Was the hope drunk / Wherein you dress'd yourself?" in Act 1 Scene 7. [4 marks]
questions.answer: In Jacobean society a wife was expected to be obedient and men were defined by courage and action. Lady Macbeth's mocking question reverses these roles: she challenges her husband's masculinity and suggests his ambition was just drunken talk. A Jacobean audience would see a wife insulting her husband as unnatural, linking her to the Witches. The clothing metaphor also mocks his hope as something he just put on, so she attacks both his manhood and his honesty.
ms: Jacobean expectation of female obedience (1 mark)
Masculinity defined by courage / action (1 mark)
Explains how her question reverses gender roles (1 mark)
Effect on audience: unnatural, threatening, linked to the supernatural (1 mark)
questions.tip: Context should make you see the quote as shocking. Explain the shock.

questions.q: Paragraph drill. Write one top-band analytical paragraph on the quotation "Darkness is cheap, and Scrooge liked it" (Stave 1), focusing on how Dickens presents Scrooge's meanness. [5 marks]
questions.answer: Dickens's short, blunt sentence links Scrooge's meanness directly to darkness. The adjective "cheap" shows that he chooses darkness because it costs nothing, so his love of money controls even his comfort. Darkness also symbolises ignorance and lack of warmth, suggesting his soul is as unlit as his rooms. The narrator's dry, ironic tone invites the reader to laugh at him, but it also prepares for the Ghost of Christmas Past, whose light Scrooge later tries to extinguish.
ms: Clear argument about meanness (1 mark)
Analysis of "cheap" (1 mark)
Symbolism of darkness (1 mark)
Narrator's tone / irony (1 mark)
Link to the wider text, e.g. light of the Ghost of Christmas Past (1 mark)
questions.tip: Comment on the narrator's voice. Dickens's tone is a method in itself.

questions.q: Paragraph drill. Write one top-band analytical paragraph on the quotation "a kind, forgiving, charitable, pleasant time" (Fred, Stave 1), focusing on how Dickens presents the spirit of Christmas. [6 marks]
questions.answer: Through Fred, Dickens presents Christmas as a set of moral values rather than a religious ceremony. The list of four adjectives builds a sense of abundance, as if the season is full of goodness. "Forgiving" is especially significant because Fred forgives Scrooge's rudeness, and "charitable" links directly to the charity collectors who arrive next. Fred is Scrooge's foil: he has far less money than Scrooge yet is happy, showing that Christmas spirit has nothing to do with money. Dickens, writing in the 'Hungry Forties', wanted readers to see Christmas as a time to help the poor, so Fred voices the author's message early in the novella.
ms: Topic sentence on the spirit of Christmas as moral values (1 mark)
Comments on the list/tricolon or listing of adjectives (1 mark)
Zooms in on one adjective with development (1 mark)
Fred as a foil to Scrooge (1 mark)
Context: 1840s poverty, Dickens's purpose (1 mark)
Link to structure (charity collectors / Scrooge's change) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Call Fred a foil and explain the contrast in detail.

questions.q: Zoom drill. In the quotation "The cold within him froze his old features" (Stave 1), zoom in on the word "froze". Explain its connotations and effect. [3 marks]
questions.answer: "Froze" suggests Scrooge's coldness is so extreme that it physically changes his face, making it stiff and lifeless. It shows his inner lack of feeling showing on the outside. This cold imagery is reversed in Stave 5, when warmth returns and he becomes cheerful.
ms: Connotation: stiff, lifeless, unable to move or feel (1 mark)
Inner coldness becoming physical / visible (1 mark)
Development: contrast with warmth in Stave 5 (1 mark)
questions.tip: Track cold and warm imagery across the whole novella.

questions.q: Zoom drill. In the quotation the description of Ignorance and Want as "wolfish" (Stave 3), zoom in on the word "wolfish". Explain its connotations and effect. [3 marks]
questions.answer: "Wolfish" dehumanises the children, presenting them as hungry, wild and dangerous. It suggests poverty turns children into predators if society ignores them, which could threaten the rich. Dickens uses the word to frighten middle-class readers into acting, not just pitying.
ms: Connotation: animal, hungry, wild (1 mark)
Dehumanising effect of poverty (1 mark)
Development: threat to society / purpose of frightening readers into action (1 mark)
questions.tip: Say what the word wants the READER to feel and do.

questions.q: Context drill. Explain how context shapes the Ghost of Christmas Present's revelation of the two children, Ignorance and Want. [4 marks]
questions.answer: In 1843 Dickens read a government report on child labour in mines and factories, and visited a Ragged School in London, and he was shocked by the conditions. Ignorance and Want are allegorical figures representing lack of education and poverty. Dickens believed that ignorance was the greater danger because it trapped the poor and could lead to crime and unrest. He uses the children to persuade middle-class readers that education and charity were urgent duties, not optional kindness.
ms: 1843 child labour report / Ragged Schools (1 mark)
Explains the allegory (ignorance = lack of education, want = poverty) (1 mark)
Dickens's view that ignorance is most dangerous (1 mark)
Purpose: persuading readers to act (1 mark)
questions.tip: Allegory + context + purpose: that combination earns full marks.

questions.q: Context drill. Explain how context shapes Dickens's description of Bob Cratchit earning "fifteen 'Bob' a-week". [4 marks]
questions.answer: Fifteen shillings a week was a low wage for a clerk with a large family in the 1840s, barely enough to survive. Dickens's pun on 'Bob' (slang for a shilling) turns Bob into a symbol of the underpaid worker. As a child, Dickens saw his family fall into debt and was sent to work in a blacking factory, so he understood how low wages trapped families. The detail makes Scrooge's meanness concrete and links it to the struggles of real Victorian workers.
ms: Explains the wage is low for the period (1 mark)
Pun on 'Bob' as slang for shilling (1 mark)
Dickens's own experience of poverty (1 mark)
Effect: makes Scrooge's meanness concrete / social criticism (1 mark)
questions.tip: Concrete numbers in a novel are always a choice. Ask why Dickens includes them.

questions.q: Paragraph drill. Write one top-band analytical paragraph on the quotation "I am as giddy as a drunken man" (Scrooge, Stave 5), focusing on how Dickens presents Scrooge's transformation. [4 marks]
questions.answer: Dickens uses a simile to show that Scrooge has become joyful and carefree. "Giddy" suggests dizziness and excitement, as if he is overwhelmed by happiness. Comparing himself to a "drunken man" is comic because the Scrooge of Stave 1 would never lose control, so the contrast shows how complete his change is.
ms: Identifies the simile (1 mark)
Explains "giddy" (joy / excitement) (1 mark)
Explains the comic effect of losing control (1 mark)
Contrast with Scrooge in Stave 1 (1 mark)
questions.tip: Compare the Stave 5 Scrooge with the Stave 1 Scrooge in every transformation paragraph.

questions.q: Paragraph drill. Write one top-band analytical paragraph on the quotation "a jolly Giant, glorious to see" (Stave 3), focusing on how Dickens presents the Ghost of Christmas Present. [5 marks]
questions.answer: Dickens presents the Ghost of Christmas Present as a figure of abundance and generosity. "Jolly" makes him warm and welcoming, while "Giant" shows that Christmas spirit is larger than Scrooge's narrow life. The alliteration of "Giant, glorious" gives the description energy. He sits on a throne of food, suggesting Christmas is about sharing plenty, which contrasts sharply with Scrooge's gruel in Stave 1. Yet under his robe he hides Ignorance and Want, showing that abundance must not blind people to poverty.
ms: Clear point about abundance / generosity (1 mark)
Analyses "jolly" or "Giant" (1 mark)
Comments on alliteration or the throne of food imagery (1 mark)
Contrast with Scrooge (1 mark)
Link to Ignorance and Want / Dickens's message (1 mark)
questions.tip: The best answers notice the dark side of the jolliest spirit.

questions.q: Zoom drill. In the quotation "Old Marley was as dead as a door-nail" (Stave 1), zoom in on the word "door-nail". Explain its connotations and effect. [3 marks]
questions.answer: A door-nail is a hammered-in nail that cannot be pulled out, so the phrase stresses that Marley is completely dead. The narrator then jokes about the phrase, creating a chatty, comic tone. This certainty makes Marley's ghost more shocking when it appears.
ms: Meaning: completely / undeniably dead (1 mark)
Narrator's comic, conversational tone (1 mark)
Development: sets up the shock of the ghost / supernatural (1 mark)
questions.tip: The opening line sets the tone of the whole novella. Comment on the narrator.

questions.q: Context drill. Explain how context shapes Dickens's presentation of Fezziwig as a generous employer in Stave 2. [4 marks]
questions.answer: In the 1840s many factory owners and businessmen paid low wages and offered no time off or support. Dickens contrasts Fezziwig, who throws a party for his workers, with Scrooge, who resents giving Bob Christmas Day. Fezziwig represents an older, kinder idea of the employer as a father figure. Dickens is arguing that employers in his own time had a moral duty to care for their workers.
ms: Victorian working conditions / low wages (1 mark)
Contrast between Fezziwig and Scrooge (1 mark)
Fezziwig as a paternal, older model of employer (1 mark)
Dickens's purpose: employers' moral duty (1 mark)
questions.tip: Context about employers always links back to Bob Cratchit.

questions.q: Paragraph drill. Write one top-band analytical paragraph on the quotation "If these shadows remain unaltered by the Future" (Ghost of Christmas Present, Stave 3), focusing on how Dickens presents the possibility of change. [6 marks]
questions.answer: Dickens uses the Ghost's conditional statement to show that the future is not fixed and can be changed by human action. The word "shadows" suggests that the visions are only possibilities, not certainties, which gives Scrooge and the reader hope. The capitalised "Future" almost personifies time, preparing for the third ghost. Crucially, the Ghost then throws Scrooge's own words about the "surplus population" back at him, so the responsibility for Tiny Tim's fate lies with Scrooge. Dickens, a Christian writer, believed in repentance and redemption, and the conditional grammar reminds readers that their choices about the poor can still save lives.
ms: Clear argument: the future is changeable / conditional (1 mark)
Analysis of the conditional "If" (1 mark)
Analysis of "shadows" (possibility, not certainty) (1 mark)
Comment on capitalisation / personification of Future, or link to third ghost (1 mark)
Link to Scrooge's own words and responsibility for Tim (1 mark)
Context: Christian redemption or Dickens's purpose for readers (1 mark)
questions.tip: Grammar is a method. 'If' is one of the most important words in the novella.

questions.q: Paragraph drill. Write one top-band analytical paragraph on the quotation "We don't live alone" (the Inspector, Act 3), focusing on how Priestley presents social responsibility. [6 marks]
questions.answer: In his final speech, Priestley uses the Inspector to state the play's socialist message directly. The collective pronoun "We" includes the Birlings and the audience, so the line breaks the fourth wall in spirit, addressing everyone in the theatre. The simple, monosyllabic sentence sounds like a moral law, contrasting with Birling's earlier speech that a man should look after himself. Priestley wrote in 1945, when Britain was voting for a welfare state, so the line urges the audience to see society as connected. The Inspector's short, firm sentences give the message authority before he leaves.
ms: Clear idea about collective responsibility / socialism (1 mark)
Analyses "We" and its inclusion of the audience (1 mark)
Comments on simple, declarative sentence form (1 mark)
Contrast with Birling's individualism (1 mark)
1945 context: welfare state / Labour victory (1 mark)
Comments on dramatic function of the final speech (1 mark)
questions.tip: Always link the Inspector's final speech back to Birling's speech in Act 1.

questions.q: Paragraph drill. Write one top-band analytical paragraph on the quotation "the Germans don't want war" (Mr Birling, Act 1), focusing on how Priestley uses dramatic irony to present Mr Birling. [5 marks]
questions.answer: Priestley uses dramatic irony to make Mr Birling look foolish. The 1945 audience knows that two world wars followed 1912, so Birling's confident prediction is completely wrong. This makes the audience distrust everything he says, including his views on business and responsibility. Priestley is undermining capitalism by making its spokesman unreliable.
ms: Identifies dramatic irony (1 mark)
Explains audience knowledge of WW1 and WW2 (1 mark)
Effect: Birling appears foolish / overconfident (1 mark)
Audience distrusts his other views (1 mark)
Links to Priestley's purpose of undermining capitalism (1 mark)
questions.tip: Dramatic irony needs you to explain what the AUDIENCE knows that the character does not.
