questions.q: Zoom drill. In the quotation the Inspector's stage direction "an impression of massiveness", zoom in on the word "massiveness". Explain its connotations and effect. [3 marks]
questions.answer: "Massiveness" suggests weight, solidity and power, as if the Inspector cannot be pushed aside. It shows his authority comes from his presence rather than his social class. This contrasts with Birling, whose power depends on money and status, so the stage direction sets up a clash between moral and social power.
ms: Connotation: size / weight / immovable power (1 mark)
Authority from presence or moral strength, not class (1 mark)
Development: contrast with Birling's status-based power (1 mark)
questions.tip: Stage directions count as quotations. Use them.

questions.q: Zoom drill. In the quotation Mr Birling's dismissive phrase "community and all that nonsense", zoom in on the word "nonsense". Explain its connotations and effect. [3 marks]
questions.answer: "Nonsense" shows Birling dismissing the idea of community as silly and not worth thinking about. It reveals his selfish capitalist values. Because the Inspector's doorbell interrupts his speech soon after, Priestley suggests that this 'nonsense' is exactly what Birling is about to be taught.
ms: Connotation: foolish, worthless, dismissive (1 mark)
Reveals capitalist / individualist values (1 mark)
Development: structural irony of the Inspector's arrival (1 mark)
questions.tip: Mention the timing of the doorbell. Priestley structures the interruption on purpose.

questions.q: Zoom drill. In the quotation Sheila's ironic description of Gerald as her "Fairy Prince", zoom in on the word "Fairy". Explain its connotations and effect. [3 marks]
questions.answer: "Fairy" connotes fantasy and fairy tales, suggesting Gerald's heroic rescue of Daisy is a story he tells himself. Sheila's sarcasm shows she now sees through the romantic image of upper-class men. It marks her growing maturity: she rejects the fairy-tale role of the grateful fiancee.
ms: Connotation: fantasy / unreal / fairy-tale (1 mark)
Sheila's sarcasm exposes Gerald's self-image (1 mark)
Development: Sheila's maturity / rejection of gender roles (1 mark)
questions.tip: Show how Sheila's language becomes sharper and more ironic as she changes.

questions.q: Context drill. Explain how context shapes Mr Birling's hope of being given "a knighthood" in Act 1. [4 marks]
questions.answer: In the Edwardian period, wealthy businessmen could rise socially by gaining titles, but the old aristocracy, like Gerald's parents, still looked down on 'new money'. Birling wants a knighthood to make his family equal to the Crofts. Priestley shows he cares about status more than morality: he is anxious about scandal because it might cost him the honour. This criticises a class system where respectability was valued above responsibility.
ms: Edwardian class system: new money vs aristocracy (1 mark)
Birling's desire to match the Crofts (1 mark)
Status over morality / fear of scandal (1 mark)
Priestley's criticism of the class system (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use Lady Croft as evidence that Birling is socially insecure.

questions.q: Context drill. Explain how context shapes Mrs Birling's role on the women's charity committee that refuses to help Eva. [4 marks]
questions.answer: Before the welfare state, poor people relied on charities, which often decided who was 'deserving' of help. Mrs Birling uses her power to judge Eva and refuse her because she was offended by her using the name 'Mrs Birling'. Priestley shows charity could be cruel and personal. Writing in 1945, when Labour promised universal benefits and the NHS, he argues that support should be a right, not a favour from the rich.
ms: Pre-welfare state reliance on charities (1 mark)
Idea of 'deserving' and 'undeserving' poor (1 mark)
Mrs Birling's prejudiced judgement (1 mark)
1945 welfare state / Priestley's argument (1 mark)
questions.tip: Context should explain why Priestley chose a CHARITY as one of the links in the chain.

questions.q: Context drill. Explain how context shapes the presence of Edna, the Birlings' maid. [4 marks]
questions.answer: In 1912 many working-class women worked as domestic servants in middle-class homes for low pay. Edna is seen but rarely heard, and the Birlings give her orders without thinking about her. She is a reminder on stage of the working class who serve the family, like Eva. Priestley uses her to show the class divide inside the Birlings' own home.
ms: Domestic service common for working-class women (1 mark)
Edna treated as invisible / given orders (1 mark)
Link to Eva and the working class (1 mark)
Priestley's purpose: class divide visible on stage (1 mark)
questions.tip: Minor characters can make strong points. Edna is Eva's living reminder.

questions.q: Paragraph drill. Write one top-band analytical paragraph on the quotation "Everything's all right now, Sheila" (Gerald, Act 3), focusing on how Priestley presents the refusal to change. [6 marks]
questions.answer: Gerald's line, offered with the ring, shows Priestley's warning that the upper class will return to their old ways as soon as the threat seems to pass. The sweeping pronoun "Everything" ignores the girl's death and their own guilt, reducing a tragedy to an inconvenience. The time word "now" suggests that for Gerald, morality depends on whether they will be caught. By offering the ring, he tries to restore the engagement and the business merger, but Sheila's refusal shows the younger generation's resistance. The phone call that follows proves him wrong, and Priestley's 1945 audience is warned not to return to 1912's complacency.
ms: Clear argument about refusal to change / complacency (1 mark)
Analyses "Everything" (1 mark)
Analyses "now" or the conditional morality (1 mark)
The ring as a symbol (1 mark)
Sheila's contrasting response (1 mark)
Structural irony of the phone call and 1945 audience (1 mark)
questions.tip: Gerald's attempt to reset is the play's biggest warning. Link it to the ending.

questions.q: Paragraph drill. Write one top-band analytical paragraph on the quotation "responsibilities as well as privileges" (the Inspector, Act 2), focusing on how Priestley presents class and responsibility. [6 marks]
questions.answer: Priestley uses the Inspector's balanced phrase to challenge Birling's view of public life. The pairing of "responsibilities" and "privileges" creates an antithesis, insisting that wealth and status come with moral duties. It answers the Birlings' reminders that Birling was Lord Mayor and is still a magistrate: public men, the Inspector implies, owe more to society, not less. The calm, formal register gives the Inspector authority without shouting. In 1945, Priestley was arguing that the upper classes who had benefited from the system should support a welfare state, so the phrase serves as a thesis for the whole play.
ms: Clear argument linking class and responsibility (1 mark)
Identifies the antithesis / balanced structure (1 mark)
Explains the meaning of the pairing (1 mark)
Link to Birling's status (magistrate, Lord Mayor) (1 mark)
Comment on the Inspector's register / authority (1 mark)
1945 context / Priestley's socialism (1 mark)
questions.tip: Short phrases are powerful when you explain their structure. Look for antithesis.

questions.q: Zoom drill. In the quotation Sheila's comment that Eric is "squiffy" in Act 1, zoom in on the word "squiffy". Explain its connotations and effect. [3 marks]
questions.answer: "Squiffy" is a light, slangy word for drunk. It suggests the family treats Eric's drinking as a joke rather than a problem. Later we learn his drinking led to his treatment of Eva, so the playful word hides something serious.
ms: Meaning: slightly drunk / slang (1 mark)
Family's casual attitude / treating it as a joke (1 mark)
Development: foreshadows Eric's later confession (1 mark)
questions.tip: Early hints in Act 1 are foreshadowing. Always say what they set up.

questions.q: Context drill. Explain how context shapes Sheila's promise "I'll never, never do it again". [4 marks]
questions.answer: Priestley wrote the play in 1945, when many young people who had lived through two wars wanted a fairer society, and Labour won a landslide. Sheila represents this younger generation: she accepts responsibility immediately and promises to change. Her repetition of "never" shows sincerity and guilt. Priestley places his hope in the young, contrasting Sheila with her parents, who refuse to change.
ms: 1945 context and the younger generation's desire for change (1 mark)
Sheila representing the young generation (1 mark)
Repetition showing sincerity (1 mark)
Contrast with the older generation / Priestley's hope (1 mark)
questions.tip: Context for Sheila is always about the 1945 young audience.

questions.q: Paragraph drill. Write one top-band analytical paragraph on the quotation "I did nothing I'm ashamed of" (Mrs Birling, Act 2), focusing on how Priestley presents Mrs Birling's attitude to responsibility. [5 marks]
questions.answer: Priestley presents Mrs Birling as defiantly unwilling to accept guilt. The negative statement "nothing" shows her total denial. The word "ashamed" reveals she thinks of morality in terms of shame and reputation rather than harm done to others. Dramatic irony increases the effect because the audience suspects that her refusal to help Eva contributed to the death of her own grandchild. Priestley uses her to represent the upper-class arrogance he wanted to change.
ms: Clear point about denial / refusal of responsibility (1 mark)
Analyses "nothing" or the negative (1 mark)
Analyses "ashamed" (shame / reputation) (1 mark)
Dramatic irony (1 mark)
Priestley's purpose / class criticism (1 mark)
questions.tip: Mrs Birling never changes. Say that clearly and explain why Priestley wants her that way.

questions.q: Paragraph drill. Write one top-band analytical paragraph on the quotation "Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!" (Ozymandias), focusing on how Shelley presents power. [6 marks]
questions.answer: Shelley presents power as arrogant and ultimately empty. The imperative "Look" shows Ozymandias commanding even other kings, and the exclamation adds pride. "Despair" is meant to make rivals feel hopeless before his greatness, but in the poem's context it is deeply ironic: the 'works' have crumbled to nothing, so the only reason to despair is that all power fades. The line is followed by the blunt "Nothing beside remains", a short sentence cut off by a caesura, which destroys the boast. As a Romantic poet who opposed tyranny, Shelley uses the inscription to warn rulers like George III that their power is temporary.
ms: Clear argument about power as arrogant / temporary (1 mark)
Imperative and exclamation (1 mark)
Irony of "despair" (1 mark)
Structure: contrast with "Nothing beside remains" / caesura (1 mark)
Context: Shelley's Romantic opposition to tyranny (1 mark)
Effect on reader (1 mark)
questions.tip: Irony is the key method in Ozymandias. Explain both meanings of 'despair'.

questions.q: Zoom drill. In the quotation "Marks of weakness, marks of woe" (London), zoom in on the word "Marks". Explain its connotations and effect. [3 marks]
questions.answer: "Marks" suggests visible, permanent damage, like scars or stains on people's faces. The repetition shows the suffering is everywhere and unavoidable. The word also echoes "mark" as a verb earlier in the line, so the speaker both notices and is marked by what he sees.
ms: Connotation: scars, stains, permanent damage (1 mark)
Repetition showing widespread suffering (1 mark)
Development: wordplay with 'mark' as noticing (1 mark)
questions.tip: Blake loves repetition with a shift in meaning. Spot it.

questions.q: Paragraph drill. Write one top-band analytical paragraph on the quotation "the hapless Soldier's sigh / Runs in blood down Palace walls" (London), focusing on how Blake presents those in power. [6 marks]
questions.answer: Blake presents those in power as directly responsible for ordinary people's suffering. The soldier's "sigh" is quiet and helpless, but Blake transforms it into a vivid image of blood running down the palace walls, a synaesthetic metaphor that turns sound into visible guilt. "Palace" stands for the monarchy, so the blood suggests the king's hands are stained by sending soldiers to die. The adjective "hapless" stresses the soldier has no control. Writing in 1794, after the French Revolution, Blake may also hint at revolution, where royal palaces really were stained with blood, making this a threat as well as a protest.
ms: Clear argument about responsibility of those in power (1 mark)
Analyses the metaphor of the sigh becoming blood (1 mark)
Analyses "Palace" as symbol of monarchy (1 mark)
Analyses "hapless" (1 mark)
Context: French Revolution / war with France / Blake's radicalism (1 mark)
Alternative reading, e.g. hint of revolution (1 mark)
questions.tip: Give two readings of an image when the poem allows it: guilt and threat.

questions.q: Zoom drill. In the quotation "an elfin pinnace" (The Prelude), zoom in on the word "elfin". Explain its connotations and effect. [3 marks]
questions.answer: "Elfin" connotes something small, magical and childlike, so the boy sees his stolen boat as a fairy-tale vessel. It shows his innocent, playful confidence. This makes the later appearance of the huge mountain more shocking, as the small, magical world is overwhelmed by nature's power.
ms: Connotation: small, magical, fairy-tale (1 mark)
Boy's innocence or playful confidence (1 mark)
Development: contrast with the huge peak (1 mark)
questions.tip: Scale is a big idea in The Prelude: small boat, huge peak.

questions.q: Paragraph drill. Write one top-band analytical paragraph on the quotation "a trouble to my dreams" (The Prelude), focusing on how Wordsworth presents the lasting effect of nature. [5 marks]
questions.answer: At the end of the extract, Wordsworth presents nature's power as something that changes the mind permanently. "Trouble" suggests disturbance and unease rather than terror, showing fear has become a lasting, uneasy thought. Placing it in "my dreams" shows it has entered his unconscious. The ending leaves the reader with the sense that the boy's confidence has been replaced with humility. This reflects the Romantic idea that nature teaches and shapes the human mind.
ms: Clear point about lasting change (1 mark)
Analyses "trouble" (1 mark)
Analyses "dreams" / unconscious (1 mark)
Comments on the poem's ending / structure (1 mark)
Romantic context of nature as teacher (1 mark)
questions.tip: Endings matter. Write about what the poem leaves the reader with.

questions.q: Zoom drill. In the quotation "I gave commands; / Then all smiles stopped together" (My Last Duchess), zoom in on the word "commands". Explain its connotations and effect. [3 marks]
questions.answer: "Commands" is cold and vague, hiding what the Duke actually ordered, which implies he had the Duchess killed. The plural suggests power used casually, as if giving orders to servants. Its vagueness is chilling: he hints at murder without admitting it, showing total control even over his own confession.
ms: Connotation: authority, orders, control (1 mark)
Implies murder / euphemism (1 mark)
Development: vagueness shows his control or chilling detachment (1 mark)
questions.tip: The Duke never says 'murder'. Explain the power of what he leaves out.

questions.q: Paragraph drill. Write one top-band analytical paragraph on the quotation "Looking as if she were alive" (My Last Duchess), focusing on how Browning presents the Duke's control. [5 marks]
questions.answer: Browning presents the Duke as preferring the Duchess as a painting rather than a living woman. The simile "as if she were alive" is chilling because it reminds the reader that she is dead. The painting can be controlled: the Duke draws the curtain and decides who looks at it. This links to Renaissance aristocratic ideas of women as possessions. The dramatic monologue lets the Duke reveal his possessiveness without realising it.
ms: Clear point about control / possession (1 mark)
Analyses the simile and the reminder of death (1 mark)
Painting as something he can control / the curtain (1 mark)
Context: women as possessions in the Renaissance (1 mark)
Dramatic monologue revealing more than intended (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use 'dramatic monologue' and explain what it reveals about the speaker.

questions.q: Context drill. Explain how context shapes Tennyson's line "Some one had blunder'd" in The Charge of the Light Brigade. [4 marks]
questions.answer: In 1854, during the Crimean War, a miscommunicated order sent the Light Brigade charging into Russian guns at Balaclava, and many were killed. Tennyson read about it in The Times. As Poet Laureate, he admits the mistake but keeps the blame vague with "Some one". He focuses on honouring the soldiers rather than attacking the commanders, which fitted his public role.
ms: Crimean War / Battle of Balaclava, 1854 (1 mark)
Miscommunicated order / The Times report (1 mark)
Vagueness of "Some one" (1 mark)
Tennyson's role as Poet Laureate shaping the tone (1 mark)
questions.tip: Context should explain the poet's tone, not just the event.

questions.q: Zoom drill. In the quotation "Dawn massing in the east her melancholy army" (Exposure), zoom in on the word "melancholy". Explain its connotations and effect. [3 marks]
questions.answer: "Melancholy" means deep sadness, so dawn, normally a symbol of hope, arrives as a sad, grey army. It reverses the usual positive meaning of morning, showing that every new day brings only more suffering. The personification also suggests nature is the real enemy, mourning in advance for the soldiers.
ms: Meaning: deep sadness / gloom (1 mark)
Reverses the usual hope of dawn (1 mark)
Development: personification of nature as enemy / mourning (1 mark)
questions.tip: Look for images that reverse what we expect (dawn as an enemy).

questions.q: Paragraph drill. Write one top-band analytical paragraph on the quotation "For love of God seems dying" (Exposure), focusing on how Owen presents the effects of war on faith. [6 marks]
questions.answer: Owen presents war as destroying not only bodies but faith itself. The phrase is ambiguous: it could mean the soldiers' love for God is dying, or God's love for them is dying, and both readings suggest spiritual abandonment. The verb "seems" shows uncertainty, as if even faith has become unreliable. The line comes as the soldiers imagine returning home and find the doors closed, so they lose both home and heaven. Owen, who had trained as a lay assistant to a vicar before the war, increasingly questioned religion after his experiences on the Western Front, and the line reflects that crisis. The pararhyme and slow rhythm make it feel heavy and hopeless.
ms: Clear argument about loss of faith (1 mark)
Explores the ambiguity of the phrase (1 mark)
Analyses "seems" or "dying" (1 mark)
Structural placement / link to the closed doors of home (1 mark)
Context: Owen's religious background and the trenches (1 mark)
Comment on sound, rhythm or pararhyme (1 mark)
questions.tip: Ambiguity + context = Level 6. Give both readings.

questions.q: Zoom drill. In the quotation "spits like a tame cat" (Storm on the Island), zoom in on the word "tame". Explain its connotations and effect. [3 marks]
questions.answer: "Tame" suggests something domestic and safe, so the sea seems harmless and familiar. But the cat 'turned savage', so the word sets up a shock: nature that seems controlled can suddenly turn violent. It shows the islanders' confidence is misplaced.
ms: Connotation: domestic, safe, controlled (1 mark)
Contrast with the cat turning savage (1 mark)
Development: nature's hidden danger / islanders' false confidence (1 mark)
questions.tip: Watch for words that promise safety and then break the promise.

questions.q: Paragraph drill. Write one top-band analytical paragraph on the quotation "King, honour, human dignity, etcetera" (Bayonet Charge), focusing on how Hughes presents the soldier's loss of ideals. [6 marks]
questions.answer: Hughes presents the soldier's patriotic ideals collapsing under the terror of battle. The list moves from the grand "King" to abstract "honour" and "human dignity", then ends with the dismissive "etcetera", which shows these values have become meaningless. The soldier drops them 'like luxuries', suggesting they are things only people far from the front can afford. The bathos of "etcetera" undercuts the language of propaganda. Hughes, writing later about WW1 and influenced by his father's experience at Gallipoli, shows how war reduces soldiers to survival instinct, and the line marks the turning point from thought back to frantic action.
ms: Clear argument about loss of ideals (1 mark)
Analyses the list / its order (1 mark)
Analyses "etcetera" / bathos (1 mark)
Links to propaganda / patriotism (1 mark)
Context: WW1, Hughes's father (1 mark)
Structural position: turning point in the poem (1 mark)
questions.tip: Bathos is a precise term. Use it when a grand list ends in something trivial.

questions.q: Context drill. Explain how context shapes Simon Armitage's "Remains". [4 marks]
questions.answer: "Remains" comes from Armitage's collection 'The Not Dead' (2008), based on interviews with British soldiers who fought in conflicts such as Iraq. The speaker is based on a real soldier suffering from PTSD after shooting a looter. Armitage uses colloquial language to give him an authentic voice. The context shows the poem is about the long-term mental cost of modern war, not the battle itself.
ms: 'The Not Dead' / interviews with real soldiers (1 mark)
Iraq or modern conflict (1 mark)
PTSD (1 mark)
Explains how context shapes the voice or message (1 mark)
questions.tip: Link the colloquial voice to the real soldier behind it.

questions.q: Zoom drill. In the quotation "Sellotape bandaged around my hand" (Poppies), zoom in on the word "bandaged". Explain its connotations and effect. [3 marks]
questions.answer: "Bandaged" brings the language of injury into a domestic scene of a mother removing cat hairs from her son's clothes. It suggests she is already wounded by the separation, or foreshadows his injury or death. The word blends home and war, showing that conflict affects families at home.
ms: Connotation: injury, wound, medical care (1 mark)
Mother's emotional pain / foreshadowing (1 mark)
Development: home and war blending (1 mark)
questions.tip: Weir mixes domestic and military language. Name that blend.

questions.q: Paragraph drill. Write one top-band analytical paragraph on the quotation "never meant to last" (Tissue), focusing on how Dharker presents human power and structures. [5 marks]
questions.answer: Dharker presents human power as something that should be fragile rather than permanent. Near the end she imagines an architect who would 'raise a structure / never meant to last', built from paper instead of brick. The negative "never" is definite, turning impermanence into a deliberate, hopeful choice rather than a failure. This paper structure is set against 'capitals and monoliths' and 'the shapes that pride can make', the solid symbols of human power. The unrhymed quatrains, heavy enjambment and final isolated line ('turned into your skin') mirror this fragile, shifting idea. Dharker's experience of living across cultures and borders suggests that the lines humans draw are artificial, so a gentler, temporary kind of structure is more human.
ms: Clear argument about fragility / temporariness of power (1 mark)
Explains that the phrase describes the deliberately temporary paper structure Dharker imagines, in contrast with the 'monoliths' of pride (1 mark)
Analyses "never" or the tone (1 mark)
Form / structure link, e.g. enjambment or the final isolated line (1 mark)
Context: Dharker's multicultural background, borders (1 mark)
questions.tip: Tissue pairs brilliantly with Ozymandias. Mention it if comparing.

questions.q: Context drill. Explain how context shapes Carol Rumens's "The Emigree". [4 marks]
questions.answer: Rumens wrote about people forced to leave their homelands because of war or oppression. The city in the poem is never named, so it can represent any place exiles have lost. The phrase about the city being "sick with tyrants" suggests political oppression. The context of refugees helps explain why the speaker clings to a bright memory that cannot be taken away.
ms: Exiles / refugees / forced migration (1 mark)
Unnamed city as universal (1 mark)
Political oppression / tyranny (1 mark)
Explains the speaker's attachment to memory (1 mark)
questions.tip: Say why the poem never names the city.

questions.q: Context drill. Explain how context shapes John Agard's "Checking Out Me History". [4 marks]
questions.answer: Agard was born in Guyana, a former British colony, and moved to Britain in 1977. Colonial education taught British history while ignoring Black and Caribbean figures such as Toussaint L'Ouverture, who led the Haitian revolution, and Mary Seacole, a nurse in the Crimean War. Agard uses Creole phonetic spelling to reject Standard English and the authority it represents. The context explains his anger: he is reclaiming an identity that colonial schooling erased.
ms: Agard's Guyanese background / British colonialism (1 mark)
Names a specific figure (Toussaint, Seacole, Nanny de Maroon) (1 mark)
Phonetic spelling / Creole as rejection of authority (1 mark)
Explains how context shapes his anger / identity (1 mark)
questions.tip: Name the figures. Specific context earns specific marks.

questions.q: Zoom drill. In the quotation "full of powerful incantations" (Kamikaze), zoom in on the word "incantations". Explain its connotations and effect. [3 marks]
questions.answer: "Incantations" are magical chants or spells, suggesting the pilot has been brainwashed with patriotic slogans before his mission. It implies the propaganda works like magic, overriding his own thoughts. This makes his decision to turn back more powerful: nature and memory break the spell.
ms: Connotation: spells / chants / magic (1 mark)
Brainwashing / propaganda / Bushido code (1 mark)
Development: the spell broken by memory of nature / home (1 mark)
questions.tip: Kamikaze is about propaganda versus memory. Words like this are the evidence.

questions.q: Context drill. Explain how context shapes the religious imagery in Carol Ann Duffy's "War Photographer". [4 marks]
questions.answer: Duffy was friends with war photographers and was interested in their struggle to record suffering for audiences who did not seem to care. The photographer develops photos 'as though this were a church', like a priest preparing Mass, which shows he treats the images with reverence. The biblical phrase 'All flesh is grass' reminds us of death. The religious context gives his job moral seriousness, contrasting with the indifference of newspaper readers.
ms: Duffy's friendship with war photographers (1 mark)
Darkroom as church / photographer as priest (1 mark)
Biblical allusion and mortality (1 mark)
Contrast with indifferent readers (1 mark)
questions.tip: Religious imagery = reverence. Readers' 'pre-lunch beers' = indifference. Contrast them.

questions.q: Context drill. Explain how context shapes Shelley's use of the sonnet form in "Ozymandias". [4 marks]
questions.answer: The sonnet was traditionally a form for love poetry. Shelley, a Romantic poet who hated tyranny, uses it to write about a cruel king, which is ironic. He breaks the usual rhyme scheme, mixing Petrarchan and Shakespearean patterns, which mirrors the broken statue and the collapse of power. Writing in 1818 under George III, Shelley uses the form itself to suggest that rigid systems of power will crumble.
ms: Sonnet traditionally associated with love (1 mark)
Shelley's Romantic / anti-tyranny views (1 mark)
Broken or irregular rhyme scheme mirroring the broken statue (1 mark)
Link to the political message (1 mark)
questions.tip: Form is context too. Explain what the form traditionally meant and how the poet bends it.

questions.q: Improve this Level 3 paragraph into a Level 6 paragraph: "Scrooge is mean at the start. Dickens says he is 'solitary as an oyster'. This is a simile. It shows he is lonely. In Victorian times many rich people were mean." Then explain three changes you made. [6 marks]
questions.answer: Improved: "Dickens opens the novella by presenting Scrooge's isolation as self-chosen: the simile 'solitary as an oyster' suggests he has sealed himself inside a hard shell, yet oysters can contain pearls, hinting that warmth is hidden within him and preparing for his redemption. This invites the Victorian middle-class reader, who may share Scrooge's indifference to the poor, to see that coldness can be changed." Changes: 1) the opening argues an idea (self-chosen isolation) instead of stating a fact; 2) the quotation is embedded and analysed in layers (shell, pearl); 3) context is linked to the reader and Dickens's purpose instead of being a vague generalisation.
ms: Rewrite opens with an argument, not a description (1 mark)
Quotation is embedded in the sentence (1 mark)
Analysis goes beyond naming the technique, with more than one layer (1 mark)
Context is linked to purpose/reader, not bolted on (1 mark)
Uses precise, ambitious vocabulary (1 mark)
Clearly explains three improvements (1 mark)
questions.tip: Never stop at 'this is a simile'. The name of the technique earns nothing on its own.

questions.q: Write a conceptualised grade 9 thesis statement for the question: "How does Shakespeare present the Witches in Macbeth?" Then explain what makes it conceptualised. [4 marks]
questions.answer: Thesis: "Shakespeare presents the Witches as catalysts rather than controllers: they never tell Macbeth to kill, but by speaking his hidden ambition aloud they expose how easily a man's free will can be seduced, a terrifying idea for a Jacobean audience who believed the devil worked through temptation." It is conceptualised because it argues a big idea (catalysts not controllers), answers 'how' and 'why', links to the whole play, and includes context.
ms: Thesis offers an arguable idea, not a list of points (1 mark)
Engages with how and why, not just what (1 mark)
Includes context or writer's purpose (1 mark)
Explanation shows understanding of 'conceptualised' (1 mark)
questions.tip: A thesis should be something someone could disagree with.

questions.q: Write one comparative topic sentence for an essay comparing how power is presented in "Ozymandias" and "My Last Duchess". [3 marks]
questions.answer: "While both Shelley and Browning expose the arrogance of rulers who believe they control others, Shelley shows that time has already destroyed Ozymandias's power, whereas Browning's Duke is still dangerous because he speaks to us directly."
ms: Names both poems or poets (1 mark)
Identifies a clear similarity (1 mark)
Identifies a clear difference using a comparative connective (whereas, while, however) (1 mark)
questions.tip: Every comparison paragraph should start by naming BOTH poems.

questions.q: Write a conclusion paragraph for an essay on "How does Priestley present responsibility in An Inspector Calls?" Your conclusion must return to the writer's purpose. [4 marks]
questions.answer: "Ultimately, Priestley presents responsibility as a choice that divides the generations: the Birlings' refusal to change shows how easily the privileged can escape guilt, while Sheila and Eric show that change is possible. By ending with the second phone call, Priestley refuses to let his 1945 audience off the hook, warning them that if they return to the selfishness of 1912, history will repeat itself in 'fire and blood and anguish'."
ms: Restates the thesis in new words (1 mark)
Summarises the key contrast in the essay (1 mark)
Returns to the writer's purpose (1 mark)
Links to the audience / context, ending with a strong final idea (1 mark)
questions.tip: A conclusion should answer 'so what?' - why did the writer want us to see this?

questions.q: Explain how to embed context into analysis rather than 'bolting it on'. Use an example from Macbeth to show the difference. [4 marks]
questions.answer: Bolted on: "Lady Macbeth says 'unsex me here'. In Jacobean times women had to obey men." Embedded: "Lady Macbeth's plea to be 'unsexed' would horrify a Jacobean audience who expected women to be obedient, because she is not just rejecting her gender but calling on spirits, which aligns her with the witches James I feared." Embedding means the context explains why the quote matters, in the same sentence, using connectives like 'because', 'which' or 'would'.
ms: Gives a bolted-on example (1 mark)
Gives an embedded example (1 mark)
Explains that context should explain the effect or meaning of the quote (1 mark)
Mentions linking words or the same sentence (1 mark)
questions.tip: If you could delete the context sentence and the paragraph still makes sense, it was bolted on.

questions.q: Explain how to plan a 30-mark Literature essay in five minutes so that it reaches Level 6. [4 marks]
questions.answer: 1) Read the question and underline the focus word (e.g. 'guilt'). 2) Write a one-sentence thesis that argues a concept. 3) Plan 4-5 paragraphs that move through the text in order (beginning, middle, end) so that you show how the idea develops, with the extract used for the first one or two. 4) Jot 1-2 short quotes, a method and a context point beside each paragraph so AO1, AO2 and AO3 are covered in every paragraph.
ms: Identifies the focus / key word (1 mark)
Writes a conceptual thesis (1 mark)
Plans paragraphs that track development across the text (1 mark)
Plans quotes, methods and context for each paragraph (1 mark)
questions.tip: Five minutes of planning saves fifteen minutes of waffle.

questions.q: Give three verbs that are better than 'shows' for analysis, and use one of them in a sentence about A Christmas Carol. [3 marks]
questions.answer: Suggests, implies, exposes (also: reveals, highlights, conveys, emphasises). Sentence: "Dickens's description of Scrooge's 'cold within' implies that his meanness is an inner emotional state rather than just a habit."
ms: Two valid verbs (1 mark)
Third valid verb (1 mark)
Uses one correctly in a relevant sentence about the text (1 mark)
questions.tip: Vary your verbs. 'Shows' ten times in an essay limits your AO1 score.

questions.q: Who says "There's daggers in men's smiles"?
ms: Donalbain says it in Act 2 Scene 3 to Malcolm before they flee, Donalbain to Ireland.
questions.tip: Malcolm and Donalbain are easy to mix up: Donalbain goes to Ireland, Malcolm to England.

questions.q: Who says "Thou hast it now: King, Cawdor, Glamis, all"?
ms: Banquo, in his soliloquy at the start of Act 3 Scene 1, suspects Macbeth 'play'dst most foully' for the crown.
questions.tip: Learn who says it AND when: examiners reward precise placement in the play.

questions.q: Who says "By the pricking of my thumbs, / Something wicked this way comes"?
ms: The Second Witch, Act 4 Scene 1, as Macbeth approaches. Even the Witches call him 'wicked'.
questions.tip: This is a great quote for Macbeth's moral decline: the Witches now see HIM as evil.

questions.q: Which method is used in "Double, double toil and trouble; / Fire burn and cauldron bubble"?
ms: Trochaic tetrameter (stressed-unstressed, four beats) with rhyming couplets makes the Witches sound like a chant or spell, unlike the iambic verse of humans.
questions.tip: Say 'trochaic' and explain the effect: it reverses the normal heartbeat rhythm, so it sounds unnatural.

questions.q: Which apparition tells Macbeth he will not be defeated until Great Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane?
options: A child crowned, with a tree in his hand
ms: The third apparition, a crowned child holding a tree, foreshadows Malcolm's soldiers carrying branches from Birnam Wood.
questions.tip: The tree in the child's hand is the clue: it predicts the camouflage in Act 5.

questions.q: Which method is most prominent in "Hover through the fog and filthy air"?
ms: The repeated 'f' sounds in 'fog' and 'filthy' are alliteration, creating a hissing, murky atmosphere around the Witches.
questions.tip: Name the sound and its effect, not just the technique.

questions.q: In Stave 1, Dickens describes Scrooge as "Hard and sharp as flint". What method is this?
ms: 'As' makes it a simile, comparing Scrooge to a hard stone that only gives off sparks, never warmth.
questions.tip: Flint makes sparks but no lasting fire: a nice extra layer for analysis.

questions.q: Who says "I will not be the man I must have been", promising to learn from the spirits?
ms: Scrooge says it to the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come in Stave 4, promising to change after his contact with the spirits (he calls it 'intercourse', meaning communication).
questions.tip: Old meanings of words matter. Explain 'intercourse' as communication.

questions.q: "Oh! But he was a tight-fisted hand at the grindstone, Scrooge!" Which method best describes this sentence?
options: Third-person omniscient narration with an intrusive, exclamatory narrator's voice
ms: The narrator interrupts with an exclamation and addresses the reader directly, giving a chatty, judgemental voice.
questions.tip: Dickens's narrator is a character in itself: comment on its tone.

questions.q: Which spirit is described as "not so like a child as like an old man"?
options: The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come
ms: The Ghost of Christmas Past looks both young and old, reflecting how memory combines childhood and age.
questions.tip: The paradox of young and old fits a spirit of memory.

questions.q: Who says of Scrooge, "His offences carry their own punishment"?
ms: Fred says it at his Christmas party in Stave 3, showing his forgiveness and pity rather than anger.
questions.tip: Fred's kindness towards Scrooge makes him a model of Christian forgiveness.

questions.q: Who says "the Germans don't want war"?
ms: Mr Birling, Act 1. Dramatic irony: the 1945 audience had lived through two world wars.
questions.tip: Learn who says it AND when: examiners reward precise placement in the play.

questions.q: Who says "lower costs and higher prices" as part of their business philosophy?
ms: Mr Birling, Act 1, when toasting the merger of Birling and Company with Crofts Limited. It sums up his profit-driven capitalism.
questions.tip: Use this to link Birling to capitalism in a single, short quote.

questions.q: Who calls Gerald the "Fairy Prince"?
ms: Sheila uses the phrase sarcastically in Act 2 after Gerald describes rescuing Daisy Renton.
questions.tip: Sarcasm is a sign of Sheila's growing maturity.

questions.q: Sheila says the Inspector is "giving us the rope". What method is this and what does it suggest?
options: A stage direction about the lighting
A metaphor suggesting he lets them condemn themselves
A simile suggesting he is helping them
ms: The metaphor, which Sheila extends into an image of the family hanging themselves, suggests the Inspector lets the family incriminate themselves through their own words.
questions.tip: Link to the Inspector's method: he lets them talk.

questions.q: The doorbell rings just as Mr Birling is telling Gerald and Eric that a man has to look after himself. What is the main dramatic effect?
options: It is a structural interruption: the Inspector arrives to challenge exactly that selfish view
It shows Birling is a good host
ms: The timing is deliberate: Priestley interrupts Birling's individualist speech with the arrival of the character who will dismantle it.
questions.tip: Timing is a method. Explain WHY something happens at that moment.

questions.q: Which poem contains the phrase "lone and level sands"?
ms: The final line of 'Ozymandias'; alliteration emphasises the endless emptiness that has swallowed the king's power.
questions.tip: Endings are the most-quoted lines. Learn them for every poem.

questions.q: Which method is used in "Cannon to right of them, / Cannon to left of them" (The Charge of the Light Brigade)?
options: Anaphora (repetition at the start of lines)
ms: Repeating 'Cannon' at the start of lines is anaphora, creating the sense of being surrounded and building a relentless rhythm.
questions.tip: Say what the repetition makes you feel: trapped, surrounded.

questions.q: Which poem uses the phrase "a huge peak, black and huge", and what method does it show?
options: The Prelude; repetition emphasising nature's overwhelming size
ms: Wordsworth repeats 'huge' to show the boy's shock; the clumsy repetition imitates a child struggling for words.
questions.tip: Repetition can show a speaker's emotional state, not just emphasis.

questions.q: In "Exposure", what is the effect of the collective pronoun in "Our brains ache"?
options: It shows the speaker is dreaming
It shows the speaker is a general
It makes the poem a dramatic monologue spoken by the enemy
It presents the suffering as shared by all the soldiers and draws the reader in
ms: 'Our' makes the experience collective, showing every soldier suffers together, and the present tense brings the reader into the moment.
questions.tip: Pronouns are methods. 'Our' vs 'I' is a precise point.

questions.q: Which poem contains "spools of suffering", and which sound technique is used?
ms: 'War Photographer': the repeated 's' sounds create a hushed, almost reverent tone in the darkroom.
questions.tip: Say what the sound does to the mood.

questions.q: Which poem contains the phrase "probably armed, possibly not"?
ms: 'Remains': the uncertainty about whether the looter was armed is the root of the soldier's guilt.
questions.tip: This short phrase is perfect for any guilt or uncertainty question.

questions.q: In "Kamikaze", the poem is narrated by a speaker reporting what the pilot's daughter said, with her words in italics. What is the effect of this?
options: It shows the poem is a sonnet
It shows the pilot is still alive and speaking
It shows the daughter is the pilot
It creates distance and layers of memory, showing how the family story is passed down and judged
ms: The layered narrative voice shows the story is reconstructed second-hand, emphasising the silence and shame imposed on the pilot.
questions.tip: Ask who is speaking and how many voices there are.

questions.q: Read this original line: "The kettle sulks on the stove." Which method is used?
ms: 'Sulks' gives the kettle a human mood, which is personification; it may reflect the speaker's own mood.
questions.tip: Ask whose feelings the object is really showing.

questions.q: Which sentence uses context most effectively?
options: Shakespeare was born in 1564 in Stratford.
In those days women were treated badly.
Macbeth was written in 1606. Lady Macbeth is evil.
Lady Macbeth's rejection of motherhood would horrify a Jacobean audience who saw women as natural nurturers.
ms: This option links context directly to a moment in the text and explains its effect on the audience.
questions.tip: Context must explain a quote or moment, not stand alone as a fact.

questions.q: In the opening stage directions of An Inspector Calls, which character is described as "her husband's social superior"?
ms: Sybil Birling is "a rather cold woman" and "her husband's social superior": she married into new money from an older, higher-status background, which explains her snobbery.
questions.tip: Do not confuse Lady Croft (who never appears) with Mrs Birling. Lady Croft is Gerald's mother and only mentioned.

questions.q: In Act 1, which character interrupts Birling's account of the strike to ask why the workers shouldn't "try for higher wages"?
ms: Eric challenges his father about sacking the striking workers. It is the first sign that the younger generation questions Birling's capitalist values.
questions.tip: Eric's challenge comes while Birling is telling the Inspector about the strike, before Eric's own part is revealed: use it to show his doubts about his father's values begin early in the play.

questions.q: In Act 2, Gerald says Daisy Renton looked "young and fresh and charming". What does this most suggest about Gerald?
options: He felt sorry for her because she was ill and poor
He was attracted mainly by her looks and youth, so his 'rescue' of her was partly for his own pleasure
He loved her as an equal and planned to marry her
He thought she was too young to be working in a bar
ms: The adjectives focus on her appearance and youth. Gerald presents himself as a rescuer from Alderman Meggarty, but he still treats her as someone who pleases him, and he ends the affair when it suits him.
questions.tip: Avoid calling Gerald simply 'kind' or simply 'a villain'. The best answers show he is both genuinely sympathetic and selfish.

questions.q: Which phrase from the opening stage directions describes Eric?
ms: Eric is "half shy, half assertive": uneasy in his family, hinting at secrets (his drinking and Eva) that come out later. "Rather provincial in his speech" is Mr Birling; "a rather cold woman" is Mrs Birling; "easy well-bred young man-about-town" is Gerald.
questions.tip: Stage directions are Priestley's own words: quote them as Priestley's methods (AO2), e.g. 'Priestley's stage directions present Eric as...'.

questions.q: Outline two things Gerald did for Daisy Renton after he met her, as he describes them in Act 2.
questions.answer: He got her away from Alderman Meggarty, who was pestering her in the bar at the Palace Variety Theatre; he let her live in his friend Charlie Brunswick's empty rooms in Morgan Terrace; he gave her money to live on (including money when the affair ended).
ms: One correct point, e.g. rescued her from Alderman Meggarty at the Palace bar (1 mark)
A second correct point, e.g. moved her into rooms in Morgan Terrace / gave her money to live on (1 mark)
questions.tip: Keep it to what Gerald did. Two vague points such as 'he was nice to her' and 'he helped her' get no marks.

questions.q: Explain how Priestley uses the end of Act 2 as a dramatic climax.
questions.answer: Mrs Birling insists the father of Eva's baby should be "made an example of" and must take the blame. Sheila realises first and tries to stop her, but Mrs Birling carries on. The audience works out it is Eric, so there is dramatic irony: Mrs Birling is condemning her own son. Eric then walks in as the curtain falls, so the act ends on a cliffhanger. Priestley shows how Mrs Birling's judgemental, class-based morality traps her own family, and keeps the audience desperate to see Eric questioned in Act 3.
ms: Identifies Mrs Birling blaming the father / demanding he is punished, ideally with a short quotation (1 mark)
Explains the dramatic irony: the audience (and Sheila) realise it is Eric before she does (1 mark)
Explains the cliffhanger effect of Eric's entrance as the curtain falls (1 mark)
Links to Priestley's purpose, e.g. her hypocrisy/class prejudice rebounds on her family, or the 'well-made play' structure building tension (1 mark)
questions.tip: Name the method (dramatic irony, cliffhanger, act structure). Just retelling what happens caps you at 1-2 marks.

questions.q: Explain how Priestley presents Gerald as having more in common with Mr Birling than with Sheila and Eric.
questions.answer: Gerald is a business ally: Birling hopes the marriage will bring Crofts and Birlings together for "lower costs and higher prices", and Gerald agrees Birling was right to sack Eva. Like Birling he is relieved, not ashamed, when he discovers the Inspector may not be real: he is the one who checks with the police and the Infirmary. In Act 3 he offers the ring back with "Everything's all right now, Sheila", showing he wants things back as they were. He is young, but Priestley places him with the older generation because his upper-class status and business interests make him resist change.
ms: Point on shared business/class interests, e.g. the merger or agreeing with Birling's sacking of Eva (1 mark)
Point on his relief/hoax investigation at the end (1 mark)
Supporting reference, e.g. "Everything's all right now, Sheila" (1 mark)
Explains Priestley's purpose: class and privilege, not just age, stop people changing (1 mark)
questions.tip: Gerald is often wrongly grouped with the 'young'. Strong answers say his age puts him with the young but his class puts him with the old.

questions.q: In Act 3, Sheila tells her parents that it "frightens me the way you talk". Explain what this shows about how Sheila has changed and why Priestley includes it.
questions.answer: Sheila has moved from the giggling, "pleased with life" daughter of Act 1 to someone who judges her parents morally. She is frightened because they are celebrating the possible hoax as if nothing happened, while she knows their actions were still real. Her fear shows she has absorbed the Inspector's message that responsibility does not depend on whether he was a real police officer. Priestley uses her as a model for his 1945 audience: the younger generation who can learn and help build a fairer post-war society, in contrast with parents who stay fixed in 1912 values.
ms: Identifies change from Act 1 (e.g. childish, materialistic, excited by the ring) to Act 3 (1 mark)
Explains why she is frightened: her parents' refusal to accept responsibility once the hoax is suspected (1 mark)
Links to the Inspector's message / her acceptance of collective responsibility (1 mark)
Explains Priestley's purpose with context, e.g. hope in the young, 1945 audience and social change (1 mark)
questions.tip: Do not stop at 'Sheila has changed'. Say what she has changed FROM and TO, and why Priestley wants the audience to notice.

questions.q: Explain three methods the Inspector uses to question the Birlings and Gerald. For each, explain its effect on the characters or the audience.
questions.answer: 1. One line of enquiry at a time: he shows the photograph to one person at a time and takes each character in turn, creating a chain of events and building tension. 2. He interrupts and controls the conversation, "cutting through, massively", so Birling's status gives him no power; the audience sees authority shift from the capitalist to the moral voice. 3. He uses blunt, emotive detail about Eva's death, e.g. "burnt her inside out", forcing the characters (and audience) to face the human cost. Other valid methods: he already seems to know everything and lets characters confess; he refuses to be impressed by Birling's connections; he plays characters off each other (Sheila sees through her mother).
ms: Method 1 identified (1 mark) with explained effect (1 mark)
Method 2 identified (1 mark) with explained effect (1 mark)
Method 3 identified (1 mark) with explained effect (1 mark)
questions.tip: Each method needs an effect. 'He interrupts them' is half a point; 'he interrupts Birling, which strips away his social power' is the full point.

questions.q:
How does Priestley present Gerald Croft as a character caught between the older and younger generations? [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: Priestley makes Gerald the play's most ambiguous character: young enough to feel real sympathy for Eva, but his class and business interests pull him back to the Birling parents, showing that privilege, not age, is what stops people changing.
Plan:
1. Act 1: an "easy well-bred young man-about-town"; the engagement as a business merger ("lower costs and higher prices"); he backs Birling over the sacking. Context: aristocratic Crofts versus new-money Birlings in 1912.
2. Act 2: his confession shows genuine feeling (he is moved by her death and leaves to walk) but also selfishness: Daisy was "young and fresh and charming", he set the terms and ended it. Sheila's mocking "fairy prince" image exposes the power imbalance. Gender context: working-class women's vulnerability.
3. Act 3: he investigates the hoax and offers the ring: "Everything's all right now, Sheila". He reverts to the older generation's relief. Sheila's "It's too soon. I must think." shows she has moved on and he has not.
4. Priestley's purpose: Gerald stands for the upper class Priestley thought would resist the post-1945 welfare state; the final phone call leaves him exposed again, suggesting no one escapes responsibility.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory and conceptualised response; a clear overall argument (thesis) running through the essay; judicious, precise references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; perceptive, convincing links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed response; apt references integrated into interpretation; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.

Level 4 (16-20 marks): clear, explained response; effective use of references to support explanation; clear explanation of the writer's methods with appropriate subject terminology; understanding of effects; clear links between context, text and task.

Level 3 (11-15 marks): some explained response; references used to support a range of relevant comments; explained comments on the writer's methods with some relevant terminology; some identification of effects; some understanding of contextual factors.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: A clear argument about Gerald's in-between position; his journey across all three acts; comparison with Sheila and Mr Birling.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Stage directions describing him; the engagement ring as symbol; his exit in Act 2; his language about Daisy; dramatic irony of his excuse in Act 1 for staying away from Sheila last summer (busy at the works); the structure of the ending and final phone call.

AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: 1912 setting (rigid class system, no votes for women, Titanic, coming war) versus 1945 audience (after two world wars, Labour landslide, welfare state); Priestley's socialism; Edwardian gender expectations. Context must be woven into the argument, not added as a separate history paragraph.

AO4 (4 marks): 4 = high performance (consistently accurate spelling and punctuation, control of meaning, wide range of vocabulary and sentence structures); 2-3 = intermediate (considerable accuracy, general control of meaning); 1 = threshold (reasonable accuracy); 0 = no marks.
questions.tip: Do not retell Gerald's affair in order. Examiners report that plot summary of Act 2 is the main reason Gerald essays stay in Level 3.

questions.q:
How far does Priestley present Eric as a character the audience should sympathise with? [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: Priestley makes Eric deliberately hard to like, a drunk who forced himself on Eva and stole from his father, yet he becomes one of the play's moral voices, so the audience's sympathy grows as he accepts responsibility that his parents refuse.
Plan:
1. Opening: "half shy, half assertive"; hints of his drinking that the family ignore; asking why workers shouldn't "try for higher wages" shows early moral instinct. Sympathy for a neglected son.
2. Act 3 confession: his treatment of Eva is shocking (she did not want him in the house, the drunken threat) and the stolen money shows the irresponsibility of privileged young men. Little sympathy here: Priestley does not excuse him.
3. Family breakdown: "You're not the kind of father..." and "you killed her" to his mother. Priestley shows the upper-middle-class family failing its own children, so blame spreads upward.
4. Ending: like Sheila he refuses the hoax escape; he accepts that what they did was real. Context: the young soldiers of WW1/WW2 who paid for their parents' mistakes; the 1945 audience was invited to trust the young to build a fairer society.
Evaluation: "how far" means a balanced judgement: sympathy is earned, not automatic.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory and conceptualised response; a clear overall argument (thesis) running through the essay; judicious, precise references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; perceptive, convincing links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed response; apt references integrated into interpretation; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.

Level 4 (16-20 marks): clear, explained response; effective use of references to support explanation; clear explanation of the writer's methods with appropriate subject terminology; understanding of effects; clear links between context, text and task.

Level 3 (11-15 marks): some explained response; references used to support a range of relevant comments; explained comments on the writer's methods with some relevant terminology; some identification of effects; some understanding of contextual factors.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: A balanced, evaluative argument answering 'how far'; Eric's behaviour judged across all three acts; contrast with his parents and Sheila.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Stage directions; his late entrance at the end of Act 2; his confession in Act 3; his outbursts at his parents; structure of the ending.

AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: 1912 setting (rigid class system, no votes for women, Titanic, coming war) versus 1945 audience (after two world wars, Labour landslide, welfare state); Priestley's socialism; Edwardian gender expectations. Context must be woven into the argument, not added as a separate history paragraph. Also: drinking culture and the vulnerability of working-class women in 1912.

AO4 (4 marks): 4 = high performance (consistently accurate spelling and punctuation, control of meaning, wide range of vocabulary and sentence structures); 2-3 = intermediate (considerable accuracy, general control of meaning); 1 = threshold (reasonable accuracy); 0 = no marks.
questions.tip: 'How far' questions need a judgement. Saying 'he is sympathetic' without weighing his treatment of Eva will not reach Level 5.

questions.q:
How does Priestley use Mr and Mrs Birling to show the dangers of refusing to change? [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: Priestley presents the Birling parents as a warning to his 1945 audience: secure in 1912 wealth and status, they cannot change even after the Inspector's lesson, and the final phone call shows that refusing to learn guarantees being "taught it" again.
Plan:
1. Birling's capitalist confidence: "like bees in a hive", "community and all that nonsense"; dramatic irony of the Titanic and "the Germans don't want war" undermines his judgement. Context: 1945 audience had lived through both wars.
2. Mrs Birling's snobbery: "a rather cold woman", "a girl of that sort", the demand that the father be "made an example of". Her prejudice destroys her own family's reputation.
3. Their reaction to the hoax: Birling mocks "the famous younger generation"; they care about scandal and the knighthood rather than Eva. Contrast with Sheila: "frightens me the way you talk".
4. Ending: the cyclical phone call. Priestley suggests societies that refuse to change face "fire and blood and anguish": a link to two world wars and his support for the welfare state.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory and conceptualised response; a clear overall argument (thesis) running through the essay; judicious, precise references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; perceptive, convincing links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed response; apt references integrated into interpretation; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.

Level 4 (16-20 marks): clear, explained response; effective use of references to support explanation; clear explanation of the writer's methods with appropriate subject terminology; understanding of effects; clear links between context, text and task.

Level 3 (11-15 marks): some explained response; references used to support a range of relevant comments; explained comments on the writer's methods with some relevant terminology; some identification of effects; some understanding of contextual factors.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Clear argument about refusal to change; both parents covered across the play; contrast with the younger generation.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Dramatic irony; stage directions; Birling's long speeches being interrupted; Mrs Birling's language of class; the cyclical structure and final phone call.

AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: 1912 setting (rigid class system, no votes for women, Titanic, coming war) versus 1945 audience (after two world wars, Labour landslide, welfare state); Priestley's socialism; Edwardian gender expectations. Context must be woven into the argument, not added as a separate history paragraph.

AO4 (4 marks): 4 = high performance (consistently accurate spelling and punctuation, control of meaning, wide range of vocabulary and sentence structures); 2-3 = intermediate (considerable accuracy, general control of meaning); 1 = threshold (reasonable accuracy); 0 = no marks.
questions.tip: Context must serve the argument. Starting a paragraph with 'In 1945 there was a Labour landslide' and not linking it to the Birlings is bolted-on context.

questions.q: Mr Birling tells Gerald and Eric that "the Germans don't want war". Why is this dramatic irony for the first audience in 1945/46?
options: The audience knew two world wars had followed, the first starting just two years after the play is set
The audience knew Birling was secretly German
The Inspector later reveals Birling is lying
Germany had already invaded Britain in 1912
ms: The play is set in 1912. The First World War began in 1914 and the audience had just lived through the Second. Birling's confident prediction is wrong, so the audience distrusts all his opinions, including his views on business and society.
questions.tip: Always explain what the irony DOES: it destroys Birling's credibility so Priestley's audience rejects his capitalist views.

questions.q: Which of these happened after the 1945 Labour election victory and reflects the values Priestley's play supports?
options: The sinking of the Titanic in 1912
The start of the First World War in 1914
Some women getting the vote in 1918
The founding of the National Health Service in 1948
ms: The NHS (1948) was part of the welfare state built after Labour's 1945 landslide: a system based on collective responsibility, the idea the Inspector argues for.
questions.tip: Use 1945 context to explain why the audience was ready for the Inspector's message, not as a random fact.

questions.q: Eva Smith later calls herself "Daisy Renton". What interpretation do many critics give of the surname "Renton"?
options: It suggests 'rent': she is used and paid for by Gerald, like something rented
It means she was a famous actress
It shows she was related to the Crofts
It is the name of her home town
ms: "Renton" can suggest renting: Gerald provides rooms and money and then ends the arrangement. A daisy is also a common, fragile flower, suggesting innocence and ordinariness.
questions.tip: Present name interpretations tentatively ('this could suggest'). Stating them as fact weakens AO1.

questions.q: In Act 1 the Inspector tells Birling it is better to "ask for the earth" than to take it. What does he mean?
options: Nobody should ever ask for a pay rise
Birling should buy more land for his factory
Workers asking for fair wages is far less wrong than the rich taking everything for themselves
Eva should have been content with her low wages
ms: Birling complains that the strikers asked for too much. The Inspector turns this around: the real greed belongs to employers who take the profits. It is a socialist challenge to Birling's values.
questions.tip: Short Inspector lines often carry Priestley's message. Explain the reversal he creates, not just the literal meaning.

questions.q: Explain the dramatic significance of the moment the Inspector arrives in Act 1.
questions.answer: Birling is lecturing Gerald and Eric that a man should look after himself and his own, mocking ideas of community as "like bees in a hive". At that moment the doorbell rings sharply and the Inspector arrives. The timing suggests the Inspector has come to challenge exactly this selfish philosophy. The lighting changes from "pink and intimate" to "brighter and harder", showing the family's comfortable illusions are about to be exposed. Priestley uses the interruption to show Birling's power being cut off, which happens repeatedly through the play.
ms: Identifies what Birling is saying just before (selfish individualism / mocking community) (1 mark)
Explains that the interruption/timing challenges Birling's views (1 mark)
Refers to the change in lighting or the sharp doorbell as a staging method (1 mark)
Links to Priestley's purpose: the Inspector as a counter-voice to capitalism / start of the moral exposure (1 mark)
questions.tip: Treat it as a play: refer to staging (sound, lighting, entrance), not just words. Examiners reward awareness of performance.

questions.q: Explain how Priestley presents the contrast between public respectability and private behaviour in An Inspector Calls.
questions.answer: The Birlings appear respectable: Birling is a former Lord Mayor and magistrate hoping for the Honours List, and Mrs Birling chairs the Brumley Women's Charity Organisation. In private, each has harmed Eva: Birling sacked her for asking for fair pay, and Mrs Birling refused her charity out of prejudice. Eric drinks heavily and steals, and Gerald keeps a mistress, while the family worries most about "scandal". Even the setting is "heavily comfortable, but not cosy", wealth without warmth. Priestley exposes the hypocrisy of the Edwardian middle class, whose reputation hid exploitation.
ms: Identifies a public role, e.g. Lord Mayor/magistrate, charity chair (1 mark)
Identifies private behaviour that contradicts it (1 mark)
Supporting reference or staging detail (1 mark)
Explains Priestley's purpose: hypocrisy of the respectable middle class (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use the theme word 'hypocrisy' and tie it to a named character's public role. General comments about 'rich people' stay vague.

questions.q: Explain how the Inspector's final speech uses rhetorical methods to deliver Priestley's message. Give three methods.
questions.answer: 1. Inclusive pronoun and short declaratives: "We don't live alone" and "We are responsible for each other" make the message apply to everyone, including the audience. 2. Repetition: "millions and millions" of Eva Smiths and John Smiths turns one girl into all working people. 3. Tricolon and prophetic warning: "fire and blood and anguish" foreshadows both world wars for the 1945 audience. The speech works almost like a sermon to the audience.
ms: One method with a correct example and effect (1 mark)
A second method with example and effect (1 mark)
A third method with example and effect (1 mark)
questions.tip: Label the technique AND say why it works on an audience. 'There is repetition' alone gets nothing.

questions.q: Explain how Priestley uses and then breaks the conventions of the detective ('whodunnit') genre in An Inspector Calls.
questions.answer: It looks like a detective play: an inspector arrives, questions suspects one by one and uncovers clues (the photograph, the diary), building suspense with cliffhanger act endings. But Priestley breaks the genre: the 'crime' is not one murder by one person but a chain of events in which everyone shares the blame, the Inspector already seems to know the answers, and the ending refuses a neat solution: the Inspector may not be real and a new phone call starts it all again. The audience is pushed from asking 'who did it?' to asking 'what is my responsibility?', which is Priestley's moral purpose.
ms: Identifies detective conventions used (inspector, interrogation, clues, suspense) (1 mark)
Explains one way the conventions are broken (shared guilt / Inspector already knows) (1 mark)
Explains the unresolved/cyclical ending as a further break (1 mark)
Explains the purpose: moves the audience from solving a crime to questioning their own responsibility (1 mark)
questions.tip: Genre terms earn credit only when linked to Priestley's message. Name the convention, then explain what breaking it achieves.

questions.q: Give two different interpretations of who or what Inspector Goole is. Explain how each one affects the play's message.
questions.answer: 1. Priestley's mouthpiece / a symbol of conscience: he speaks for socialism and collective responsibility, so whether he is a real policeman does not matter; the message is what counts. 2. A supernatural or time figure: "Goole" sounds like "ghoul", he seems to know the future, and Priestley was interested in theories of time (such as J.W. Dunne's). On this reading he is a warning from the future, giving the family a second chance that the final phone call tests. Either way, the characters who focus only on whether he was real (Mr and Mrs Birling, Gerald) miss the point.
ms: First interpretation identified (1 mark) with its effect on the message explained (1 mark)
Second interpretation identified (1 mark) with its effect on the message explained (1 mark)
questions.tip: Offer interpretations tentatively ('perhaps', 'could be read as'). Grade 9 answers keep more than one reading open.

questions.q:
How does Priestley present the ways the Birling family try to protect their reputation? [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: Priestley shows that the Birlings value reputation above morality: their first instinct is always to hide, deny or buy their way out, and this obsession with appearances exposes the hollowness of Edwardian middle-class respectability.
Plan:
1. Status in Act 1: Birling's knighthood hopes, his time as Lord Mayor, his attempts to impress the Inspector with names (the Chief Constable). The setting is "heavily comfortable, but not cosy".
2. Denial and cover-up: Mrs Birling claims "I accept no blame for it"; Birling wants the theft hushed up and offers "I'd give thousands". The Inspector's reply undercuts money as a solution.
3. Act 3 hoax: Gerald and Birling investigate the Inspector rather than their behaviour; Birling's main worry is public scandal. Contrast with Sheila and Eric, who refuse to pretend.
4. Ending: the final phone call shows reputation cannot shield them. Context: Priestley attacking a class system that hid exploitation; the post-war audience's wish for an honest, fairer society.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory and conceptualised response; a clear overall argument (thesis) running through the essay; judicious, precise references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; perceptive, convincing links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed response; apt references integrated into interpretation; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.

Level 4 (16-20 marks): clear, explained response; effective use of references to support explanation; clear explanation of the writer's methods with appropriate subject terminology; understanding of effects; clear links between context, text and task.

Level 3 (11-15 marks): some explained response; references used to support a range of relevant comments; explained comments on the writer's methods with some relevant terminology; some identification of effects; some understanding of contextual factors.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Argument about reputation versus morality; covers several family members and the whole play; contrast between generations.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Stage directions on setting and character; dialogue showing denial; Birling's interrupted speeches; dramatic irony; the cyclical ending.

AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: 1912 setting (rigid class system, no votes for women, Titanic, coming war) versus 1945 audience (after two world wars, Labour landslide, welfare state); Priestley's socialism; Edwardian gender expectations. Context must be woven into the argument, not added as a separate history paragraph. Also: the importance of respectability and honours to the Edwardian middle class.

AO4 (4 marks): 4 = high performance (consistently accurate spelling and punctuation, control of meaning, wide range of vocabulary and sentence structures); 2-3 = intermediate (considerable accuracy, general control of meaning); 1 = threshold (reasonable accuracy); 0 = no marks.
questions.tip: A list of 'Birling cares about reputation, Mrs Birling cares about reputation...' is repetitive. Build an argument that develops, ideally ending with how the young reject it.

questions.q:
How does Priestley use the ending of An Inspector Calls to explore whether people are able to change? [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: Priestley's ending divides the characters into those who change and those who refuse, then uses the final phone call to suggest that change is a choice everyone, including the audience, must keep making.
Plan:
1. The hoax discovery: Gerald and Birling's relief; Birling mocks "the famous younger generation". Change, for them, was only fear of scandal.
2. Sheila and Eric refuse to return to normal: "It's too soon. I must think."; "frightens me the way you talk". Priestley's hope lies in the young.
3. Structure: the phone call announcing a girl has died and an inspector is on his way creates a cyclical structure. Dramatic tension is reset; the audience realises the lesson will be repeated until learned.
4. Context: the Inspector's warning of "fire and blood and anguish" links to the wars the 1945 audience had lived through; Priestley's socialism and the welfare state offered a chance to change as a society.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory and conceptualised response; a clear overall argument (thesis) running through the essay; judicious, precise references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; perceptive, convincing links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed response; apt references integrated into interpretation; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.

Level 4 (16-20 marks): clear, explained response; effective use of references to support explanation; clear explanation of the writer's methods with appropriate subject terminology; understanding of effects; clear links between context, text and task.

Level 3 (11-15 marks): some explained response; references used to support a range of relevant comments; explained comments on the writer's methods with some relevant terminology; some identification of effects; some understanding of contextual factors.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Clear argument about change as a choice; covers both the hoax section and the final twist; distinguishes characters.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Cyclical structure; the final phone call; stage directions in Act 3; contrasting dialogue between generations; dramatic irony.

AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: 1912 setting (rigid class system, no votes for women, Titanic, coming war) versus 1945 audience (after two world wars, Labour landslide, welfare state); Priestley's socialism; Edwardian gender expectations. Context must be woven into the argument, not added as a separate history paragraph.

AO4 (4 marks): 4 = high performance (consistently accurate spelling and punctuation, control of meaning, wide range of vocabulary and sentence structures); 2-3 = intermediate (considerable accuracy, general control of meaning); 1 = threshold (reasonable accuracy); 0 = no marks.
questions.tip: Write about the ending as a METHOD (structure and its effect on the audience). Explaining only what happens in the last pages is retelling.

questions.q:
How does Priestley use dramatic devices to criticise the attitudes of the upper and middle classes in An Inspector Calls? [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: Priestley turns the theatre itself against the comfortable classes: lighting, timing, irony and structure all work to expose the Birlings' attitudes so that the audience judges them.
Plan:
1. Setting and lighting: "heavily comfortable, but not cosy"; lighting from "pink and intimate" to "brighter and harder" as the truth is exposed.
2. Dramatic irony: the Titanic and "the Germans don't want war" make Birling's capitalist confidence ridiculous to a 1945 audience.
3. The Inspector's entrances and interruptions: he arrives as Birling mocks community, and cuts through his speeches "massively"; the end of Act 2 uses irony against Mrs Birling.
4. Structure: one-character-at-a-time questioning creates a chain of events; the cyclical ending denies the family an escape. Context: Priestley's socialism and Edwardian class hierarchy.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory and conceptualised response; a clear overall argument (thesis) running through the essay; judicious, precise references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; perceptive, convincing links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed response; apt references integrated into interpretation; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.

Level 4 (16-20 marks): clear, explained response; effective use of references to support explanation; clear explanation of the writer's methods with appropriate subject terminology; understanding of effects; clear links between context, text and task.

Level 3 (11-15 marks): some explained response; references used to support a range of relevant comments; explained comments on the writer's methods with some relevant terminology; some identification of effects; some understanding of contextual factors.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: A clear argument that the devices serve Priestley's criticism of class; range of devices across the whole play.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Stage directions, lighting, entrances and exits, dramatic irony, cliffhangers, cyclical structure, the Inspector as dramatic device.

AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: 1912 setting (rigid class system, no votes for women, Titanic, coming war) versus 1945 audience (after two world wars, Labour landslide, welfare state); Priestley's socialism; Edwardian gender expectations. Context must be woven into the argument, not added as a separate history paragraph.

AO4 (4 marks): 4 = high performance (consistently accurate spelling and punctuation, control of meaning, wide range of vocabulary and sentence structures); 2-3 = intermediate (considerable accuracy, general control of meaning); 1 = threshold (reasonable accuracy); 0 = no marks.
questions.tip: Avoid a device-by-device list with no argument. Every paragraph should say what class attitude the device exposes.
