questions.q: Ozymandias: How many voices can the reader hear in the poem?
options: Four: the speaker, the traveller, the sculptor and Ozymandias
Three: the speaker, the traveller and Ozymandias (through the inscription)
ms: The speaker ("I met a traveller") reports the traveller's words, and the traveller quotes Ozymandias's inscription. The sculptor is described but never speaks.
questions.tip: The layered voices distance us from Ozymandias: his power reaches us only second-hand, which is part of Shelley's point.

questions.q: Ozymandias: In "The hand that mocked them, and the heart that fed", whose hand and whose heart are meant?
options: The sculptor's hand and the king's heart
The traveller's hand and the speaker's heart
The king's hand and the sculptor's heart
The king's hand and the king's heart
ms: The sculptor's hand 'mocked' (copied and also ridiculed) the king's passions; the king's heart 'fed' them. The artist outlives the tyrant by recording his cruelty.
questions.tip: 'Mocked' has a double meaning (imitated / ridiculed). Explaining both meanings is a quick route to Level 5+ analysis.

questions.q: Ozymandias: Explain how Shelley uses the final line, "The lone and level sands stretch far away", to present ideas about power.
questions.answer: The empty desert is all that surrounds the "colossal Wreck". The alliteration of "lone and level" creates a flat, slow sound that mirrors the endless, featureless sand. "Stretch far away" suggests vast distance and time, making the king's ambition seem tiny. Ending on nature rather than the statue shows that time and nature outlast human power, so the king's boast is ironic.
ms: Identifies the image of emptiness / the desert surrounding the ruin (1 mark)
Comments on a method, e.g. alliteration of 'lone and level' or the long vowel sounds (1 mark)
Explains the effect of vastness of space/time (1 mark)
Links to the message: nature and time outlast human power (1 mark)
questions.tip: Don't just say 'it shows power doesn't last'. Show HOW the sound and the position as the last line create that idea.

questions.q: Ozymandias: Explain the irony in the inscription "Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!"
questions.answer: Ozymandias meant other rulers to despair because they could never match his great works. The imperative "Look" and the exclamation show his arrogance. But the next line is "Nothing beside remains": the works have vanished. Now the 'Mighty' should despair for a different reason: because all their power will also crumble. The short caesura-broken sentence after the boast makes the collapse sudden. Shelley uses this reversal to mock tyrants, including the rulers of his own time.
ms: Explains what Ozymandias originally meant (1 mark)
Comments on the language of command/arrogance (1 mark)
Explains the reversal created by 'Nothing beside remains' (1 mark)
Explains the new meaning / Shelley's purpose (1 mark)
questions.tip: Irony answers must explain BOTH meanings: what was intended and what it now means. One meaning only is half the answer.

questions.q: Ozymandias: Explain how Shelley's context as a Romantic and political radical shapes the message of the poem. Refer to the poem in your answer.
questions.answer: Shelley was a Romantic who opposed tyranny and the monarchy of his day (George III and the Regency). He writes about an ancient Egyptian king, but the "sneer of cold command" fits any oppressive ruler. Romantic poets valued nature over human creation: the "lone and level sands" outlast the king. The poem also celebrates the artist: the sculptor "well those passions read", suggesting art and truth survive while tyrants fall. The broken sonnet form, mixing rhyme patterns, could reflect Shelley's rejection of rules. The poem was written in 1817 in a sonnet competition with his friend Horace Smith and published in 1818. Together these show a warning to the powerful: all tyranny is temporary.
ms: Accurate context: Shelley's radical/anti-monarchy views (1 mark)
Linked to a reference about the tyrant, e.g. 'sneer of cold command' (1 mark)
Accurate Romantic context: nature's power over humans (1 mark)
Linked to a reference, e.g. 'lone and level sands' (1 mark)
Point on art/the sculptor or form as rebellion with reference (1 mark)
Overall explanation of the message as a warning to the powerful (1 mark)
questions.tip: Bolted-on context ('Shelley was born in 1792') earns nothing. Every context fact must explain a quotation.

questions.q: London: In which collection did William Blake publish 'London'?
ms: 'London' is in Songs of Experience (1794), Blake's poems about a corrupted, fallen world, paired against Songs of Innocence.
questions.tip: Lyrical Ballads is Wordsworth and Coleridge. Mixing up Romantic poets loses AO3 credibility.

questions.q: London: What is the main effect of the repeated "every" in "In every cry of every Man" and the next line "In every infant's cry of fear"?
options: It shows the speaker is exaggerating for comedy
It shows only children suffer in London
It shows suffering is universal: no one in London escapes it
It creates a cheerful, regular rhythm
ms: The anaphora ('In every...') and repetition of 'every' builds an overwhelming list: men, infants, all voices. Suffering is everywhere and inescapable.
questions.tip: Name the technique (anaphora/repetition) and the effect (inescapable suffering). Don't just say 'it emphasises'.

questions.q: London: Explain the effect of the word "chartered" in the opening lines.
questions.answer: "Chartered" means mapped out, owned and controlled by law and commerce. Even the streets and the natural river Thames are owned, suggesting people and nature are controlled by the wealthy and powerful. A charter can also be a document granting rights or freedoms, so the word is ironic: London's people have no real freedom. The repetition ("chartered street" and "chartered Thames") stresses that control covers everything, man-made and natural.
ms: Meaning: owned/mapped/controlled (1 mark)
Effect: even nature (the Thames) is controlled by those in power (1 mark)
Second meaning: charters grant rights, so the word is ironic (1 mark)
Comments on the repetition and its effect (1 mark)
questions.tip: Single-word analysis is gold, but explain more than one meaning. 'Chartered means controlled' alone is a Level 3 comment.

questions.q: London: Explain how Blake criticises the Church and the monarchy in the third stanza.
questions.answer: Blake links the "Chimney-sweeper's cry" to the "blackening Church": the soot-blackened buildings suggest the Church is morally stained because it ignores child labour. "Appals" can mean both 'shocks' and 'covers like a pall (a funeral cloth)', so the Church is both horrified and guilty. "The hapless Soldier's sigh / Runs in blood down Palace walls" suggests soldiers die for the monarchy; the image of blood on the palace blames the royal family. With the French Revolution (1789) in mind, the image may also warn of revolution against rulers.
ms: Explains the Church criticism linked to child chimney sweeps (1 mark)
Analyses a word, e.g. 'blackening' or 'appals' (1 mark)
Explains the monarchy criticism through the soldier's blood on 'Palace walls' (1 mark)
Relevant context, e.g. French Revolution or child labour, linked to the image (1 mark)
questions.tip: Blake criticises INSTITUTIONS, not just 'rich people'. Name the Church and the monarchy precisely.

questions.q: London: Explain how Blake uses the final stanza to present a society that corrupts life from birth to death.
questions.answer: The final stanza opens "But most through midnight streets I hear", so it is the climax. The "youthful Harlot's curse" shows young women forced into prostitution by poverty. Her curse "Blasts the new-born Infant's tear", suggesting disease (such as sexually transmitted infection) passed to babies, so life is ruined from birth. The oxymoron "Marriage hearse" joins a beginning (marriage) with death (a hearse): even love and family are poisoned. The stanza moves from birth to marriage to death, showing the whole cycle of life corrupted. The harsh plosives ("Blasts", "blights") make the anger audible. Blake suggests a society that exploits the poor destroys every stage of life.
ms: Identifies the stanza as a climax ('most') (1 mark)
Explains the harlot as a victim of poverty (1 mark)
Explains the infant image as corruption from birth (1 mark)
Analyses the oxymoron 'Marriage hearse' (1 mark)
Comments on sound, e.g. plosives 'Blasts'/'blights' (1 mark)
Explains the overall idea of life corrupted from birth to death (1 mark)
questions.tip: Avoid moral judgement of the 'Harlot'. Blake presents her as a victim of the system, and saying so shows sensitive reading.

questions.q: My Last Duchess: Who is the Duke speaking to?
options: An envoy (agent) of a Count, arranging the Duke's next marriage
ms: The silent listener represents a Count whose daughter the Duke plans to marry. This makes the monologue a chilling warning about how the next wife must behave.
questions.tip: Remember the listener: it turns the poem from a memory into a threat aimed at the next Duchess.

questions.q: My Last Duchess: What is most strongly implied by "I gave commands; / Then all smiles stopped together"?
options: The Duchess died of grief after a quarrel
The Duke ordered the painter to stop painting her smile
The Duchess stopped smiling because she missed her family
The Duke had the Duchess killed or silenced because she smiled at others
ms: The Duke's cold, brief statement, with the caesura after 'commands', implies he ordered her death. The euphemism makes it more sinister.
questions.tip: Never read this poem as grief or loving memory. Examiners flag 'the Duke misses his wife' as a basic misreading.

questions.q: My Last Duchess: Explain what "The curtain I have drawn for you" reveals about the Duke.
questions.answer: The Duke keeps the portrait behind a curtain that only he opens (no one draws back "The curtain I have drawn for you, but I"). This shows his need for control: in life the Duchess smiled at everyone, but now he decides who sees her smile. The painting turns her into a possession he can display like art. The emphasis on "I" at the line ending shows his ego and possessiveness. It suggests his jealousy and his view of women as objects.
ms: Explains that only the Duke opens the curtain (1 mark)
Links this to control over the Duchess (1 mark)
Explains the painting as a possession/object (1 mark)
Comments on a method, e.g. the stress on 'I' or enjambment (1 mark)
questions.tip: Link the curtain to the CHANGE: in life he couldn't control her smiles; in death he can. That contrast lifts the answer.

questions.q: My Last Duchess: Explain how Browning uses the final lines, where the Duke points out a statue of Neptune "Taming a sea-horse", to reveal the Duke's character.
questions.answer: The Duke moves straight from hinting at his wife's death to showing off another piece of art, which shows how little she matters to him. The statue shows Neptune, god of the sea, "Taming a sea-horse": a powerful male controlling a wild creature, which mirrors how the Duke tamed (and destroyed) his wife. He also boasts it was cast in bronze "for me", stressing ownership. Ending on this object warns the envoy, and the next Duchess, that she will also be 'tamed'.
ms: Comments on the Duke's casual shift to another artwork (1 mark)
Explains the symbolism of taming a sea-horse (male power/control) (1 mark)
Links to the Duke's treatment of the Duchess (1 mark)
Explains the warning to the envoy/next wife or the possessive 'for me' (1 mark)
questions.tip: The ending is a method (structure). Say WHY Browning ends there, not just what the Duke says.

questions.q: My Last Duchess: A student writes: "The Duke is a grieving husband remembering his lost wife." Explain why this is a misreading. Use evidence and comment on Browning's methods.
questions.answer: The Duke is not grieving; he is boasting and justifying himself. Evidence: he resents that she was "too soon made glad" and that her looks went everywhere, treating her friendliness as disloyalty. He is angry she ranked his "nine-hundred-years-old name" with anybody's gift, showing pride in status above love. He refuses to discuss it with her: "I choose / Never to stoop". "I gave commands; / Then all smiles stopped together" suggests he had her killed. Methods: the dramatic monologue lets him reveal more than he intends (dramatic irony); the rhyming couplets show his control, but heavy enjambment suggests his anger spilling over. He then moves straight on to the dowry and a bronze statue. Browning presents jealousy, pride and the abuse of patriarchal power.
ms: States the correct reading: pride/jealousy, not grief (1 mark)
Evidence of jealousy of her smiles/friendliness (1 mark)
Evidence of pride in status, e.g. 'nine-hundred-years-old name' (1 mark)
Evidence that he ordered her death ('I gave commands') (1 mark)
Method: dramatic monologue / dramatic irony revealing more than he intends (1 mark)
Method: form (couplets and enjambment) or the shift to the dowry/statue (1 mark)
questions.tip: Reading the poem as grief or love is a common, costly misreading. Anchor every point in the Duke's jealousy and need for control.

questions.q: Storm on the Island: Which pronoun is used throughout to present a community facing the storm together?
ms: 'We' presents a collective island community preparing and enduring together, starting with 'We are prepared'.
questions.tip: Use the pronoun to discuss community and shared vulnerability, not just 'the speaker'.

questions.q: Storm on the Island: Heaney writes that the sea "spits like a tame cat" that has "Turned savage". What is the main effect?
options: Personification: the sea is friendly company
Metaphor: the sea is calm and gentle
Simile: something familiar and safe suddenly becomes dangerous
ms: The simile takes a domestic, 'tame' animal and makes it 'savage': nature that seemed harmless can turn on the islanders without warning.
questions.tip: Comment on the enjambment too: 'Turned savage' arrives on the next line, enacting the sudden switch.

questions.q: Storm on the Island: Explain how Heaney uses military language, such as "strafes invisibly" and "Space is a salvo", to present the storm.
questions.answer: "Strafes" means attacking with gunfire from low-flying aircraft, and a "salvo" is a burst of gunfire. Heaney presents the storm as an enemy launching an air attack on the islanders. "Invisibly" stresses the enemy cannot be seen or fought back, increasing fear. The phrase "bombarded by the empty air" continues the semantic field and adds a paradox: something empty can attack. The extended war metaphor shows nature as a powerful, relentless enemy, and may hint at political conflict.
ms: Explains the meaning of 'strafes' or 'salvo' (1 mark)
Explains the storm as an attacking enemy (1 mark)
Comments on 'invisibly'/the paradox of empty air (1 mark)
Comments on the overall effect / semantic field / possible conflict reading (1 mark)
questions.tip: Say 'semantic field of war' and explain the effect. Listing military words without meaning is technique spotting.

questions.q: Storm on the Island: Explain how the opening ("We are prepared") and the ending ("a huge nothing that we fear") create a shift in tone.
questions.answer: The poem opens with a short, confident declarative: "We are prepared". The islanders believe their squat houses and good slate make them safe. By the end, confidence turns to fear: "a huge nothing that we fear". The paradox of a "huge nothing" shows the threat is invisible and impossible to defend against. The single-stanza form makes the change gradual: the conversational voice drifts from practical boasting to anxiety. Heaney suggests human preparation is powerless against nature (or possibly against conflict).
ms: Explains the confident tone of the opening (1 mark)
Explains the fearful tone of the ending (1 mark)
Analyses the paradox 'huge nothing' (1 mark)
Explains the overall message / structure of the shift (1 mark)
questions.tip: Track the change across the poem, ideally naming a turning point ('But no:'). Comparing only the first and last lines feels thin.

questions.q: Storm on the Island: Explain how the title and Heaney's context open up a political reading of the poem. Use the poem to support your answer.
questions.answer: Heaney grew up on a farm in County Derry, Northern Ireland, and the poem was published in Death of a Naturalist (1966). The title may pun on "Stormont", the Northern Ireland parliament, so the storm could stand for political tension. The military lexis ("strafes invisibly", "Space is a salvo") supports a reading about conflict. "We are prepared" could suggest a community bracing for violence, and "a huge nothing that we fear" could be fear of an invisible threat. However, the poem predates the worst of the Troubles (from the late 1960s), so this reading should be tentative: it works best as a second layer on top of the literal storm.
ms: Accurate context: Heaney's Northern Irish rural background (1 mark)
Explains the Stormont pun (1 mark)
Links military language to the political reading (1 mark)
Second reference supporting the reading (1 mark)
Shows tentativeness / awareness the reading is an interpretation (1 mark)
Keeps the literal nature reading alongside (1 mark)
questions.tip: Don't claim the poem IS about the Troubles. Present it as an alternative interpretation with evidence. Over-certainty loses AO1 marks.

questions.q: The Prelude: What does the boy do at the start of the extract?
options: Takes a boat that is not his and rows it out onto the lake
Climbs a mountain to watch the sunset
Swims across the lake for a dare
ms: He finds a boat tied to a willow tree and takes it: 'an act of stealth / And troubled pleasure'. The guilt prepares for nature's 'punishment'.
questions.tip: The stealing matters: it gives the boy guilt, so nature's response can be read as a moral lesson.

questions.q: The Prelude: Where is the main volta (turning point) in the extract?
options: When he describes the moon on the water
When the boy unties the boat
When a huge peak rises up from behind the ridge
ms: The appearance of 'a huge peak, black and huge' turns the mood from confident pleasure to fear and awe.
questions.tip: Name the volta and describe the mood before and after it. That is a ready-made structure paragraph.

questions.q: The Prelude: Explain how Wordsworth presents the boy's feelings BEFORE the mountain appears.
questions.answer: He feels excited but guilty: the theft is "an act of stealth / And troubled pleasure", an oxymoron-like pairing of joy and unease. He is confident, rowing "like one who rows, / Proud of his skill", and the boat goes "heaving through the water like a swan", a simile suggesting grace and pride. The setting is beautiful and calm: "Small circles glittering idly in the moon". This peaceful, proud mood makes the later fear more shocking.
ms: Identifies mixed guilt and pleasure, with reference (1 mark)
Identifies pride/confidence, with reference (1 mark)
Analyses a method, e.g. the swan simile or light imagery (1 mark)
Explains how this sets up the contrast with what follows (1 mark)
questions.tip: Note the guilt is there from the start ('troubled pleasure'). Saying he is simply 'happy' misses the nuance.

questions.q: The Prelude: Explain how the ending of the extract presents the lasting effect of the experience on the speaker.
questions.answer: For many days afterwards his brain worked with "a dim and undetermined sense / Of unknown modes of being": he cannot fully understand what he saw. "There hung a darkness, call it solitude / Or blank desertion" shows his mind is emptied of comfort. The listing of what is gone ("no pleasant images of trees, / Of sea or sky") shows nature now feels strange. Instead "huge and mighty forms, that do not live / Like living men" haunt him and "were a trouble to my dreams". Nature's power has permanently changed how he thinks: it is a moment of spiritual growth, as the full poem's subtitle, Growth of a Poet's Mind, suggests.
ms: Identifies the lasting confusion/unease (1 mark)
Analyses a phrase, e.g. 'blank desertion' or 'unknown modes of being' (1 mark)
Explains the 'huge and mighty forms' haunting his dreams (1 mark)
Explains the idea of lasting change / spiritual growth (1 mark)
questions.tip: The ending is about the mind, not the mountain. Focus on psychological effect to show a perceptive reading.

questions.q: The Prelude: Explain how Wordsworth's Romantic beliefs about nature and the sublime are shown in the extract.
questions.answer: Romantics believed nature was a powerful moral teacher. At the start nature guides him ("led by her"), personified as female and almost motherly. The sublime is a mixture of awe and terror at nature's vastness: the peak is "black and huge" and seems alive, it "Upreared its head" and "Strode after me", so he flees "with trembling oars". Nature appears to punish his theft, teaching humility. The experience changes his imagination for days afterwards ("huge and mighty forms"), showing the Romantic idea that nature shapes the mind. The Prelude is autobiographical and was published in 1850, after his death.
ms: Accurate context: Romantic view of nature as teacher (1 mark)
Linked reference, e.g. 'led by her' (1 mark)
Accurate explanation of the sublime (awe and terror) (1 mark)
Linked reference to the peak, e.g. 'Upreared its head' / 'Strode after me' (1 mark)
Explains nature humbling/punishing him (1 mark)
Explains the lasting effect on his mind as Romantic idea (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Sublime' is not just 'beautiful'. Using it to mean pretty is a common error; it means awe mixed with terror.

questions.q: Exposure: What is presented as the soldiers' main enemy?
ms: Owen says the bullets are less deadly than the snow-filled air; the cold, wind and snow are what kill the men. The real war is against nature and waiting.
questions.tip: Make the point that the human enemy is almost absent. That is what makes the poem so bleak.

questions.q: Exposure: What technique is used in "Dawn massing in the east her melancholy army"?
options: Personification and military metaphor: dawn becomes an attacking army
Onomatopoeia: the sound of the dawn
Simile: dawn is compared to a soldier using 'like'
ms: Dawn is personified as a general 'massing' troops. Instead of hope, the new day brings another attack of cold and misery.
questions.tip: Dawn normally symbolises hope. Explaining how Owen reverses that symbol is a high-level point.

questions.q: Exposure: Explain how Owen uses sound in "Sudden successive flights of bullets streak the silence".
questions.answer: The sibilance (repeated 's' sounds in "Sudden successive", "streak", "silence") imitates the whistle and hiss of bullets cutting through the air. The sound breaks up the stillness, just as the bullets break the silence. Yet the next line says the bullets are less deadly than the air, so the moment of action is brief and meaningless. The sound effect makes the reader experience the soldiers' nervous, sudden alerts in a war where "nothing happens".
ms: Identifies sibilance (1 mark)
Explains how it imitates the bullets (1 mark)
Explains the contrast with silence/stillness (1 mark)
Links to the wider idea that the weather is deadlier / futility (1 mark)
questions.tip: Say what the sound actually imitates and why it matters. 'Sibilance creates an effect' with no explanation gets one mark at best.

questions.q: Exposure: Explain how Owen presents a loss of faith and hope in the later stanzas, including "For love of God seems dying".
questions.answer: The soldiers dream of home, but "on us the doors are closed": they feel shut out and forgotten. They "turn back to our dying", accepting death. "For love of God seems dying" can mean their love for God is dying, or God's love for them is dying: either way faith is collapsing. The present-tense "seems dying" makes the loss ongoing. Owen, who had been religious, questions how a loving God could allow such suffering, challenging the idea of a holy, patriotic war.
ms: Identifies the soldiers' sense of rejection/hopelessness, with reference (1 mark)
Explains the double meaning of 'love of God' (1 mark)
Comments on a method, e.g. tense, half-line ending (1 mark)
Links to Owen's purpose: challenging religious/patriotic justification of war (1 mark)
questions.tip: Explore the ambiguity: both meanings together score higher than picking one.

questions.q: Exposure: Explain how Owen uses form and structure to reflect the soldiers' experience.
questions.answer: The poem has eight stanzas of five lines with a regular pattern, reflecting monotonous, repetitive days. Each stanza ends with a short half-line, often "But nothing happens", which drains energy from the stanza and stresses futility. The refrain repeats like the endless waiting. Pararhyme (half-rhyme, e.g. "knive us" / "nervous") creates an uneasy, unfinished sound, like a world out of tune. Rhetorical questions ("What are we doing here?") show confusion. The ending returns to "But nothing happens", so the poem is cyclical: no progress is made, mirroring the stalemate of trench warfare in winter 1917.
ms: Comments on stanza regularity reflecting monotony (1 mark)
Explains the short final lines (1 mark)
Explains the refrain 'But nothing happens' (1 mark)
Explains pararhyme and its effect (1 mark)
Comments on rhetorical questions or cyclical structure (1 mark)
Links structure to stalemate/futility of WW1 (1 mark)
questions.tip: Structure points need effects. 'There are eight stanzas' is a fact, not analysis.

questions.q: Which two of these poems are both written in blank verse (unrhymed iambic pentameter)?
options: My Last Duchess and The Prelude
The Prelude and Storm on the Island
ms: The Prelude and Storm on the Island both use (loose) blank verse, giving a natural, speaking voice. London has quatrains with ABAB rhyme, Exposure uses pararhyme, Ozymandias is a sonnet and My Last Duchess uses rhyming couplets.
questions.tip: Form comparisons are easy marks if you know them cold. Learn one form fact for every poem.

questions.q: Ozymandias and My Last Duchess both present a powerful man through a work of art. Which statement best describes a key DIFFERENCE?
options: The statue was made to criticise the king, while the painting was made to praise the Duke
Ozymandias is presented as kind, while the Duke is cruel
Ozymandias is still alive, while the Duke is dead
Ozymandias's statue now shows his power has been destroyed by time, while the Duke still controls his painting and his power continues
ms: The broken statue is a 'colossal Wreck' in an empty desert: power is gone. The Duke keeps the Duchess's portrait behind a curtain he controls and is arranging a new marriage: his power is still active and dangerous.
questions.tip: A good comparison finds a difference INSIDE a similarity. Both use art, but one shows power ended, one shows power still at work.

questions.q: Explain one similarity and one difference in how 'London' and 'Exposure' present suffering caused by those in power.
questions.answer: Similarity: both show ordinary people suffering because of decisions made by those in power. Blake's soldier's sigh "Runs in blood down Palace walls", blaming the monarchy; Owen's soldiers are left in freezing trenches asking "What are we doing here?", questioning the leaders who sent them. Difference: Blake's suffering is caused directly by institutions (Church, monarchy, commerce: "chartered" streets), while in Exposure the immediate killer is the weather, "merciless iced east winds", and the authorities are almost absent. Blake's tone is angry and accusing; Owen's is weary and hopeless.
ms: Valid similarity identified (1 mark)
Similarity supported with a reference from each poem (1 mark)
Valid difference identified (1 mark)
Difference supported with references and explained (1 mark)
questions.tip: Use comparative connectives ('similarly', 'whereas') in the same sentence. Two separate mini-answers do not count as comparison.

questions.q: Explain one similarity and one difference in how nature is presented as powerful in 'The Prelude' and 'Exposure'.
questions.answer: Similarity: in both, nature is personified as an active force that overwhelms humans: the peak "Strode after me", and in Exposure the winds "knive us" and snowflakes come "feeling for our faces". Difference: Wordsworth's nature is sublime and teaches a lesson; the boy is frightened but grows from it. Owen's nature is purely destructive and pointless: it kills the soldiers ("All their eyes are ice") and offers no meaning. Wordsworth writes as a Romantic who reveres nature; Owen reverses Romantic ideas, showing nature as an enemy.
ms: Valid similarity (personification / overwhelming force) (1 mark)
Supported with references from both poems (1 mark)
Valid difference (moral teacher vs killer) (1 mark)
Difference explained with reference or context (1 mark)
questions.tip: Don't stop at 'both show nature is powerful'. That is the question. Say HOW the power differs.

questions.q: Compare how Browning in 'My Last Duchess' and Blake in 'London' use form and structure to present control.
questions.answer: MLD: a dramatic monologue in strict rhyming couplets and iambic pentameter; the regular form mirrors the Duke's need for control, but heavy enjambment lets his anger spill over the line breaks, showing control slipping. The listener never speaks, so the Duke controls the whole conversation. London: four regular quatrains with ABAB rhyme and a steady beat, like the trudging speaker; the rigid pattern mirrors the "mind-forged manacles" that trap the people. Similarity: both use regular patterns to reflect control. Difference: in MLD the form shows a controller's mind; in London it shows the experience of the controlled. Blake builds to a climax in the final stanza ("But most"), while Browning ends abruptly, switching to the statue to show the Duke's coldness.
ms: Form point on MLD (couplets/monologue) with effect (1 mark)
Second MLD point, e.g. enjambment or silent listener (1 mark)
Form point on London (quatrains/rhyme/rhythm) with effect (1 mark)
Second London point, e.g. climactic final stanza or anaphora (1 mark)
Clear similarity drawn (1 mark)
Clear difference drawn: controller's view vs the controlled (1 mark)
questions.tip: Form points must link to the idea of control. 'MLD has rhyming couplets' alone is technique spotting.

questions.q: Compare how 'Ozymandias' and 'Storm on the Island' present the limits of human power.
questions.answer: Similarity: both show human power or preparation defeated by greater forces. Ozymandias boasts "Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!", but "Nothing beside remains". Heaney's islanders say "We are prepared", but end with "a huge nothing that we fear". Difference: Shelley's limit is time: decay happens over thousands of years. Heaney's limit is the immediate violence of a storm. Shelley's tone is ironic and mocking towards a tyrant; Heaney's is anxious and sympathetic towards an ordinary community. Structure: both turn on a reversal (Shelley's volta at the inscription; Heaney's "But no:"). Context: Shelley's anti-tyranny Romanticism versus Heaney's rural Northern Irish life and a possible political reading.
ms: Similarity: human power/preparation defeated (1 mark)
References from both poems supporting the similarity (1 mark)
Difference: time vs immediate natural force (1 mark)
Difference in tone/attitude: mocking a tyrant vs sympathy for a community (1 mark)
Structural comparison (reversal/volta) (1 mark)
Relevant context linked to the comparison (1 mark)
questions.tip: Keep both poems in every point. Examiners reward 'interwoven' comparison, not two separate halves.

questions.q: Compare how poets present the ways power can be challenged or undermined in "Ozymandias" and in one other poem from "Power and conflict". [30 marks]
questions.answer:
Chosen second poem: London.
Thesis: Both Romantic poets challenge tyranny, but Shelley does it through irony and the long view of time, showing that power collapses on its own, while Blake challenges power in the present, exposing institutions whose cruelty is still active.
Plan:
1. How power is shown: the "sneer of cold command" of a single tyrant versus the faceless control of "chartered" streets and "mind-forged manacles". Shelley's power is personal; Blake's is systemic.
2. How power is undermined: Shelley's irony ("Look on my Works... despair!" then "Nothing beside remains"); Blake's accusing images ("Runs in blood down Palace walls"). Shelley lets time do the work; Blake demands change now.
3. Who challenges: the sculptor who "well those passions read" (art outlives tyranny) versus the poet-witness who "marks" every face. Both suggest the artist's voice can resist power.
4. Form and context: Shelley's broken sonnet versus Blake's rigid quatrains; Shelley's radical politics and Blake's response to the French Revolution and child labour.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory and conceptualised comparison of both poems; a clear overall argument (thesis) running through the essay; judicious, precise references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; perceptive, convincing links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed comparison of both poems; apt references integrated into interpretation; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.

Level 4 (16-20 marks): clear, explained comparison of both poems; effective use of references to support explanation; clear explanation of the writer's methods with appropriate subject terminology; understanding of effects; clear links between context, text and task.

Level 3 (11-15 marks): some explained comparison of both poems; references used to support a range of relevant comments; explained comments on the writer's methods with some relevant terminology; some identification of effects; some understanding of contextual factors.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Critical comparison of how power is challenged; judicious references from both poems; a clear comparative thesis.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Irony, voice and framing in Ozymandias; repetition, anaphora, oxymoron and imagery in London; sonnet form vs quatrains; endings.
AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Romanticism; Shelley's opposition to monarchy and tyranny; Blake and the French Revolution; child labour and industrial London.
questions.tip: Choose the second poem to fit the question, not because it's your favourite. A weak match makes comparison feel forced.

questions.q: Compare how poets present the effects of a frightening experience on people in "The Prelude" and in one other poem from "Power and conflict". [30 marks]
questions.answer:
Chosen second poem: Exposure.
Thesis: Both poets show nature producing fear, but in The Prelude fear is a lesson that leads to growth, while in Exposure fear is endless and pointless, a sign of how war strips young men of meaning.
Plan:
1. The source of fear: the sudden, personified peak that "Upreared its head" versus the slow, constant cold and "merciless iced east winds". One sudden, one relentless.
2. Physical response: "with trembling oars I turned" versus soldiers "Worried by silence", "curious, nervous". Both show bodies controlled by fear.
3. Structure: Wordsworth's volta changes the mood once; Owen's repeated refrain "But nothing happens" traps the reader in waiting. Both use the endings to show fear lasting: "a trouble to my dreams" versus "All their eyes are ice".
4. Context: Wordsworth's Romantic sublime (fear that teaches) versus Owen's WW1 trench experience (fear that destroys); Owen reverses Romantic nature.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory and conceptualised comparison of both poems; a clear overall argument (thesis) running through the essay; judicious, precise references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; perceptive, convincing links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed comparison of both poems; apt references integrated into interpretation; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.

Level 4 (16-20 marks): clear, explained comparison of both poems; effective use of references to support explanation; clear explanation of the writer's methods with appropriate subject terminology; understanding of effects; clear links between context, text and task.

Level 3 (11-15 marks): some explained comparison of both poems; references used to support a range of relevant comments; explained comments on the writer's methods with some relevant terminology; some identification of effects; some understanding of contextual factors.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Critical comparison of different kinds of fear; judicious references from both; a clear comparative argument.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Personification, volta and blank verse in The Prelude; refrain, pararhyme, half-line endings and sibilance in Exposure; endings of both poems.
AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Romanticism and the sublime; WW1 trench warfare, winter 1917; Owen as a soldier-poet.
questions.tip: Don't spend a whole paragraph on WW1 history. Context should be one or two sentences that explain the TYPE of fear each poet shows.

questions.q: Compare how poets present the suffering of ordinary people in "London" and in one other poem from "Power and conflict". [30 marks]
questions.answer:
Chosen second poem: Exposure.
Thesis: Blake and Owen both speak for people with no voice, but Blake blames the powerful institutions directly, while Owen shows a suffering so pointless that the very idea of meaning, even God, seems to be dying.
Plan:
1. Who suffers: Blake's chimney sweeps, soldiers, harlots and infants (a city-wide list); Owen's anonymous "we" in the trenches. Both use collective, universal suffering.
2. Language of suffering: "Marks of weakness, marks of woe" and "the Marriage hearse" versus "Our brains ache" and "All their eyes are ice". Blake's oxymoron vs Owen's blunt imagery.
3. Blame: Blake points at "Church" and "Palace"; Owen's enemy is the weather and the futility ("What are we doing here?"), with authority unseen. Owen's loss of faith ("For love of God seems dying") vs Blake's attack on the Church.
4. Form and voice: Blake's first-person observer in regular quatrains versus Owen's first-person plural with refrain. Context: industrial London in 1794 vs WW1 trenches in 1917.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory and conceptualised comparison of both poems; a clear overall argument (thesis) running through the essay; judicious, precise references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; perceptive, convincing links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed comparison of both poems; apt references integrated into interpretation; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.

Level 4 (16-20 marks): clear, explained comparison of both poems; effective use of references to support explanation; clear explanation of the writer's methods with appropriate subject terminology; understanding of effects; clear links between context, text and task.

Level 3 (11-15 marks): some explained comparison of both poems; references used to support a range of relevant comments; explained comments on the writer's methods with some relevant terminology; some identification of effects; some understanding of contextual factors.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Critical comparison of suffering and who is to blame; judicious references; comparative thesis.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Anaphora, oxymoron, imagery and quatrains in London; pararhyme, refrain, personification, rhetorical questions in Exposure; voice (I vs we).
AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Industrial revolution, child labour, French Revolution; WW1, trench conditions, Owen's experience.
questions.tip: Keep to suffering. Drifting into 'both poems are about power' loses focus on the task (AO1).

questions.q: Compare how poets present control in "My Last Duchess" and in one other poem from "Power and conflict". [30 marks]
questions.answer:
Chosen second poem: London.
Thesis: Both poems show control that reaches into private lives: Browning gives us the controller's own voice, so we see control from the inside, while Blake shows the effects of control on a whole city, where people are trapped even in their minds.
Plan:
1. Who controls: the Duke ("I gave commands") versus faceless institutions ("chartered" streets, Church and Palace). Individual tyranny versus systemic control.
2. Control over others' bodies and feelings: the Duke controls the Duchess's smile even after death ("The curtain I have drawn for you"); Blake's "mind-forged manacles" control thought.
3. Form: strict couplets with enjambment (control slipping into rage) versus regular quatrains and anaphora (relentless, trapped rhythm).
4. Endings and context: the Duke's warning via "Taming a sea-horse" (patriarchal power, Renaissance Italy, Browning's Victorian readers) versus "the Marriage hearse" (Blake's 1794 London). Both endings show control continuing into the future.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory and conceptualised comparison of both poems; a clear overall argument (thesis) running through the essay; judicious, precise references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; perceptive, convincing links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed comparison of both poems; apt references integrated into interpretation; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.

Level 4 (16-20 marks): clear, explained comparison of both poems; effective use of references to support explanation; clear explanation of the writer's methods with appropriate subject terminology; understanding of effects; clear links between context, text and task.

Level 3 (11-15 marks): some explained comparison of both poems; references used to support a range of relevant comments; explained comments on the writer's methods with some relevant terminology; some identification of effects; some understanding of contextual factors.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Critical comparison of control; perceptive references from both poems; a conceptualised comparative thesis.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Dramatic monologue, dramatic irony, couplets and enjambment, symbolism of art in MLD; repetition, oxymoron, imagery and quatrains in London.
AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Renaissance Italy and Alfonso II; Victorian views of marriage; Blake's Songs of Experience and attack on institutions.
questions.tip: Don't say the Duke 'loved his wife too much'. Misreading the Duke as grieving or romantic is a frequent and costly error.

questions.q: Compare how poets present a sense of helplessness in "Exposure" and in one other poem from "Power and conflict". [30 marks]
questions.answer:
Chosen second poem: Storm on the Island.
Thesis: Both poems trap a group ("we") who can only wait for a natural force to strike, but Heaney's islanders begin confident and slowly lose it, whereas Owen's soldiers are helpless from the first line and sink further into despair.
Plan:
1. Openings: "We are prepared" versus "Our brains ache". Confidence vs suffering from the start.
2. Waiting and inaction: "We just sit tight" versus "But nothing happens". Both show helpless waiting; Owen's refrain makes it endless.
3. Nature as enemy, with military language in both: "strafes invisibly", "Space is a salvo" versus "Dawn massing in the east her melancholy army". Heaney uses war as a metaphor for nature; Owen shows nature worse than war.
4. Endings: "a huge nothing that we fear" versus "All their eyes are ice". Fear of an invisible threat versus actual death. Context: rural Northern Ireland (and a possible political reading) versus WW1 trenches.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory and conceptualised comparison of both poems; a clear overall argument (thesis) running through the essay; judicious, precise references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; perceptive, convincing links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed comparison of both poems; apt references integrated into interpretation; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.

Level 4 (16-20 marks): clear, explained comparison of both poems; effective use of references to support explanation; clear explanation of the writer's methods with appropriate subject terminology; understanding of effects; clear links between context, text and task.

Level 3 (11-15 marks): some explained comparison of both poems; references used to support a range of relevant comments; explained comments on the writer's methods with some relevant terminology; some identification of effects; some understanding of contextual factors.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Critical comparison of helplessness; collective voice in both; judicious references; comparative argument.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Collective pronouns; military semantic field; refrain; pararhyme vs blank verse; single stanza vs eight regular stanzas; endings.
AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: WW1, winter 1917, Owen's experience; Heaney's rural Northern Irish background; the Stormont pun as a tentative political reading.
questions.tip: Heaney's war imagery is a METAPHOR; Owen's war is literal. Spotting that difference is the kind of detail that earns Level 6.

questions.q: Compare how poets present the ways art and objects reveal the truth about powerful people in "My Last Duchess" and in one other poem from "Power and conflict". [30 marks]
questions.answer:
Chosen second poem: Ozymandias.
Thesis: In both poems a work of art outlives its subject and exposes what the powerful man wanted hidden, but Shelley's statue reveals the truth through the artist's skill, while Browning's painting reveals the truth through the Duke's own boasting about it.
Plan:
1. The artworks: "my last Duchess painted on the wall" (kept, displayed, controlled) versus "Two vast and trunkless legs of stone" (ruined, abandoned).
2. The artist: the sculptor "well those passions read" and "mocked" the king, capturing his "sneer of cold command"; Fra Pandolf captures the Duchess's smile, which provokes the Duke's jealousy. Art tells the truth.
3. Voice and framing: Shelley's layered narrators distance us from the king; Browning's dramatic monologue puts us in the room with the Duke, so the truth leaks through his words ("I gave commands").
4. Final objects and context: the empty desert versus the bronze "Taming a sea-horse". Shelley's Romantic view that tyranny is temporary versus Browning's Victorian exposure of patriarchal power.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory and conceptualised comparison of both poems; a clear overall argument (thesis) running through the essay; judicious, precise references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; perceptive, convincing links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed comparison of both poems; apt references integrated into interpretation; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.

Level 4 (16-20 marks): clear, explained comparison of both poems; effective use of references to support explanation; clear explanation of the writer's methods with appropriate subject terminology; understanding of effects; clear links between context, text and task.

Level 3 (11-15 marks): some explained comparison of both poems; references used to support a range of relevant comments; explained comments on the writer's methods with some relevant terminology; some identification of effects; some understanding of contextual factors.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Critical comparison of art as revealing truth; perceptive references from both; conceptualised thesis.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Framing narrative and irony in Ozymandias; dramatic monologue and dramatic irony in MLD; sonnet vs couplets; symbolism of the statue/painting/bronze.
AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Shelley's Romanticism and politics; Rameses II; Browning, Alfonso II and the Renaissance; Victorian attitudes to marriage.
questions.tip: Don't just compare 'what the art looks like'. Ask what the art REVEALS and how each poet makes it reveal it.

questions.q:
Q27.1 style. Read the poem.

"The Allotment" (original poem)
My grandad's hands were maps of soil and rain,
the creases brown with forty years of digging.
He'd lift a potato like a newborn,
brush off the dirt, and grin as if he'd made it.

Now weeds have climbed the fence he mended twice.
His shed leans in, a tired old man itself,
and through the cracked glass, rusted on its nail,
his spade still waits for someone's hands to fit.

I take it down. It's heavier than I thought.
I push it in. The earth gives, just a little.

In "The Allotment", how does the poet present the speaker's feelings about their grandfather? [24 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: The speaker's feelings move from admiring memory to grief, and finally to a hesitant sense of inheritance: the allotment becomes a way of keeping the grandfather alive.
Plan:
1. Admiration and tenderness: the metaphor "hands were maps of soil and rain" presents a lifetime of work written on his body; the simile "like a newborn" shows his gentle care and pride ("grin as if he'd made it").
2. Loss: the volta at "Now" shifts to decay: weeds "climbed the fence he mended twice". The personified shed, "a tired old man itself", reflects the grandfather's ageing and absence, showing the speaker sees him everywhere.
3. Longing: the spade "still waits for someone's hands to fit": personification and enjambment suggest an empty space the speaker feels they should fill.
4. Inheritance: the final couplet uses short, simple sentences ("I take it down.") to slow the moment; "heavier than I thought" suggests the weight of grief and responsibility; "The earth gives, just a little" ends on a hopeful but tentative note.
Form: four-line stanzas of memory and absence, then a two-line ending of action, like a turn from past to present.
ms: Level 6 (21-24 marks): critical, exploratory and conceptualised response to the task and the poem; judicious references; analysis of the poet's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader.
Level 5 (17-20 marks): thoughtful, developed response; apt references integrated into interpretation; examination of methods with effective use of terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects.
Level 4 (13-16 marks): clear, explained response; effective references; clear explanation of methods with appropriate terminology; understanding of effects.
Level 3 (9-12 marks): some explained response; references support a range of relevant comments; explained comments on methods with some relevant terminology; some identification of effects.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Admiration, love, grief and a tentative sense of continuing the grandfather's work; development of feelings across the poem.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Metaphor of hands as maps; simile 'like a newborn'; personification of the shed and spade; volta at 'Now'; enjambment; short sentences and the final two-line stanza; past to present tense shift.
AO3 is not assessed on unseen poetry: give no credit for guesses about the poet's life or era.
questions.tip: Track how feelings CHANGE through the poem. Working through line by line with no argument tends to stay in Level 4.

questions.q:
Q27.1 style. Read the poem.

"Last Bus" (original poem)
The last bus hums its one long yellow note
through streets that someone else has switched to sleep.
Upstairs, the front seat. Mine. The window fogs;
I write my name, then wipe it, then rewrite it.

Below, the city shrugs its shoulders off:
the kebab shop, the shutters, someone's laugh
spilled out of a doorway, rolling down the hill.
The driver doesn't know I'm here. Nobody does.

And for these twenty minutes, I'm the king
of every lit-up window that we pass.

In "Last Bus", how does the poet present the speaker's feelings about travelling home alone at night? [24 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: The speaker presents the journey as a rare moment of freedom and private power, but small details hint at loneliness beneath the excitement.
Plan:
1. Calm, dreamy atmosphere: synaesthesia/metaphor "one long yellow note" mixes sound and colour; "switched to sleep" makes the city feel like a machine turned off, setting up a private world.
2. Ownership and identity: the minor sentence "Mine." shows pride in the front seat; writing, wiping and rewriting the name (repetition) suggests a young person trying out who they are.
3. The city below: personification "the city shrugs its shoulders off" suggests relaxation; the list of night details and the laugh "spilled out of a doorway" create a lively but distant world the speaker only watches.
4. Loneliness and power: "Nobody does." (short sentence) could feel isolating or freeing; the final two-line stanza, "I'm the king / of every lit-up window", uses enjambment and hyperbole to celebrate imagined control, while "for these twenty minutes" reminds us it is temporary.
ms: Level 6 (21-24 marks): critical, exploratory and conceptualised response to the task and the poem; judicious references; analysis of the poet's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader.
Level 5 (17-20 marks): thoughtful, developed response; apt references integrated into interpretation; examination of methods with effective use of terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects.
Level 4 (13-16 marks): clear, explained response; effective references; clear explanation of methods with appropriate terminology; understanding of effects.
Level 3 (9-12 marks): some explained response; references support a range of relevant comments; explained comments on methods with some relevant terminology; some identification of effects.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Freedom, independence, pride and a hint of loneliness; awareness that the feeling is temporary.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Synaesthesia/metaphor; minor sentences; repetition; personification of the city; listing; enjambment into the final two-line stanza; hyperbole of 'king'; contrast between upstairs and 'Below'.
AO3 is not assessed on unseen poetry: give no credit for guesses about the poet's life or era.
questions.tip: Don't settle for one feeling. The best answers notice tension (freedom vs loneliness) and explore both.

questions.q:
Q27.1 style. Read the poem.

"Exam Hall" (original poem)
The clock is louder here than anywhere.
Two hundred pens are holding in their breath.
The radiator ticks as if it's counting
down the seconds I have left to think.

My mind's a cupboard someone's emptied out,
the shelves still marked with labels: dates, quotes, names.
I close my eyes. I find the first one. Then
another. One by one, I stack them back.

In "Exam Hall", how does the poet present the experience of anxiety? [24 marks]
questions.answer:
Thesis: The poet presents anxiety as something that distorts the senses and empties the mind, but the poem's structure shows it can be calmly overcome, one small step at a time.
Plan:
1. Heightened senses: the hyperbole "louder here than anywhere" shows how panic amplifies small sounds; the personified pens "holding in their breath" spread the tension through the whole room.
2. Time pressure: the radiator "ticks as if it's counting / down" uses enjambment so the line itself runs out, mirroring the speaker's fear of running out of time.
3. The empty mind: the metaphor "My mind's a cupboard someone's emptied out" presents panic as theft or loss; the labels ("dates, quotes, names") show the knowledge is still there, just out of reach.
4. Recovery: short sentences ("I close my eyes. I find the first one.") slow the pace; enjambment across "Then / another" mirrors steady progress; "One by one, I stack them back" completes the cupboard metaphor, ending in control.
Form: two balanced quatrain-like stanzas: the first is panic, the second recovery.
ms: Level 6 (21-24 marks): critical, exploratory and conceptualised response to the task and the poem; judicious references; analysis of the poet's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader.
Level 5 (17-20 marks): thoughtful, developed response; apt references integrated into interpretation; examination of methods with effective use of terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects.
Level 4 (13-16 marks): clear, explained response; effective references; clear explanation of methods with appropriate terminology; understanding of effects.
Level 3 (9-12 marks): some explained response; references support a range of relevant comments; explained comments on methods with some relevant terminology; some identification of effects.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Panic, pressure, blankness and recovery; how the speaker regains control.

AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Hyperbole; personification of the pens and radiator; enjambment; extended metaphor of the cupboard; listing; short sentences and caesura; two-stanza structure of problem and solution.
AO3 is not assessed on unseen poetry: give no credit for guesses about the poet's life or era.
questions.tip: Use the whole poem. Many answers spend all their time on the first stanza and miss the turn to recovery.

questions.q:
Q27.2 style. Read both poems.

"The Allotment" (original poem)
My grandad's hands were maps of soil and rain,
the creases brown with forty years of digging.
He'd lift a potato like a newborn,
brush off the dirt, and grin as if he'd made it.

Now weeds have climbed the fence he mended twice.
His shed leans in, a tired old man itself,
and through the cracked glass, rusted on its nail,
his spade still waits for someone's hands to fit.

I take it down. It's heavier than I thought.
I push it in. The earth gives, just a little.

"Recipe" (original poem)
My mother never wrote the recipe.
It lived inside her wrists: a pinch, a shake,
a handful judged by weight, the way you judge
a baby's sleep by listening at the door.

I stand where she once stood, phone propped on the tin,
her voice on speaker: Not that much. Now wait.
The onions soften slowly into gold.
The kitchen fills with something like her arms.

It's not quite hers. It never will be. Still,
my brother takes a second bowl, and smiles.

In both "The Allotment" and "Recipe" the speakers describe a relationship with an older family member. What are the similarities and/or differences between the methods the poets use to present these relationships? [8 marks]
questions.answer:
Plan:
1. Hands and the body: both poets focus on the older relative's hands, "hands were maps of soil and rain" vs the recipe that "lived inside her wrists". Both use metaphor to show skill learned over a lifetime, but the grandfather's hands are marked by labour while the mother's knowledge is instinctive.
2. Absence and presence: The Allotment uses personified objects (the shed, the waiting spade) to show the grandfather is gone; Recipe has the mother still present through her voice on speaker, shown in short direct speech ("Not that much. Now wait."). One poem is grief; the other is distance.
3. Endings: both end with the speaker trying to carry on the relative's work, with short sentences and caesura ("I push it in." vs "It's not quite hers. It never will be."). The Allotment ends on the earth giving "just a little"; Recipe ends on the brother's smile. Both end tentatively hopeful, but Recipe's ending looks forward to another person.
4. Structure: both use three stanzas (two of four lines, then two lines), with a turn to the present; similar shape, both moving from the older person to the speaker.
ms: Level 4 (7-8 marks): exploratory comparison of the poets' methods (language, structure, form) and their effects, with judicious references from both poems and terminology used judiciously.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): thoughtful comparison of the poets' methods and their effects, with apt references and effective terminology.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): relevant comparison of methods, with some explanation of effects and some relevant terminology.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): some links between the methods used, with little explanation; references may be descriptive.

AO2 indicative content: Metaphors of hands/wrists; personification (shed, spade) vs direct speech; short sentences and caesura in both endings; matching three-stanza structure ending on a two-line stanza; tense shifts.
Only comparison of METHODS earns marks here (AO2 only). Comparing what the poems are about, or analysing one poem without the other, scores little.
questions.tip: 27.2 is about METHODS only. Spending your time on what the poems mean, without comparing techniques, keeps you in Level 1 or 2.

questions.q:
Q27.2 style. Read both poems.

"Last Bus" (original poem)
The last bus hums its one long yellow note
through streets that someone else has switched to sleep.
Upstairs, the front seat. Mine. The window fogs;
I write my name, then wipe it, then rewrite it.

Below, the city shrugs its shoulders off:
the kebab shop, the shutters, someone's laugh
spilled out of a doorway, rolling down the hill.
The driver doesn't know I'm here. Nobody does.

And for these twenty minutes, I'm the king
of every lit-up window that we pass.

"Exam Hall" (original poem)
The clock is louder here than anywhere.
Two hundred pens are holding in their breath.
The radiator ticks as if it's counting
down the seconds I have left to think.

My mind's a cupboard someone's emptied out,
the shelves still marked with labels: dates, quotes, names.
I close my eyes. I find the first one. Then
another. One by one, I stack them back.

In both "Last Bus" and "Exam Hall" the speakers describe a moment when they are alone with their thoughts. What are the similarities and/or differences between the methods the poets use to present these moments? [8 marks]
questions.answer:
Plan:
1. Personification of surroundings: "the city shrugs its shoulders off" (relaxed) vs pens "holding in their breath" (tense). Same method, opposite moods.
2. Sound: the bus "hums its one long yellow note" (soothing, continuous) vs the clock "louder here than anywhere" and the radiator "ticks" (pressing, repetitive). Sound shows calm in one and anxiety in the other.
3. Short sentences: "Mine." and "Nobody does." show confidence or isolation; "I close my eyes. I find the first one." show deliberate steps to regain calm. Both use them for control, but in different ways.
4. Endings: Last Bus builds to the hyperbole "I'm the king" through enjambment; Exam Hall ends on the completed cupboard metaphor "I stack them back". Both end with the speaker in control, but one is a fantasy of power and one is quiet recovery.
ms: Level 4 (7-8 marks): exploratory comparison of the poets' methods (language, structure, form) and their effects, with judicious references from both poems and terminology used judiciously.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): thoughtful comparison of the poets' methods and their effects, with apt references and effective terminology.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): relevant comparison of methods, with some explanation of effects and some relevant terminology.
Level 1 (1-2 marks): some links between the methods used, with little explanation; references may be descriptive.
AO2 indicative content: Personification; sound imagery; minor/short sentences; enjambment; extended metaphor vs hyperbole; endings.
Only comparison of METHODS earns marks here (AO2 only). Comparing what the poems are about, or analysing one poem without the other, scores little.
questions.tip: Use 'whereas' and 'similarly' in every point. Two separate mini-analyses are not comparison.

questions.q:
Read the poem.

"Recipe" (original poem)
My mother never wrote the recipe.
It lived inside her wrists: a pinch, a shake,
a handful judged by weight, the way you judge
a baby's sleep by listening at the door.

I stand where she once stood, phone propped on the tin,
her voice on speaker: Not that much. Now wait.
The onions soften slowly into gold.
The kitchen fills with something like her arms.

It's not quite hers. It never will be. Still,
my brother takes a second bowl, and smiles.

Explain how the poet uses the final two lines to present the speaker's feelings.
questions.answer: "It's not quite hers. It never will be." Short sentences and caesura create a pause of sadness: the speaker accepts they can never fully replace their mother's cooking. "Still," at the end of the line acts as a turning point (volta) that introduces hope. The brother taking "a second bowl, and smiles" shows the food still brings love and comfort to the family. The ending moves from loss to quiet pride: the tradition continues even if it changes.
ms: Comments on short sentences/caesura showing acceptance or sadness (1 mark)
Explains the turn at 'Still' (1 mark)
Explains the brother's reaction as comfort/success (1 mark)
Overall feeling: loss balanced with pride/hope (1 mark)
questions.tip: Say what the punctuation DOES. 'There are full stops' on its own is not analysis.

questions.q: Read this line from an original poem: "The radiator ticks as if it's counting". Which technique is used?
ms: The radiator is given a human action (counting). This makes the room seem to join in the speaker's anxiety about time.
questions.tip: 'As if' signals a comparison, but the strongest label here is personification: the radiator is given a human action (counting). Pathetic fallacy needs weather or nature reflecting mood.

questions.q: An original poem about a dead grandfather ends: "I take it down. It's heavier than I thought. / I push it in. The earth gives, just a little." What is the most likely effect of the short sentences?
options: They speed the poem up to show excitement
They slow the pace, making a small action feel weighty and emotional
They create a cheerful, sing-song rhythm
They show the speaker is confused and cannot finish sentences
ms: Short, simple sentences force pauses, so each action feels deliberate and significant. 'Heavier' suggests the emotional weight of continuing his work.
questions.tip: Link sentence length to emotion. Saying 'short sentences create tension' every time, whatever the poem, is a generic comment.

questions.q: Which sentence is the best example of 'bolted-on' context that would NOT earn much AO3 credit?
options: "Blake's attack on the 'blackening Church' reflects his anger that the Church ignored child chimney sweeps."
"Owen, writing from the trenches, reverses the Romantic idea that nature is kind."
"Priestley was born in Bradford in 1894 and fought in the First World War."
"Birling's prediction that war won't come would seem ridiculous to a 1945 audience who had lived through two."
ms: A biographical fact with no link to the text or task is bolted on. The other three use context to explain a quotation or idea.
questions.tip: Test every context sentence: does it explain WHY the writer wrote this or HOW an audience would react? If not, cut it.

questions.q: Which is the strongest thesis for "Compare how poets present people being overwhelmed by nature in 'Storm on the Island' and 'The Prelude'"?
options: "Both poets present nature as overwhelming, but Heaney's storm is an invisible enemy a community can only endure, while Wordsworth's mountain is a moral teacher that changes one boy's mind for ever."
"In this essay I will compare Storm on the Island and The Prelude."
"Heaney uses lots of military language and Wordsworth uses personification."
"Both poems are about nature and they both show it is very powerful."
ms: The best thesis gives a clear argument with both a similarity and a precise difference. The others are vague, describe the essay, or just list techniques.
questions.tip: A thesis is an ARGUMENT. If it could be the start of any essay on any two poems, it is too vague.

questions.q:
Read this weak paragraph about An Inspector Calls.

"In Act 1, Mr Birling gives a speech at dinner. He talks about the Titanic and says it is unsinkable. Then he says there won't be a war. Then the doorbell rings and the Inspector comes in. This shows Birling is wrong."

Explain FOUR ways to improve this paragraph and write one improved sentence.
questions.answer: Improvements: 1. Start with an argument (topic sentence) about Priestley's purpose, not the plot. 2. Embed short quotations ("unsinkable, absolutely unsinkable") instead of retelling. 3. Name and analyse the method: dramatic irony, and the repetition in Birling's line showing overconfidence. 4. Link to context and audience: the 1945 audience knew the Titanic sank and two wars followed, so they reject his capitalist views too. Improved sentence: "Priestley uses dramatic irony to destroy Birling's authority: his repeated 'unsinkable, absolutely unsinkable' would make a 1945 audience laugh, so they learn to distrust everything he says about business and society."
ms: Identifies retelling/plot summary as the problem and suggests an argument-led topic sentence (1 mark)
Suggests embedded quotation(s) (1 mark)
Suggests naming and analysing a method, e.g. dramatic irony (1 mark)
Suggests linking to context/audience and writes a clearly improved sentence (1 mark)
questions.tip: Retelling the plot is the biggest reason AIC essays stay in Level 3. Every sentence should be about Priestley's choices.

questions.q:
Read this weak paragraph about Exposure.

"Owen uses alliteration in 'Sudden successive flights of bullets streak the silence'. He also uses personification. He also uses repetition with 'But nothing happens'. These techniques make the poem more interesting for the reader."

Rewrite this into a grade 8-9 paragraph and explain what you changed.
questions.answer:
Rewritten: "Owen suggests that the real horror of the trenches is not combat but futile waiting. The sibilance of 'Sudden successive flights of bullets streak the silence' imitates the hiss of gunfire, yet the moment passes without consequence, swallowed by the refrain 'But nothing happens'. By ending stanza after stanza on this flat half-line, Owen traps the reader in the soldiers' stalemate, challenging the heroic war poetry his readers at home expected."
What changed: the paragraph starts with an idea, not a technique; it uses precise terminology (sibilance, refrain, half-line) and explains the EFFECT of each; it drops the generic 'makes it interesting'; it links methods together into one argument; it adds context (readers at home, heroic war poetry).
ms: Opens with an argument/idea rather than a technique (1 mark)
Uses precise terminology with explained effects (1 mark)
Removes generic comments and links methods to meaning (1 mark)
Integrates context or the writer's purpose (1 mark)
questions.tip: Technique spotting (listing devices with 'it makes it interesting') is flagged in examiner reports every year. Effect beats label.

questions.q: Write a thesis statement for the question "How does Priestley present the theme of responsibility in An Inspector Calls?" Then explain what makes it effective.
questions.answer:
Example thesis: "Priestley presents responsibility as a choice that divides the generations: while the Birling parents see it only as legal guilt to be avoided, Sheila and Eric come to accept it as a moral duty to others, a lesson Priestley urges his 1945 audience to build a fairer society on."
Why it works: it gives a clear argument (not just 'responsibility is important'); it shows a conceptual distinction (legal vs moral responsibility, older vs younger); it links to Priestley's purpose and context.
ms: Thesis states a clear, arguable position (1 mark)
Thesis contains a conceptual idea or contrast (e.g. generations, legal vs moral) (1 mark)
Links to the writer's purpose/audience (1 mark)
questions.tip: Don't repeat the question back ('Priestley presents responsibility in many ways'). That isn't a thesis.

questions.q:
Read this weak comparison paragraph.

"In Ozymandias the king is arrogant. He says 'Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!' This shows he is proud. In My Last Duchess the Duke is also arrogant. He says 'Never to stoop'. This shows he is proud too."

Explain how to improve it and write an improved version.
questions.answer:
Problems: it treats the poems separately, uses only 'also' as comparison, repeats 'shows he is proud', and has no analysis of methods or differences.
Improved: "Both rulers reveal their arrogance through their own words, but while Ozymandias's imperative 'Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!' is undercut by the ruins around it, so his pride becomes a joke against him, the Duke's 'Never to stoop' is still in force: his refusal to lower himself led to the Duchess's death and threatens the next wife. Shelley uses irony to show pride destroyed by time; Browning uses dramatic monologue to show pride that remains dangerous."
Changes: comparison within each sentence; a precise difference; methods named (imperative, irony, dramatic monologue); effects explained.
ms: Identifies the problem of separate, sequential treatment (1 mark)
Improved version compares within sentences using a precise similarity AND difference (1 mark)
Names and analyses methods in both poems (1 mark)
Explains effects/purposes rather than repeating 'shows he is proud' (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Also' is the weakest comparative word. Use 'whereas', 'while', 'in contrast' and say what the difference MEANS.

questions.q:
Read the poem, then the weak unseen poetry paragraph written about it.

"Exam Hall" (original poem)
The clock is louder here than anywhere.
Two hundred pens are holding in their breath.
The radiator ticks as if it's counting
down the seconds I have left to think.

My mind's a cupboard someone's emptied out,
the shelves still marked with labels: dates, quotes, names.
I close my eyes. I find the first one. Then
another. One by one, I stack them back.

Weak paragraph:
"The poet probably wrote this poem because they failed an exam when they were young and it made them sad. In the 1990s exams were very stressful. The poem uses a metaphor 'My mind's a cupboard someone's emptied out'."

Explain what is wrong and how to improve it for question 27.1.
questions.answer:
What's wrong: it guesses about the poet's life and adds historical 'context'. AO3 is not assessed on unseen poetry, so this earns nothing and wastes time. It also names the metaphor without analysing it.
Improvement: focus on AO1 (argument about anxiety) and AO2 (methods and effects). For example: "The metaphor 'My mind's a cupboard someone's emptied out' presents panic as a kind of theft: the speaker's knowledge feels stolen rather than forgotten. Yet the shelves are 'still marked with labels', suggesting the information is still there, which prepares for the calm ending where they 'stack them back'."
ms: Identifies that biographical/historical guesses earn no credit (AO3 not assessed) (1 mark)
Identifies that the metaphor is named but not analysed (1 mark)
Improved version analyses the metaphor's connotations (1 mark)
Improved version links the method to the poem's overall argument/structure (1 mark)
questions.tip: In unseen poetry, never invent the poet's life story. Examiners give it no marks and it signals weak focus on the text.

questions.q: In the An Inspector Calls question on Paper 2, how many marks are available for AO3 (context)?
ms: The 34 marks split as AO1 12, AO2 12, AO3 6 and AO4 4. Context is the smallest share, so it should support your argument, not dominate it.
questions.tip: With only 6 marks, a whole paragraph of history is poor value. Weave context into analytical points.

questions.q: Who says "There's daggers in men's smiles" after Duncan's murder?
ms: Donalbain says it to Malcolm in Act 2 Scene 3 before they flee. It sums up the theme of appearance versus reality: friendly faces may hide murderers.
questions.tip: Malcolm and Donalbain are easy to mix up. Donalbain flees to Ireland; Malcolm flees to England.

questions.q: In Act 2 Scene 2, Lady Macbeth says that "Had he not resembled / My father as he slept" she would have killed Duncan herself. What does this reveal?
options: She has limits: a trace of conscience or human feeling she cannot overcome
She is lying to make Macbeth feel guilty
She is completely fearless and has no feelings
ms: Despite calling on spirits to 'unsex' her, she could not kill a man who looked like her father. It foreshadows her later breakdown.
questions.tip: Use this line to challenge a simple 'Lady Macbeth is evil' reading. Examiners reward alternative interpretations.

questions.q: Explain how Shakespeare presents Macbeth's fear of Banquo in Act 3 Scene 1.
questions.answer: In his soliloquy Macbeth says "To be thus is nothing, / But to be safely thus": being king means nothing unless he is secure. He admits "Our fears in Banquo / Stick deep", showing fear rooted inside him. He envies Banquo's "royalty of nature" and wisdom, showing Banquo is the better man. He resents the "fruitless crown" and "barren sceptre": he has no heir, while the Witches promised Banquo's sons would be kings. The soliloquy shows his paranoia growing, leading him to hire murderers.
ms: Reference to Macbeth's insecurity, e.g. 'To be thus is nothing' (1 mark)
Explains fear of Banquo's qualities/the prophecy about his sons (1 mark)
Analyses a method, e.g. 'fruitless crown' imagery or the soliloquy form (1 mark)
Explains how the fear drives the plot/his decline into tyranny (1 mark)
questions.tip: Name the soliloquy as a method: it shows the audience Macbeth's private fears that he hides from Banquo in public.

questions.q: Explain how Lady Macbeth's language changes between Act 1 Scene 5 and Act 5 Scene 1.
questions.answer: In Act 1 Scene 5 she speaks in commanding verse, using imperatives to call on darkness: "come, thick night". She seems in control and summons evil. In Act 5 Scene 1 she sleepwalks and speaks in broken prose, showing her mind has collapsed. Her words repeat the past: "Here's the smell of the blood still" shows guilt she can't wash away, reversing her earlier confidence that water would clear them. "What's done cannot be undone" echoes and reverses her earlier "what's done is done" (Act 3 Scene 2), showing she now sees the murder as permanent and haunting.
ms: Act 1 Scene 5: commanding verse/imperatives with reference (1 mark)
Act 5 Scene 1: fragmented prose showing breakdown (1 mark)
Reference to guilt imagery, e.g. blood (1 mark)
