Explains the echo/reversal of 'what's done' (1 mark)
questions.tip: Comment on verse versus prose. Shakespeare's shift in form is a method the examiners specifically reward.

questions.q:
Starting with this moment in the play, explore how far Shakespeare presents Banquo as a threat to Macbeth.

Write about:
- how Shakespeare presents Banquo at the start of Act 3 Scene 1
- how Shakespeare presents Banquo in the play as a whole. [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]

(Act 3 Scene 1 opens with Banquo alone, reflecting that Macbeth now has everything the Witches promised: "Thou hast it now: King, Cawdor, Glamis, all". He suspects Macbeth "play'dst most foully for't", but reminds himself that the Witches also promised his own descendants would be kings. Macbeth then enters as king, warmly invites Banquo to a "solemn supper" that night, and casually asks whether he is riding out that afternoon and whether Fleance goes with him.)
questions.answer:
Thesis: Shakespeare makes Banquo a threat to Macbeth less through anything he does than through what he is: a loyal, suspicious witness and the father of future kings. That combination turns him into Macbeth's conscience and his rival.
Plan:
1. The extract: Banquo's suspicion ("play'dst most foully for't") shows he knows the truth, but his silence is ambiguous; perhaps he too is tempted by the prophecy. Macbeth's friendly questions about Fleance are dramatic irony: he is planning murder.
2. Act 1: Banquo as foil. He warns that "instruments of darkness" deceive, while Macbeth is drawn in. Context: Banquo as James I's ancestor, so Shakespeare keeps him noble.
3. Macbeth's soliloquy: "Our fears in Banquo / Stick deep"; the "fruitless crown" and "barren sceptre". Banquo threatens Macbeth's legacy and his sense of himself.
4. Act 3 Scene 4 and Act 4 Scene 1: the ghost and the line of kings. Dead, Banquo is more dangerous: he breaks Macbeth's public composure and shows the future belongs to Banquo's line. Divine right: the rightful order will be restored.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory and conceptualised response; a clear overall argument (thesis) running through the essay; judicious, precise references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; perceptive, convincing links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed response; apt references integrated into interpretation; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.

Level 4 (16-20 marks): clear, explained response; effective use of references to support explanation; clear explanation of the writer's methods with appropriate subject terminology; understanding of effects; clear links between context, text and task.

Level 3 (11-15 marks): some explained response; references used to support a range of relevant comments; explained comments on the writer's methods with some relevant terminology; some identification of effects; some understanding of contextual factors.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Clear argument about why Banquo threatens Macbeth; extract and whole play both covered; 'how far' judgement.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Soliloquy; dramatic irony in Macbeth's questions; imagery of the 'fruitless crown'; the ghost as a staging device; the show of kings; Banquo as foil.

AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Jacobean context: James I, the divine right of kings, the Great Chain of Being, the Gunpowder Plot, belief in witchcraft; Shakespeare flattering James by presenting Banquo (James's claimed ancestor) positively. Context must explain the text, not sit in a separate paragraph.

AO4 (4 marks): 4 = high performance (consistently accurate spelling and punctuation, control of meaning, wide range of vocabulary and sentence structures); 2-3 = intermediate (considerable accuracy, general control of meaning); 1 = threshold (reasonable accuracy); 0 = no marks.
questions.tip: Use the extract AND the whole play. Examiners report many answers that only cover the extract, which caps the mark.

questions.q: Give three things that happen to or are done by Macduff during the play.
questions.answer: Any three: he discovers Duncan's murdered body (Act 2); he refuses to attend Macbeth's coronation at Scone; he flees to England to join Malcolm; his wife and children are murdered on Macbeth's orders; he hears the news from Ross; he kills Macbeth in the final battle, revealing he was 'from his mother's womb / Untimely ripped'.
ms: First correct event (1 mark)
Second correct event (1 mark)
Third correct event (1 mark)
questions.tip: Be precise: Macduff goes to England, not Ireland. Donalbain is the one who goes to Ireland.

questions.q: Why does Shakespeare present Banquo as a noble, loyal character?
options: Banquo was the real murderer of Duncan in history
Audiences of the time disliked Macbeth's family
King James I claimed to be descended from Banquo
ms: James I traced his line to Banquo, so Shakespeare presents Banquo positively and shows his descendants as future kings. In Holinshed's source, Banquo helped kill Duncan, which Shakespeare changed.
questions.tip: This is a strong AO3 point only when linked to a moment, e.g. the show of eight kings in Act 4 Scene 1.

questions.q: In Act 3 Scene 2 Lady Macbeth says "what's done is done". In Act 5 Scene 1 she says "What's done cannot be undone". What does the change most clearly show?
options: She has become more confident since becoming queen
She now realises guilt is permanent and the murder can never be put behind her
She has forgotten what she did
ms: The first is dismissive: forget it and move on. The echo in Act 5 reverses it: the deed haunts her for ever. Shakespeare shows guilt destroying her mind.
questions.tip: Spotting echoes across the play is a whole-text skill. Two linked quotes in one point show 'judicious' references.

questions.q: Explain how Shakespeare explores the theme of fate versus free will through Macbeth's aside in Act 1 Scene 3: "If chance will have me king, why, chance may crown me".
questions.answer: At first Macbeth suggests he can leave it to fate: if he is meant to be king, it will happen without his action ("chance may crown me"). This shows a moment of hesitation and moral restraint. But the fact he is already thinking about it, and has "horrid" images of murder earlier in the aside, shows the prophecy has awakened his ambition. The Witches never tell him to kill; Macbeth chooses to act. Banquo hears prophecies too but does not act on them, suggesting free will matters. For a Jacobean audience, this raises the question of whether evil is chosen or caused by the supernatural.
ms: Explains the literal meaning: leaving it to fate/chance (1 mark)
Explains how this shows initial restraint/hesitation (1 mark)
Explains that he later chooses to act / the Witches never command (1 mark)
Supports with comparison to Banquo or Jacobean context (1 mark)
questions.tip: Don't argue that the Witches 'made' Macbeth do it. The best answers weigh fate against choice.

questions.q: Explain how Shakespeare uses the apparitions in Act 4 Scene 1 to explore the theme of equivocation.
questions.answer: The apparitions give answers that sound reassuring but are deceptive. The bloody child says "Be bloody, bold, and resolute" because "none of woman born / Shall harm Macbeth", but Macduff was born by caesarean ('untimely ripped'). The crowned child says he will not be defeated until Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane, which seems impossible but happens when soldiers carry branches. These are equivocations: true statements that mislead. They make Macbeth overconfident and reckless. For a Jacobean audience, equivocation recalled the Gunpowder Plot trials, linking it to treason and evil.
ms: Explains one apparition's prophecy and how it misleads (1 mark)
Explains a second prophecy and how it misleads (1 mark)
Defines equivocation as truthful but deceptive language (1 mark)
Explains its effect on Macbeth or links to Jacobean context (1 mark)
questions.tip: Define equivocation in your answer. Many students use the word without showing they know what it means.

questions.q:
Starting with this moment in the play, explore how Shakespeare presents the idea that killing a king disturbs the natural world.

Write about:
- how Shakespeare presents the natural world in Act 2 Scene 4
- how Shakespeare presents the link between nature and order in the play as a whole. [30 marks]
AO4 [4 marks]

(In Act 2 Scene 4, the morning after Duncan's murder, Ross and an Old Man describe strange events: although it is daytime "dark night strangles the travelling lamp"; a falcon was killed by "a mousing owl"; and Duncan's horses "Turned wild in nature" and are said to have eaten each other. The Old Man calls it "unnatural, / Even like the deed that's done". Macduff enters and reports that Macbeth has been named king.)
questions.answer:
Thesis: Shakespeare presents regicide as a crime against the whole created order: nature itself rebels in Act 2 Scene 4, and the play only heals when a rightful king is restored, reflecting the Jacobean belief in the divine right of kings.
Plan:
1. The extract: personified darkness that "strangles" the sun (verb of murder); the falcon killed by an owl reverses the natural hierarchy just as Macbeth (a subject) kills his king; horses "Turned wild in nature". Pathetic fallacy turns the whole world into a mirror of the crime.
2. Before the murder: Macbeth's "Stars, hide your fires" and Lady Macbeth's "come, thick night": they ask nature to hide their crime, so darkness becomes linked to evil.
3. Disorder in the mind: lost sleep ("Macbeth does murder sleep"), hallucinations and sleepwalking: the natural order of the body is broken too.
4. Restoration: Birnam Wood moving to Dunsinane and Malcolm's coronation. Nature (the trees) becomes part of the army that restores order. Context: Great Chain of Being, divine right, James I and the Gunpowder Plot.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory and conceptualised response; a clear overall argument (thesis) running through the essay; judicious, precise references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; perceptive, convincing links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed response; apt references integrated into interpretation; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.

Level 4 (16-20 marks): clear, explained response; effective use of references to support explanation; clear explanation of the writer's methods with appropriate subject terminology; understanding of effects; clear links between context, text and task.

Level 3 (11-15 marks): some explained response; references used to support a range of relevant comments; explained comments on the writer's methods with some relevant terminology; some identification of effects; some understanding of contextual factors.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Clear argument about regicide and natural order; extract and whole play; development through the play to restoration.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Pathetic fallacy; personification; animal imagery and reversed hierarchy; light/dark imagery; sleep imagery; structure of disorder then restoration.

AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Jacobean context: James I, the divine right of kings, the Great Chain of Being, the Gunpowder Plot, belief in witchcraft; Shakespeare flattering James by presenting Banquo (James's claimed ancestor) positively. Context must explain the text, not sit in a separate paragraph.

AO4 (4 marks): 4 = high performance (consistently accurate spelling and punctuation, control of meaning, wide range of vocabulary and sentence structures); 2-3 = intermediate (considerable accuracy, general control of meaning); 1 = threshold (reasonable accuracy); 0 = no marks.
questions.tip: The Great Chain of Being is only worth AO3 marks if you use it to explain the falcon and the owl, not if you define it in a separate paragraph.

questions.q: Explain how Shakespeare presents Duncan as a good but flawed king. Give three points.
questions.answer: 1. Generous and fair: he rewards loyalty, naming Macbeth Thane of Cawdor after the battle. 2. Trusting: about the traitor Cawdor he says "There's no art / To find the mind's construction in the face", then immediately trusts Macbeth, another traitor (dramatic irony). 3. Holy and gentle: Macbeth himself admits Duncan has been a good, humble ruler and his virtues will "plead like angels". His flaw is naivety: he cannot see through appearances, which makes him vulnerable.
ms: Point on generosity/rewarding loyalty (1 mark)
Point on trusting nature / dramatic irony (1 mark)
Point on holy/virtuous kingship or naivety as his flaw (1 mark)
questions.tip: Duncan is a model of kingship but not perfect. Showing the flaw (naivety) gives your answer a more critical edge.

questions.q: Who says "Another idol has displaced me"?
ms: Belle, Scrooge's former fiancée, says it in Stave 2 when she ends their engagement. The 'idol' is money: 'a golden one'.
questions.tip: Link Belle to the theme of greed replacing love: it explains WHY Scrooge is alone in Stave 1.

questions.q: In Stave 1 the narrator says: "Darkness is cheap, and Scrooge liked it." What does this suggest?
options: Scrooge is miserly, and darkness also hints at his cold, unloving nature
Scrooge cannot afford candles because he is poor
Scrooge is afraid of the light
ms: Literally, he saves money by not lighting candles. Symbolically, darkness links him to moral coldness and the absence of warmth and goodness.
questions.tip: Short narrator comments often carry Dickens's judgement. Give the literal and symbolic meaning.

questions.q: Explain how Dickens presents Fezziwig as a contrast to Scrooge.
questions.answer: Fezziwig is a joyful, generous employer who closes work early on Christmas Eve and throws a party for his workers, apprentices and neighbours. Scrooge, in contrast, begrudges Bob Cratchit even a day off and keeps his office cold. Scrooge himself says Fezziwig's power lies in small things, making work "a pleasure or a toil", showing that a boss's kindness costs little but matters greatly. Dickens uses Fezziwig as a model of responsible employment to criticise employers like Scrooge, and Scrooge immediately thinks of how he treated Bob, the first sign of change.
ms: Describes Fezziwig's generosity/party (1 mark)
Contrasts with Scrooge's treatment of Bob (1 mark)
Explains Scrooge's own response/realisation (1 mark)
Explains Dickens's purpose: model employer / social responsibility (1 mark)
questions.tip: Always say WHY Dickens includes a minor character. Description alone stays at the bottom of the mark range.

questions.q: Explain how Dickens uses the Cratchit family's reaction to Scrooge in Stave 3 to show his effect on others.
questions.answer: When Bob toasts "Mr Scrooge... the Founder of the Feast", Mrs Cratchit reacts with anger, calling him an "odious, stingy, hard, unfeeling man". Her list of adjectives shows how Scrooge's meanness hurts the people who depend on him. Bob's toast is generous and forgiving, showing Christian goodness. The family only drinks reluctantly, and the mention of Scrooge casts "a dark shadow" over the party for a while. Watching this, Scrooge sees how others see him, a step towards his change. Dickens shows readers that the actions of the rich directly affect poor families' happiness.
ms: Reference to Bob's toast and its generosity (1 mark)
Analysis of Mrs Cratchit's list of adjectives (1 mark)
Explains the effect on the family/Scrooge seeing himself through others' eyes (1 mark)
Explains Dickens's purpose: the wealthy's effect on the poor (1 mark)
questions.tip: 'Founder of the Feast' is ironic: Scrooge provides almost nothing. Explain the irony for a higher mark.

questions.q:
Starting with this extract, explore how Dickens uses Scrooge's past to make the reader sympathise with him.

Write about:
- how Dickens presents Scrooge's childhood in this extract
- how Dickens uses Scrooge's past in the novel as a whole. [30 marks]

(In Stave 2 the Ghost of Christmas Past takes Scrooge to his old school. The Ghost says "A solitary child, neglected by his friends, is left there still." Scrooge sees his younger self reading alone in a cold, bare classroom while the other boys have gone home for Christmas, and he weeps at the sight. He recalls the characters from the books he read as a boy, and then wishes he had given something to a boy singing a carol at his door the night before.)
questions.answer:
Thesis: Dickens uses Scrooge's past to show that his coldness was made, not born: by revealing a lonely, neglected child, he makes the reader pity Scrooge and believe that the present Scrooge can still be redeemed.
Plan:
1. The extract: "A solitary child, neglected by his friends" echoes the "solitary as an oyster" description in Stave 1, linking the lonely boy to the lonely man. Scrooge weeping shows hidden feeling; the carol-singer regret is his first moral change.
2. Fan's arrival: his loving sister brings him home; her early death (and Fred being her son) explains both his pain and why Fred matters.
3. Fezziwig and Belle: warmth and love were once possible for him. Belle's "Another idol has displaced me" shows the moment greed replaced love: sympathy mixed with judgement.
4. Purpose and context: Dickens's own childhood work in a blacking factory; Victorian neglect of poor and lonely children; Ignorance and Want in Stave 3 extend the idea that neglected children become a danger to society. The structure of the staves makes the past the first step in redemption.
ms: Level 6 (26-30 marks): critical, exploratory and conceptualised response; a clear overall argument (thesis) running through the essay; judicious, precise references; analysis of the writer's methods with subject terminology used judiciously; exploration of effects on the reader/audience; perceptive, convincing links between context, text and task.

Level 5 (21-25 marks): thoughtful, developed response; apt references integrated into interpretation; examination of the writer's methods with effective use of subject terminology; thoughtful consideration of effects; thoughtful links between context, text and task.

Level 4 (16-20 marks): clear, explained response; effective use of references to support explanation; clear explanation of the writer's methods with appropriate subject terminology; understanding of effects; clear links between context, text and task.

Level 3 (11-15 marks): some explained response; references used to support a range of relevant comments; explained comments on the writer's methods with some relevant terminology; some identification of effects; some understanding of contextual factors.
AO1 (12 marks) indicative content: Clear argument about sympathy and redemption; extract linked to the whole novella; balanced view of sympathy and judgement.
AO2 (12 marks) indicative content: Narrator's voice; repetition of 'solitary'; Scrooge's emotional reactions; structure of the staves; the contrasting scenes (school, Fezziwig, Belle); symbolism.

AO3 (6 marks) indicative content: Victorian context: the 1834 Poor Law and workhouses; Malthus and the 'surplus population'; child poverty; Dickens's own childhood in a blacking factory; Christian ideas of charity and redemption; Dickens's purpose to change readers' attitudes.
questions.tip: There is no AO4 for A Christmas Carol, but don't drop accuracy. Spend the time on whole-text links instead of retelling Stave 2.

questions.q: Give two things Scrooge does in Stave 5 to show he has changed.
questions.answer: Any two: sends the prize turkey to the Cratchits; promises a large donation to the charity collector he turned away; goes to Fred's house for Christmas dinner; raises Bob Cratchit's salary; becomes 'a second father' to Tiny Tim.
ms: First correct action (1 mark)
Second correct action (1 mark)
questions.tip: Be specific: 'he is nicer' does not count. Name the action.

flashcards.front: "brave Macbeth" - who says it and what does it show?
flashcards.back: The Captain (Act 1.2). Macbeth begins as a loyal, admired warrior, which makes his fall tragic.

flashcards.front: "Fair is foul, and foul is fair"
flashcards.back: Witches, Act 1.1. Paradox: appearances deceive; moral order is inverted.
Macbeth's aside, Act 1.4, after Malcolm is named heir. Light/dark imagery: he wants to hide his evil desires.
Lady Macbeth, Act 1.5. Asks spirits to remove her femininity so she can be cruel; links her to the supernatural.

flashcards.front: "Look like th' innocent flower, / But be the serpent under't"
flashcards.back: Lady Macbeth, Act 1.5. Deception; serpent alludes to Satan in Eden.
Macbeth's soliloquy, Act 1.7. He admits ambition is his only motive: his hamartia.

flashcards.front: "When you durst do it, then you were a man"
flashcards.back: Lady Macbeth, Act 1.7. She manipulates him by questioning his masculinity.

flashcards.front: "Is this a dagger which I see before me"
flashcards.back: Macbeth, Act 2.1. Hallucination: guilt or the supernatural pulling him to murder.
Macbeth, Act 2.2. Sleep = innocence and peace; he has destroyed his own peace of mind.

flashcards.front: "O, full of scorpions is my mind, dear wife!"
flashcards.back: Macbeth, Act 3.2. Paranoia and torment after becoming king.

flashcards.front: "Be innocent of the knowledge, dearest chuck"
flashcards.back: Macbeth to Lady Macbeth, Act 3.2. He now plans murder alone: power shifts.

flashcards.front: "I am in blood / Stepp'd in so far"
flashcards.back: Macbeth, Act 3.4. He feels going back is as hard as going on: trapped in evil.
Lady Macbeth sleepwalking, Act 5.1. Guilt breaks her mind; she cannot wash away the imagined blood.
Macbeth, Act 5.5. Nihilism: after Lady Macbeth's death life feels meaningless.

flashcards.front: "this dead butcher and his fiend-like queen"
flashcards.back: Malcolm, in the final scene. Final judgement on the Macbeths; order restored.

flashcards.front: "I must also feel it as a man"
flashcards.back: Macduff, Act 4.3. Grief for his family; true masculinity includes emotion.
Banquo, Act 1.3. He distrusts the Witches; foil to Macbeth.
King of Scotland. Trusting and generous; murdered by Macbeth in Act 2. Represents rightful, divinely appointed kingship.
Duncan's elder son, named Prince of Cumberland. Flees to England, tests Macduff, becomes king at the end.
Banquo's son. Escapes the murderers in Act 3, so Banquo's line (ancestors of James I) survives.
Macbeth has Lady Macduff and her children murdered in Act 4.2: his most pointless, tyrannical act.
Offstage, reportedly by suicide, in Act 5. Her death is announced with a cry of women.

flashcards.front: Who is the Porter and why is he included?
flashcards.back: The drunk gatekeeper in Act 2.3. Comic relief, imagines he is porter of hell-gate, jokes about an 'equivocator'.
1: prophecies, plan. 2: Duncan murdered. 3: Macbeth king, Banquo killed, ghost. 4: apparitions, Macduff's family killed. 5: Lady Macbeth's madness and death, Macbeth killed.

flashcards.front: Macbeth's character arc in one line
flashcards.back: Brave warrior, tempted, murderer, paranoid tyrant, nihilist, dies fighting.

flashcards.front: Lady Macbeth's character arc in one line
flashcards.back: Dominant and ambitious, coaches Macbeth, sidelined, guilt-ridden, sleepwalks, dies.
Macbeth's final defiance in Act 5.8: some of his warrior courage returns even when he knows he is doomed.
Scottish thanes. Ross carries news (including Macduff's family's murder); Lennox becomes sarcastic and suspicious of Macbeth in Act 3.6.

flashcards.front: When was Macbeth written and for whom?
flashcards.back: About 1606, for King James I, who claimed descent from Banquo.
Belief that monarchs are chosen by God; killing a king is a sin against God.
God's fixed order of the universe: God, angels, king, nobles, commoners, animals. Regicide breaks it, so nature becomes chaotic.
1605 Catholic plot to blow up James I and Parliament. Makes regicide in Macbeth highly topical.
James I's 1597 book on witchcraft. Shows his belief that witches threatened kings.
1590s Scotland: witches accused of raising storms against James's ship. Links to the Witches' storms.
Speaking ambiguously to deceive. The Porter mentions an 'equivocator' (Father Garnet, Gunpowder Plot). The apparitions equivocate.
Shakespeare's historical source. He changed it to make Banquo innocent, flattering James I.
Macbeth's 'vaulting ambition' drives the tragedy. Unchecked ambition destroys the self and the kingdom.
Shown through blood imagery, hallucinations, lost sleep and Lady Macbeth's madness.
"Fair is foul", the serpent under the flower, Duncan's misplaced trust in Cawdor and Macbeth.
Lady Macbeth links manhood to violence; Macduff shows men can feel grief; Macbeth's violence becomes monstrous.
Good kings (Duncan, Edward, Malcolm) contrast with the tyrant Macbeth. Malcolm lists the 'king-becoming graces'.
The Witches predict but do not command. Banquo hears the same prophecies but chooses not to act.
Represents guilt and violence: daggers, 'Neptune's ocean', 'damned spot', 'I am in blood'.
Borrowed robes: the crown fits Macbeth like 'a giant's robe' on a 'dwarfish thief' - he is not a rightful king.
Light = goodness/God; darkness = evil. 'Stars, hide your fires', 'Come, thick night', Lady Macbeth needs a candle in 5.1.
Four stressed-unstressed beats, used by the Witches ('Double, double toil and trouble'). Sets them apart from humans.
Nobles speak in verse. Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking in prose shows her mind breaking down.
A character speaks thoughts alone on stage. Macbeth's in 1.7 and 2.1 reveal conscience and ambition.
High status, hamartia (fatal flaw), downfall, anagnorisis (realisation), catharsis for the audience.
Darkness in daytime, a falcon killed by an owl, Duncan's horses eating each other: nature is disordered.
English king who heals by touch (Act 4.3). Symbol of holy kingship; James I also 'touched' for scrofula.
Expected to be obedient wives and mothers. Lady Macbeth's ambition and rejection of motherhood would shock.

flashcards.front: When was A Christmas Carol published?
flashcards.back: December 1843.

flashcards.front: Why are the chapters called staves?
flashcards.back: A stave is a verse of a song: the novella is structured like a Christmas carol, in 5 staves.
Stave 1. Scrooge is closed off, but an oyster may hide a pearl: potential for goodness.
Stave 1. Listing of harsh verbs shows Scrooge's greed.
Scrooge to the charity collectors, Stave 1. Shows his cruelty and support for harsh systems.
Scrooge, Stave 1 (Malthusian idea). Thrown back at him by the Ghost of Christmas Present.

flashcards.front: "I wear the chain I forged in life"
flashcards.back: Marley's Ghost, Stave 1. Sins create a self-made punishment.
Marley's Ghost, Stave 1. Real business is caring for others: key moral message.

flashcards.front: "A small matter... to make these silly folks so full of gratitude"
flashcards.back: Ghost of Christmas Past about Fezziwig's party, Stave 2. Scrooge defends Fezziwig, realising employers' power.
Stave 2. Belle releases Scrooge because money has replaced her in his heart.
Tiny Tim, Stave 3 and the final line of the book. Message of Christian goodwill.
Two wretched children under the Ghost of Present's robe, Stave 3. Allegory of society's neglect. Ignorance has 'Doom' written on his brow.

flashcards.front: "I will honour Christmas in my heart"
flashcards.back: Scrooge, Stave 4, at his grave: a promise to change.

flashcards.front: "I am as light as a feather"
flashcards.back: Scrooge, Stave 5. Joy and freedom, contrast with Marley's heavy chain.
Stave 5: Scrooge becomes this to Tiny Tim, who does not die.
Strange, childlike yet old, with a bright light from its head. Shows Scrooge's lonely school days, Fan, Fezziwig, Belle.
Jolly giant in a green robe, surrounded by feast food. Shows the Cratchits, miners, Fred's party.

flashcards.front: Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come
flashcards.back: Silent, hooded, only points. Shows Scrooge's unmourned death and Tiny Tim's death.
Scrooge's loving younger sister who brought him home from school. Fred's mother; died young.
Scrooge's old employer, a kind, generous boss. Model of a good employer.
Scrooge's nephew. Cheerful, forgiving, represents the Christmas spirit.
Scrooge's underpaid clerk (15 shillings a week). Loving father; represents the deserving poor.
A rag-and-bone dealer in Stave 4 who buys the dead Scrooge's stolen belongings.
Aged 12, worked in a blacking factory while his father was in the Marshalsea debtors' prison.
Forced poor people into harsh workhouses. Dickens criticised it.
Economist who argued population growth would outstrip food; used to justify not helping the poor.
Free schools for poor children that Dickens visited and supported; linked to the warning about Ignorance.
He chose a story instead of a political pamphlet to have far greater impact on readers.
Anyone can change; Scrooge's transformation is a Christian rebirth on Christmas Day.
The wealthy must care for the poor: 'Mankind was my business'.
Cratchits and Fred show love and warmth; Scrooge's isolation is self-chosen.
Stave 5 mirrors Stave 1: same people (Fred, Bob, collectors), but Scrooge treats them kindly.
Scrooge is linked to cold, fog and darkness; in Stave 5 he is linked to light and warmth.
Wealthy factory owner, former Lord Mayor, hoping for a knighthood. Capitalist; refuses to accept responsibility.
Arthur's wife, socially superior to him. Chairs the charity that refuses Eva. Cold and prejudiced.
The Birlings' daughter, engaged to Gerald. Changes most, accepts responsibility.
The Birlings' son. Drinks heavily, got Eva pregnant, stole money. Accepts guilt and condemns his parents.
Son of Sir George and Lady Croft. Had an affair with Eva (as Daisy Renton). Returns to complacency.
Mysterious visitor who exposes each character's role. Priestley's mouthpiece for socialism.
Working-class young woman who dies after swallowing disinfectant. Represents the exploited poor.
The Birlings' maid. A reminder of the working class serving the family.
1. Sacked by Birling. 2. Sacked from Milwards by Sheila. 3. Gerald's mistress. 4. Eric gets her pregnant. 5. Refused help by Mrs Birling. 6. Dies.
Birling describing himself: pride in capitalism.
Birling on the Titanic: dramatic irony exposes his poor judgement.
Mrs Birling: class prejudice towards Eva.
Sheila, Act 1: she starts to show empathy and challenge her father.
Her language matures: from childish 'mummy' to a more adult 'mother', showing independence.
Eric to Birling: he couldn't turn to his father, showing family failure.
Eric to Mrs Birling in Act 3: he blames her for the death of Eva and his child.
Early in Act 1 Sheila teases Gerald that he never came near her "all last summer"; he claims he was busy at the works. He actually met Daisy at the Palace bar.
A drunk, lecherous councillor Gerald rescues Daisy from: shows corruption of powerful men.
Symbol of a business-like engagement. Sheila returns it in Act 2.
The Inspector shows it to one person at a time, so each may have seen a different girl.
A girl has died and an inspector is coming: the family must face it all again.
She demands the father be made an example, unaware it is Eric. Strong dramatic irony at the end of Act 2.
Change: Sheila and Eric. No change: Mr and Mrs Birling, Gerald.
Set in 1912 (before WW1, Titanic); written 1945, performed 1945-46.
Yorkshire writer and socialist; fought in WW1; wartime radio Postscripts; co-founded the Common Wealth Party.
Belief that society should share wealth and responsibility, protecting the vulnerable.
Economic system where private owners run businesses for profit. Represented by Birling.
Labour landslide; led to the NHS (1948) and the welfare state. Matches Priestley's message.
The Inspector's final speech: the play's key message of collective responsibility.
The Inspector's warning: links to WW1 and WW2.
Key phrase from the Inspector's speech: Eva represents every vulnerable worker.
Individual and collective. The play asks who is to blame: everyone.
Upper class exploits and judges the working class; the Birlings value status.
The young (Sheila, Eric) change; the old (Birlings) don't: hope lies with the young.
Women judged by looks; Eva exploited by men; Sheila grows; Mrs Birling enforces class.
'pink and intimate' becomes 'brighter and harder' when the Inspector arrives: comfortable illusions replaced by truth.
A 'heavily comfortable' house, but not cosy: wealth without warmth.
One place, one evening, continuous time: claustrophobic, the family can't escape.
A tightly plotted play with a climax and resolution, often a mystery. Priestley subverts it.
Medieval drama teaching right and wrong. One interpretation (not stated by Priestley) sees the Inspector as a judge figure and the characters as linked to the seven deadly sins.
A popular critical reading, not stated by Priestley: Birling = greed, Sheila = envy, Gerald = lust, Eric = gluttony (drink), Mrs Birling = pride. Present it as 'some critics suggest'.
The 1945 audience knew the Titanic sank and two wars came, so Birling looks foolish.
The Inspector's name suggests a ghostly, otherworldly figure.
No vote (until 1918 for some women); limited rights; working-class women especially vulnerable.
Real wave of industrial unrest, including the 1912 national coal strike. Context for Eva's factory strike.
Power and pride are temporary; time and nature destroy tyrants, while art survives.
"sneer of cold command"; "Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!"; "lone and level sands".
Shelley (1818), Romantic radical. Based on Rameses II's statue; attacks tyranny and monarchy.
Sonnet with an irregular rhyme scheme: breaks rules like broken power. Framed narrative via a traveller.
Industrial London is full of suffering caused by corrupt institutions (Church, monarchy).
"mind-forg'd manacles"; "marks of weakness, marks of woe"; "chartered street"; "youthful Harlot's curse".
Blake (1794), Romantic, Songs of Experience. Opposed industrialisation and the Church's hypocrisy; French Revolution era.
Four regular quatrains, ABAB rhyme, steady rhythm like trudging through streets. Repetition of 'every'.
Nature's power humbles human pride and leaves a lasting spiritual effect.
"led by her"; "a huge peak, black and huge"; "huge and mighty forms".
Wordsworth, Romantic. Autobiographical epic, published 1850 after his death.
Blank verse; volta when the peak appears; mood shifts from confident to fearful to troubled.
The Duke's arrogance and jealousy show the abuse of patriarchal power.
"Looking as if she were alive"; "I gave commands"; "Then all smiles stopped together".
Browning (1842). Based on Alfonso II, Duke of Ferrara (16th century), whose young wife died suspiciously.
Dramatic monologue in rhyming couplets with heavy enjambment: control masking obsession.

flashcards.front: Charge of the Light Brigade: message
flashcards.back: Celebrates soldiers' courage and obedience despite a military blunder.

flashcards.front: Charge of the Light Brigade: key quotes
flashcards.back: "Theirs not to reason why"; "Into the valley of Death"; "Some one had blunder'd"; "Honour the Light Brigade".

flashcards.front: Charge of the Light Brigade: context
flashcards.back: Tennyson, Poet Laureate, 1854. Battle of Balaclava, Crimean War; about 600 cavalry.

flashcards.front: Charge of the Light Brigade: form
flashcards.back: Dactylic dimeter imitating galloping; repetition and refrains; six stanzas.
Soldiers suffer more from the freezing weather and futile waiting than from the enemy.
"Our brains ache"; "But nothing happens"; "merciless iced east winds that knive us"; "All their eyes are ice".
Wilfred Owen, WW1 soldier poet, written 1917-18; killed one week before the Armistice.
Eight five-line stanzas; pararhyme; each stanza ends on a short half-line, and "But nothing happens" recurs as a refrain, creating anticlimax.
Humans are powerless against nature; possibly a metaphor for the Troubles.

flashcards.front: Storm on the Island: key phrases
flashcards.back: "We are prepared"; "exploding comfortably"; "spits like a tame cat"; "a huge nothing that we fear".
Seamus Heaney (1966), Northern Irish. Title may pun on Stormont.
Single block stanza of blank verse, like a fortress; conversational tone; enjambment.
Patriotic ideals collapse in the terror of battle; the soldier becomes an animal fighting to survive.
"Suddenly he awoke"; "yellow hare"; "like luxuries"; "King, honour, human dignity, etcetera".
Ted Hughes (1957). His father fought in WW1 at Gallipoli; Hughes imagines the experience.
Starts in medias res; time slows in stanza 2 (a pause of confusion); ends with explosive action.
A soldier is haunted by guilt and trauma (PTSD) after killing a looter.
"On another occasion"; "probably armed, possibly not"; "dug in behind enemy lines"; "blood-shadow".
Simon Armitage (2008), from The Not Dead, based on testimony of soldiers in Iraq.
Shift from 'we' to 'I'; colloquial voice; final couplet-like lines; flashback cycle.
A mother's grief and fear as her son leaves for war; memory and loss at home.
"Armistice Sunday"; "steeled the softening of my face"; "play at being Eskimos"; "the dove pulled freely".
Jane Weir (2009), textile designer; commissioned by Carol Ann Duffy in 2009 for a collection on modern conflict.
Free verse, long enjambed lines, caesura; dramatic monologue to her son.
The photographer is traumatised by what he records, while the public quickly forgets.
"spools of suffering"; "ordered rows"; "All flesh is grass"; "they do not care".
Carol Ann Duffy (1985), inspired by friends Don McCullin and Philip Jones Griffiths.
Four regular six-line stanzas with rhyme: order the photographer imposes on chaos.
Human systems of power (maps, money, borders) are fragile; humanity should be open and light.
"Paper that lets the light"; "never meant to last"; "your skin".
Imtiaz Dharker (2006), born in Pakistan, grew up in Glasgow; explores identity and borders.
Free verse in unrhymed quatrains, single final line: lighter, like the ideas it praises.
An exile holds on to idealised childhood memories of a city now ruled by tyranny.
"There once was a country"; "sunlight-clear"; "my city"; "evidence of sunlight".
Carol Rumens (1993). The city is unnamed, so it stands for many refugees' homelands.
Three stanzas with recurring light imagery, ending on sunlight; fairy-tale opening; first person.
Black and Caribbean history has been hidden by a Eurocentric education; the speaker reclaims identity.

flashcards.front: Checking Out Me History: key phrases
flashcards.back: "Dem tell me"; "Toussaint L'Ouverture"; "healing star"; "carving out me identity".
John Agard, born 1949 in Guyana, moved to the UK in 1977. Uses Caribbean Creole.
Dialect, phonetic spelling, no standard punctuation; italic stanzas on Black heroes; repetition.
A pilot's choice to live leads to lifelong shame and rejection: the conflict between duty and humanity.
"Her father embarked"; "cairns of pearl-grey pebbles"; "no longer the father".
Beatrice Garland (2013). WW2 Japanese kamikaze pilots; surviving was seen as deep dishonour.
Third-person narrative through the daughter; final stanzas shift into the daughter's own voice; seven stanzas.
Storm on the Island, The Prelude, Exposure, (Ozymandias - time and nature destroy power).

flashcards.front: Power of humans / tyranny: best pairs
flashcards.back: Ozymandias, My Last Duchess, London, Tissue.

flashcards.front: Effects of conflict on soldiers: pairs
flashcards.back: Remains, Exposure, Bayonet Charge, Charge of the Light Brigade, Kamikaze.
Remains, Poppies, The Emigree, War Photographer, Kamikaze, The Prelude.
Checking Out Me History, The Emigree, Tissue, Kamikaze, My Last Duchess.
Poppies, War Photographer, Kamikaze, Remains.
Ozymandias, My Last Duchess, The Prelude (the boy's pride), Charge of the Light Brigade.
Remains and War Photographer (both haunted after the event).
Ozymandias (statue), My Last Duchess (portrait), War Photographer (photos), Tissue (paper).
Glorifies: Charge of the Light Brigade. Criticises: Exposure, Bayonet Charge, Remains.
My Last Duchess, Remains, Poppies, The Emigree: speakers reveal themselves.
Both arrogant rulers judged through art; Ozymandias's power is gone, the Duke's is still active.

flashcards.front: Exposure vs Storm on the Island
flashcards.back: Both show nature as an enemy using military language; Owen's soldiers are dying, Heaney's islanders endure.
One moment changes a life: Remains = guilt for killing; Kamikaze = shame for surviving.
Memory of a lost loved one/place; Poppies is grief, The Emigree is defiant love.

flashcards.front: London vs Checking Out Me History
flashcards.back: Both attack institutions (Church/monarchy vs education) using repetition and anger.

flashcards.front: Bayonet Charge vs Charge of the Light Brigade
flashcards.back: Both show charges; Hughes shows terror and lost ideals, Tennyson glorifies obedience.
Both Romantic: nature dwarfs human pride, but Wordsworth learns personally while Shelley mocks a tyrant.
Both show human-made power is temporary; Shelley ironic, Dharker hopeful.
Both haunted by images of death; photographer can't make the public care, soldier can't escape memory.
Shared idea, poem A method + quote + effect, comparative connective, poem B method + quote + effect, context for both.
Similarly, likewise, in contrast, whereas, however, conversely, both poets...
Sonnet (Ozymandias), dramatic monologue (MLD), single block stanza (Storm), regular stanzas (War Photographer, London), free verse (Poppies, Tissue).

About 30-35 minutes for 27.1 and 10-15 minutes for 27.2. Read each poem twice.
Structure, Meaning, Imagery, Language, Effect: a quick way to annotate an unseen poem.
A sentence runs over a line break: creates flow, speed, or emphasis on the next word.
A pause in the middle of a line (punctuation): creates hesitation, shock or emphasis.
A turn in mood or argument, often in sonnets.
No regular rhyme or metre: can suggest freedom, natural speech or chaos.
Ten syllables, five unstressed-stressed beats: like a heartbeat, natural speech.
Two consecutive rhyming lines: can create closure, control or emphasis.
A group of words linked by meaning, e.g. military words used for a storm.
Placing contrasting ideas close together to highlight difference.
Repeated 's' sounds: can be soft, soothing or sinister.
Harsh b, p, t, d, k sounds: suggest anger, violence or force.
The voice or character speaking the poem, not necessarily the poet.
The attitude or mood of the voice, e.g. bitter, nostalgic, reverent.
Open with an overview thesis answering the question, then work through the poem's journey.
