flashcards.front: [Macbeth: early doubt] "Present fears / Are less than horrible imaginings"
flashcards.back: Macbeth, 1.3 aside. Analysis: his imagination outruns reality; murder is already in his mind. Method: aside, antithesis of real fears vs imagined horrors. Context: Jacobean fear that the devil tempts through thoughts.

flashcards.front: [Macbeth: ambition] "I have no spur / To prick the sides of my intent"
flashcards.back: Macbeth, 1.7 soliloquy. Analysis: no moral reason to kill, only ambition. Method: extended horse-riding metaphor. Link: Lady Macbeth enters as the 'spur'. Context: free will vs fate in tragedy.

flashcards.front: [Macbeth: imagination] "a dagger of the mind, a false creation"
flashcards.back: Macbeth, 2.1. Analysis: hallucination shows a conscience-torn mind. Method: soliloquy, rhetorical questions. Context: could be read as demonic temptation by a Jacobean audience.

flashcards.front: [Macbeth: guilt] "Wake Duncan with thy knocking! I would thou couldst!"
flashcards.back: Macbeth, 2.2. Analysis: instant regret after the murder. Method: exclamation, apostrophe to the knocking. Context: guilt as a sign of a soul that knows it has sinned.

flashcards.front: [Macbeth: insecurity] "To be thus is nothing; / But to be safely thus"
flashcards.back: Macbeth, 3.1. Analysis: the crown is worthless without safety; paranoia begins. Method: antithesis. Context: usurpers could never feel secure under divine right.

flashcards.front: [Macbeth: no heirs] "Upon my head they placed a fruitless crown"
flashcards.back: Macbeth, 3.1. Analysis: power with no future; Banquo's line will rule. Method: infertility imagery. Context: James I claimed descent from Banquo.

flashcards.front: [Macbeth: manipulation] "Ay, in the catalogue ye go for men"
flashcards.back: Macbeth to the murderers, 3.1. Analysis: he now manipulates manhood like Lady Macbeth did. Method: dog-breed comparison, questioning. Context: Jacobean masculinity as courage.
Macbeth, 3.4. Analysis: violence is cyclical and demands more. Method: repetition, fatalistic tone. Context: biblical idea that murdered blood cries for justice.

flashcards.front: [Macbeth: tyranny] "The very firstlings of my heart"
flashcards.back: Macbeth, 4.1. Analysis: he will act on impulse without thinking, leading to Macduff's family being killed. Method: repetition/parallelism. Context: tyranny as rule by impulse.

flashcards.front: [Macbeth: emptiness] "I have almost forgot the taste of fears"
flashcards.back: Macbeth, 5.5. Analysis: he has become numb, a moral death. Method: sensory metaphor of taste. Link: contrast with his terror in 2.1.

flashcards.front: [Macbeth: despair] "a tale / Told by an idiot"
flashcards.back: Macbeth, 5.5. Analysis: life is meaningless to him. Method: metaphor, nihilistic tone. Context: tragedy shows the spiritual cost of sin.

flashcards.front: [Macbeth: defiance] "I'll fight till from my bones my flesh be hack'd"
flashcards.back: Macbeth, 5.3. Analysis: he returns to the warrior of 1.2, but now fighting for a stolen crown. Method: violent, physical imagery; determined future tense. Context: the tragic hero keeps a trace of courage, which makes his fall more tragic.
Lady Macbeth, 1.5. Analysis: she summons darkness to hide sin from heaven. Method: imperative, light/dark imagery. Link: needs a light in 5.1. Context: witchcraft fears.

flashcards.front: [Lady Macbeth: manipulation] "Was the hope drunk / Wherein you dress'd yourself?"
flashcards.back: Lady Macbeth, 1.7. Analysis: mocks his ambition as drunken talk. Method: rhetorical question, clothing metaphor. Context: wife insulting husband reverses Jacobean gender roles.

flashcards.front: [Lady Macbeth: false confidence] "A little water clears us of this deed"
flashcards.back: Lady Macbeth, 2.2. Analysis: she trivialises guilt. Method: dramatic irony reversed in 5.1. Context: guilt cannot be washed away in a Christian worldview.
Lady Macbeth, 3.2. Analysis: gaining the crown brought no joy. Method: antithesis, monosyllables. Link: first crack before her breakdown.
Lady Macbeth, 5.1. Analysis: she now fears damnation. Method: prose, fragmented speech. Context: Jacobean belief in hell and divine punishment.

flashcards.front: [Lady Macbeth: permanent guilt] "all the perfumes of Arabia"
flashcards.back: Lady Macbeth, 5.1. Analysis: no luxury can remove the smell of blood; guilt is permanent. Method: hyperbole, sensory imagery. Link: echoes Macbeth's 'Neptune's ocean'.

flashcards.front: [Banquo: suspicion] "I fear / Thou play'dst most foully for't"
flashcards.back: Banquo, 3.1. Analysis: he suspects Macbeth but stays silent, compromising himself. Method: soliloquy. Context: Banquo as ancestor of James I is shown as mostly virtuous.

flashcards.front: [Banquo: resisting temptation] "Merciful powers, / Restrain in me the cursed thoughts"
flashcards.back: Banquo, 2.1. Analysis: he has the same temptation but prays against it, a foil to Macbeth. Method: prayer/apostrophe. Context: free will to resist evil.

flashcards.front: [Duncan: misplaced trust] "There's no art / To find the mind's construction in the face"
flashcards.back: Duncan, 1.4. Analysis: appearance hides reality; ironic as Macbeth enters next. Method: dramatic irony. Context: kingship needs judgement of men.

flashcards.front: [Duncan: kindness] "This castle hath a pleasant seat"
flashcards.back: Duncan, 1.6. Analysis: dramatic irony; he praises the place he will die. Method: dramatic irony, pastoral imagery. Context: hospitality was sacred, so the murder breaks the laws of guest and host.
Macduff, 4.3. Analysis: tender grief for his children. Method: emotive adjective; contrast with Macbeth's numbness. Context: masculinity can include feeling.
Macduff, 5.8. Analysis: Macbeth is now demonic. Method: imperative, metaphor. Context: tyrant as devil; restoring God's order.
Malcolm, 5.8. Analysis: order is restored with God's blessing. Method: repetition/wordplay. Context: divine right of kings.
Witches, 4.1. Analysis: chant suggests a spell. Method: trochaic tetrameter, rhyming couplets. Context: Daemonologie and James I's fear of witches.

flashcards.front: [Witches: Macbeth now wicked] "Something wicked this way comes"
flashcards.back: Second Witch, 4.1. Analysis: even the Witches see Macbeth as evil. Method: rhyming couplet. Link: shows how far he has fallen.
Ross, 2.4. Analysis: nature murdered like Duncan; darkness by day. Method: personification, pathetic fallacy. Context: Great Chain of Being broken by regicide.
Macduff, 2.3. Analysis: the murder is the ultimate chaos. Method: personification of Confusion as an artist. Context: regicide as sacrilege.

flashcards.front: [Clothing imagery] "like a giant's robe / Upon a dwarfish thief"
flashcards.back: Angus, 5.2. Analysis: Macbeth is too small for the kingship he stole. Method: simile, clothing motif. Context: illegitimate king.

flashcards.front: [Appearance vs reality] "False face must hide what the false heart doth know"
flashcards.back: Macbeth, 1.7. Analysis: commits to deception. Method: rhyming couplet ending the scene, repetition of 'false'. Context: link to equivocation and the Gunpowder Plot.

flashcards.front: [Sleep] "Sleep that knits up the ravell'd sleave of care"
flashcards.back: Macbeth, 2.2. Analysis: sleep heals; he has destroyed his own peace. Method: metaphor of knitting. Link: Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking.

flashcards.front: [Scrooge: meanness] "Darkness is cheap, and Scrooge liked it"
flashcards.back: Stave 1. Analysis: miserliness controls even comfort. Method: short declarative sentence, light/dark symbolism. Context: Victorian businessmen saving at the expense of comfort and others.

flashcards.front: [Scrooge: coldness] "The cold within him froze his old features"
flashcards.back: Stave 1. Analysis: inner coldness made physical. Method: cold imagery, personification. Link: warmth returns in Stave 5.
Stave 1. Analysis: unyielding; flint sparks but never warms. Method: simile. Context: Dickens's caricature of the Victorian miser.
Stave 1, to Marley. Analysis: he blames indigestion for the ghost, refusing to believe. Method: humour, list of foods. Link: resistance to change.

flashcards.front: [Scrooge: lonely childhood] "a solitary child, neglected by his friends"
flashcards.back: Stave 2. Analysis: explains his isolation; evokes sympathy. Method: pathos. Context: Dickens's own lonely childhood and the blacking factory.
Stave 2 after seeing Belle's family. Analysis: memory has become unbearable; he is beginning to feel. Method: exclamation, imperative.

flashcards.front: [Scrooge: new man] "I am not the man I was"
flashcards.back: Stave 4. Analysis: declares redemption. Method: simple declarative, past vs present. Context: Christian repentance.

flashcards.front: [Scrooge: joy] "as giddy as a drunken man"
flashcards.back: Stave 5. Analysis: complete loss of his old control. Method: simile, comic tone. Link: contrast with 'solitary as an oyster'.
Stave 2. Analysis: money is a false god replacing love. Method: religious lexis. Context: Christian warnings about worshipping wealth.

flashcards.front: [Belle: cause of greed] "You fear the world too much"
flashcards.back: Stave 2. Analysis: greed comes from fear of poverty, a sympathetic reading. Method: dialogue. Context: insecurity of Victorian economy; Dickens's father's debt.

flashcards.front: [Fred: Christmas spirit] "a kind, forgiving, charitable, pleasant time"
flashcards.back: Stave 1. Analysis: Christmas as moral values. Method: list of adjectives. Context: Dickens popularising the Victorian Christmas.

flashcards.front: [Fred: forgiveness] "His offences carry their own punishment"
flashcards.back: Stave 3. Analysis: Fred pities rather than hates Scrooge. Method: dialogue. Context: Christian forgiveness.

flashcards.front: [Fezziwig: good employer] "as great as if it cost a fortune"
flashcards.back: Scrooge, Stave 2. Analysis: Scrooge argues against his own values. Method: dialogue, irony. Context: employers' duty to workers.

flashcards.front: [Christmas Present] "a jolly Giant, glorious to see"
flashcards.back: Stave 3. Analysis: abundance and generosity. Method: alliteration, description. Link: hides Ignorance and Want under his robe.

flashcards.front: [Christmas Past] "not so like a child as like an old man"
flashcards.back: Stave 2. Analysis: memory mixes youth and age. Method: paradox. Link: light from its head shows truth.

flashcards.front: [Christmas Yet to Come] "shrouded in a deep black garment"
flashcards.back: Stave 4. Analysis: death and the unknown future. Method: Gothic imagery, silence. Context: Victorian fear of death and judgement.
Stave 3, Ignorance and Want. Analysis: poverty dehumanises. Method: list of adjectives, allegory. Context: 1843 child labour report, Ragged Schools.
Ghost of Christmas Present, Stave 3. Analysis: prophetic warning to society. Method: imperative. Context: fear of social unrest in the 1840s.

flashcards.front: [Future] "If these shadows remain unaltered by the Future"
flashcards.back: Stave 3. Analysis: the future can change. Method: conditional grammar. Context: Christian redemption.
Bob, Stave 3. Analysis: bitter irony; Scrooge gives nothing. Method: irony, Mrs Cratchit's angry reaction. Context: low wages.
Stave 3. Analysis: low wages trap the family. Method: pun on 'Bob' (shilling). Context: Victorian clerks' pay; Dickens's family debt.

flashcards.front: [Death] "Why show me this, if I am past all hope?"
flashcards.back: Scrooge at his grave, Stave 4. Analysis: he realises change is still possible. Method: rhetorical question. Context: Christian repentance before judgement.

flashcards.front: [Narrator] "Old Marley was as dead as a door-nail"
flashcards.back: Stave 1 opening. Analysis: chatty narrator; certainty sets up the ghost. Method: simile, direct address. Context: ghost-story tradition at Christmas.
Stave 1. Analysis: Scrooge works others hard and gives nothing. Method: idiom, exclamatory narrator. Context: Victorian work ethic.

flashcards.front: [Redemption] "I will live in the Past, the Present, and the Future!"
flashcards.back: Scrooge, Stave 4. Analysis: he promises to learn from all three spirits; time becomes a moral teacher. Method: tricolon, capitalised abstract nouns, exclamation. Context: Christian repentance and the novella's three-ghost structure.

flashcards.front: [Birling: dramatic irony] "the Germans don't want war"
flashcards.back: Act 1. Analysis: confidently wrong, so the audience distrusts him. Method: dramatic irony. Context: 1945 audience had lived through two world wars.
Act 1. Analysis: profit over people. Method: antithesis-like pairing. Context: Edwardian capitalism, strikes of 1912.
Act 1. Analysis: he values honours over morality; fears scandal. Method: dialogue, dramatic irony. Context: 'new money' vs aristocracy.
Act 1. Analysis: dismisses social responsibility. Method: dismissive noun; interrupted by the doorbell. Context: Priestley's socialism challenges this.
Opening stage direction. Analysis: defined by status, not warmth. Method: stage direction. Context: Edwardian upper-middle-class respectability.

flashcards.front: [Mrs Birling: denial] "I did nothing I'm ashamed of"
flashcards.back: Act 2. Analysis: total denial; morality as reputation. Method: negative statement, dramatic irony. Context: judgemental charity before the welfare state.

flashcards.front: [Mrs Birling: blame] "the father of the child"
flashcards.back: Act 2. Analysis: blames Eric without knowing. Method: dramatic irony at the Act 2 curtain. Context: one critical reading links her to pride, one of the seven deadly sins (Priestley never says this).

flashcards.front: [Sheila: change] "I'll never, never do it again"
flashcards.back: Act 1. Analysis: sincere guilt. Method: repetition. Context: the younger generation of 1945.
Act 2. Analysis: the Inspector lets them condemn themselves. Method: metaphor of hanging. Link: her growing perception.
Act 2, about Gerald. Analysis: she sees through upper-class romantic self-image. Method: irony, sarcasm. Context: rejection of passive female role.
Act 1, Sheila on Eric. Analysis: drinking treated as a joke. Method: slang, foreshadowing. Context: upper-class male privilege.
Act 3. Analysis: minimises his assault on Eva. Method: euphemism, vague 'a chap'. Context: sexual exploitation of working-class women.
Opening stage direction. Analysis: charming, confident aristocrat. Method: stage direction. Context: aristocracy and business merging.
Act 3. Analysis: returns to complacency, offers the ring back. Method: sweeping pronoun; ring as symbol. Context: warning to the 1945 audience.
Act 1 stage direction. Analysis: moral weight and authority. Method: stage direction. Context: power not based on class.
Act 2. Analysis: wealth brings duties. Method: antithesis. Context: Priestley's socialism.
Act 3 final speech. Analysis: society is connected. Method: collective pronoun, declarative. Context: 1945 welfare state.
Act 3. Analysis: guilt is shared; no one can hide. Method: blunt verb 'kill', addressed to every family member. Context: collective responsibility.
Opening stage direction for when the Inspector arrives. Analysis: interrogation exposes the family. Method: symbolic lighting. Context: change from 'pink and intimate'.
Opening stage direction. Analysis: wealth without warmth; the family lacks love. Method: stage direction, contrast. Context: Edwardian middle-class materialism.
Act 3 ending. Analysis: the cycle restarts; guilt cannot be escaped. Method: cyclical structure, cliffhanger. Context: Priestley's interest in time theories (J.W. Dunne).

flashcards.front: [Eva as symbol] "millions and millions of Eva Smiths"
flashcards.back: Act 3. Analysis: she stands for all workers. Method: repetition, hyperbole. Context: pre-welfare-state poverty.

flashcards.front: [Ozymandias] "Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!"
flashcards.back: Analysis: arrogant boast, now ironic. Method: imperative, exclamation, irony. Context: Shelley's hatred of tyranny.
Analysis: blunt collapse of power. Method: short sentence straight after the boast, ended by a caesura. Effect: time defeats tyranny.
Analysis: oppression is everywhere. Method: anaphora of 'every'. Context: laws restricting the poor in 1790s London.
Analysis: monarchy guilty of soldiers' deaths; hint of revolution. Method: metaphor, synaesthesia. Context: French Revolution.
Analysis: love and life destroyed by disease and poverty. Method: oxymoron. Context: sexually transmitted disease and prostitution in Blake's London.
Analysis: childish, magical confidence. Method: fairy-tale adjective. Link: contrast with the huge peak.
Analysis: confidence replaced by fear. Method: verb choice, structural reversal of the opening. Context: the sublime.
Analysis: nature's power stays in his mind. Method: abstract adjectives, ending. Context: Romantic nature as teacher.

flashcards.front: [My Last Duchess] "Looking as if she were alive"
flashcards.back: Analysis: prefers her as a controllable portrait. Method: simile, dramatic monologue. Context: women as possessions in the Renaissance.

flashcards.front: [My Last Duchess] "I choose / Never to stoop"
flashcards.back: Analysis: pride and refusal to communicate. Method: enjambment emphasising 'Never'. Context: aristocratic status.
Analysis: the final statue symbolises his urge to control. Method: symbolism at the ending. Link: compare with Ozymandias's statue.

flashcards.front: [Charge of the Light Brigade] "Theirs not to reason why"
flashcards.back: Analysis: praises obedience. Method: anaphora with 'Theirs not to'. Context: Victorian duty and the Crimean War.

flashcards.front: [Charge of the Light Brigade] "Honour the Light Brigade"
flashcards.back: Analysis: commands public memory. Method: imperative ending. Context: Tennyson as Poet Laureate.

flashcards.front: [Exposure] "Dawn massing in the east her melancholy army"
flashcards.back: Analysis: hope becomes an enemy. Method: personification, military metaphor. Context: 1917 winter on the Western Front.
Analysis: loss of faith. Method: ambiguity. Context: Owen's religious background.

flashcards.front: [Storm on the Island] "spits like a tame cat"
flashcards.back: Analysis: familiar nature turns savage. Method: simile and enjambment. Context: rural Irish island life.
Analysis: ideals dropped in terror. Method: list ending in bathos. Context: WW1 propaganda.
Analysis: uncertainty fuels guilt. Method: antithesis, colloquial tone. Context: Iraq, rules of engagement.
Analysis: domestic scene full of injury. Method: semantic field of wounds. Context: modern conflicts, Armistice.
Analysis: suffering ordered and stored. Method: sibilance, alliteration. Context: photojournalism.
Analysis: Dharker imagines a paper structure built to be temporary, set against the 'monoliths' of pride. Method: definite negative, enjambment. Context: borders and identity.
Analysis: the city is oppressed, but memory stays bright. Method: personification of the city. Context: exile and refugees.

flashcards.front: [Checking Out Me History] "carving out me identity"
flashcards.back: Analysis: reclaiming selfhood. Method: final line, metaphor of carving, Creole grammar. Context: colonial education.
Analysis: propaganda as a spell. Method: magical lexis. Context: Bushido code and WW2.

flashcards.front: Thesis: How is Macbeth presented as a tragic hero?
flashcards.back: Shakespeare makes Macbeth tragic because he is never blind to his crimes: his clear moral vision, not his ambition alone, is what destroys him, so the audience pities a man who chooses evil while fully understanding it.

flashcards.front: Thesis: How is Lady Macbeth presented?
flashcards.back: Lady Macbeth's power is real but borrowed from the supernatural: she can command her husband but not her own conscience, and her collapse shows that rejecting one's nature is unsustainable.
Banquo is Macbeth's moral mirror: he hears the same prophecy and feels the same temptation, so his resistance proves that Macbeth's fall is a choice, not fate.
Macduff redefines masculinity as courage joined with feeling, and his victory shows that true manhood, not ruthless ambition, restores the natural order.

flashcards.front: Thesis: How are the Witches presented?
flashcards.back: The Witches are catalysts, not controllers: they speak Macbeth's ambition aloud but never command him, exposing how easily free will can be seduced.

flashcards.front: Thesis: How does Shakespeare present guilt?
flashcards.back: Guilt is the natural order fighting back inside the mind: neither Macbeth nor Lady Macbeth can command it, and it destroys them in opposite ways at opposite times.

flashcards.front: Thesis: How does Shakespeare present kingship?
flashcards.back: Kingship is a sacred trust, not a prize: Duncan and Malcolm show it as service under God, while Macbeth's reign shows a stolen crown can only be held through fear.

flashcards.front: Thesis: How does Shakespeare present violence?
flashcards.back: Violence in Macbeth is judged by its target: the same brutality that makes a hero on the battlefield makes a tyrant when turned on the king.

flashcards.front: Thesis: How is Scrooge presented as changing?
flashcards.back: Dickens presents Scrooge's change as a recovery of what he once was: his redemption is a return to the feeling boy of Stave 2, proving that greed is learned and can be unlearned.

flashcards.front: Thesis: How does Dickens present poverty?
flashcards.back: Dickens presents poverty as a social choice, not a natural fact: by forcing Scrooge to see the poor as individuals, he forces readers to see their own responsibility.

flashcards.front: Thesis: How does Dickens present the Cratchits?
flashcards.back: The Cratchits show that poverty cannot destroy love but can destroy lives: their warmth makes Scrooge's coldness shameful, and Tiny Tim's fate makes it deadly.

flashcards.front: Thesis: How does Dickens present Christmas?
flashcards.back: Christmas is presented as a moral season that tests generosity: those who share it (Fred, Fezziwig, the Cratchits) are rich in spirit, and Scrooge's rejection of it is a rejection of humanity.

flashcards.front: Thesis: How does Dickens use the ghosts?
flashcards.back: The ghosts are a teaching method: Past shows cause, Present shows consequence, and Yet to Come shows choice, so the supernatural becomes a structured lesson in redemption.

flashcards.front: Thesis: How does Dickens present loneliness?
flashcards.back: Loneliness is both Scrooge's punishment and his cause: neglected as a child, he chooses isolation as an adult, and Dickens shows connection is the only cure.

flashcards.front: Thesis: How is Mr Birling presented?
flashcards.back: Priestley makes Birling the confident voice of capitalism and then destroys his credibility with dramatic irony, so the audience rejects both the man and the system he speaks for.
Sheila is Priestley's model of the conscience awakening: she moves from a sheltered daughter to the Inspector's ally, proving the young can break free of their parents' values.

flashcards.front: Thesis: How is the Inspector presented?
flashcards.back: The Inspector is less a policeman than a moral force: his mysterious identity matters less than his message, which judges the Birlings and the audience alike.
Gerald is the most dangerous character because he is the most likeable: his real kindness makes his final return to complacency a warning that charm hides exploitation.
Eric is the damaged product of a family that gives money instead of guidance, yet his acceptance of guilt shows even the most flawed young person can be redeemed.

flashcards.front: Thesis: How does Priestley present class?
flashcards.back: Class is presented as a system that lets the privileged harm the poor without seeing it, and Eva's absence from the stage shows how invisible the working class is to the Birlings.

flashcards.front: Thesis: How does Priestley present the generations?
flashcards.back: Priestley divides the family by age to argue that the future belongs to those willing to change: the old cling to 1912 while the young look towards 1945.

flashcards.front: Thesis: How does Priestley present responsibility?
flashcards.back: Responsibility is a choice the play forces on everyone: the Inspector gives each Birling the same evidence, so their responses, not their guilt, are what Priestley judges.

flashcards.front: Thesis: Compare power of humans (Ozymandias + My Last Duchess)
flashcards.back: Both expose the arrogance of rulers, but time has already defeated Shelley's king while Browning's Duke remains dangerous, so one poem offers comfort and the other a warning.

flashcards.front: Thesis: Compare effects of conflict (Remains + Kamikaze)
flashcards.back: Both show a single choice in conflict shaping a whole life, but Armitage's soldier is haunted by what he did, whereas Garland's pilot is punished for what he refused to do.

flashcards.front: Thesis: Compare identity (Checking Out Me History + The Emigree)
flashcards.back: Both speakers hold on to an identity that authority tries to erase, but Agard fights back with anger, while Rumens's speaker protects hers through love and memory.
Both present nature as stronger than human will, but Wordsworth's nature teaches the boy humility, while Owen's nature simply kills the soldiers it surrounds.
A host had a sacred duty to protect guests. Duncan is Macbeth's king, kinsman and guest, so the murder breaks three bonds at once (Macbeth says so in 1.7).
Jesuit priest executed in 1606 for the Gunpowder Plot; defended 'equivocation' (misleading truths). The Porter's 'equivocator' joke points to him.
James I believed he descended from Banquo. Shakespeare makes Banquo noble and shows his heirs as kings (the line of eight kings in 4.1) to flatter James.
Suicide was a mortal sin; suicides could be denied Christian burial. Lady Macbeth's death completes her damnation in Jacobean eyes.
The 1840s: food shortages, high bread prices, poverty and unrest in Britain. A Christmas Carol (1843) appeared in the middle of it.
Government report on children in mines and factories. It shocked Dickens, who first planned a pamphlet and wrote A Christmas Carol instead.
Dickens visited this school for poor children in 1843. The experience inspired Ignorance and Want.
Christmas traditions (cards, trees, family feasts) grew popular in the 1840s. Dickens helped make Christmas a festival of family and charity.
Dickens's father was imprisoned for debt in the Marshalsea (1824). Dickens, aged 12, worked in Warren's Blacking Factory, which shaped his sympathy for the poor.
In 1912 women could not vote in general elections; suffragettes were campaigning. Some women gained the vote in 1918 and all women over 21 in 1928.

Before 1945 Britain had only limited welfare (old age pensions from 1908, the 1911 National Insurance Act) and no NHS. The 1942 Beveridge Report proposed a full welfare state; Labour built it after 1945.
Priestley's 'Postscripts' radio talks (1940) were hugely popular and argued for a fairer post-war Britain. He was taken off air partly for being too left-wing.

flashcards.front: First performance of An Inspector Calls
flashcards.back: First staged in 1945 in Moscow (the Soviet Union) because no London theatre was available, then in London in 1946.
Britain, France and the Ottoman Empire against Russia. The Light Brigade's charge at Balaclava (1854) was a disastrous misunderstanding of orders.
Late 18th-early 19th century movement (Wordsworth, Blake, Shelley) valuing nature, emotion, imagination and the individual, and often opposing tyranny.
A Romantic idea: nature so vast and powerful that it creates awe mixed with fear. Seen in The Prelude's mountain.
Japanese warrior code of honour and loyalty. Kamikaze pilots who returned were often shamed for failing their duty.
Best with: My Last Duchess (pride of rulers, art outlasting power), Tissue (temporary human power), London (abuse of power). Key contrast: time defeats Ozymandias; the Duke is still powerful.
Best with: Checking Out Me History (institutions controlling people), Ozymandias (tyranny), The Emigree (a city under oppression). Key contrast: Blake's despair vs Agard's defiance.
Best with: Storm on the Island (power of nature), Exposure (nature as hostile), Bayonet Charge (sudden fear changing a young man). Key contrast: nature teaches Wordsworth; it kills Owen's soldiers.
Best with: Ozymandias (pride, art and power), Tissue (paper/art vs control), Checking Out Me History (control of a story). Key contrast: dramatic monologue vs framed sonnet.

flashcards.front: Pairings: The Charge of the Light Brigade
flashcards.back: Best with: Bayonet Charge (realities of battle), Exposure (heroism vs futility), Kamikaze (duty and obedience). Key contrast: glorification vs disillusion.
Best with: Storm on the Island (nature as enemy), The Prelude (nature's power), War Photographer (reality of conflict ignored at home). Key contrast: waiting in silence vs sudden violence.
Best with: The Prelude (nature's power humbling humans), Exposure (weather as enemy), Ozymandias (human confidence undermined). Key contrast: collective 'We' vs a lone boy.
Best with: Charge of the Light Brigade (soldiers in battle), Remains (effects of conflict on a soldier), Exposure (futility). Key contrast: frozen moment of doubt vs Tennyson's unquestioning charge.
Best with: War Photographer (guilt, memories that will not fade), Kamikaze (one decision with lifelong consequences), Poppies (aftermath). Key contrast: perpetrator's guilt vs witness's guilt.
Best with: War Photographer (impact on those at home), The Emigree (memory and loss), Kamikaze (family and conflict). Key contrast: maternal grief vs a photographer's professional distance.
Best with: Remains (trauma and memory), Poppies (people at home), Exposure (ignored reality of war). Key contrast: controlled form vs Armitage's colloquial breakdown.
Best with: Ozymandias (human power is temporary), My Last Duchess (art and documents vs control), Checking Out Me History (recorded identity). Key contrast: Dharker's gentle hope vs Shelley's irony.
Best with: Checking Out Me History (identity and the past), Poppies (memory and loss), London (a city of oppression). Key contrast: loving memory vs Blake's bleak present.
Best with: London (oppressive institutions), The Emigree (identity), Tissue (who writes the record). Key contrast: anger and rebellion vs Rumens's quiet loyalty.
Best with: Remains (consequences of a decision), Charge of the Light Brigade (duty vs individual), Poppies (family impact). Key contrast: refusing to kill vs being haunted by killing.
1) The title. 2) The speaker and who they address. 3) The volta or shift. 4) The ending. 5) Two or three standout images. Then write.
Track I/you/we. A shift (e.g. 'I' to 'we') often shows connection or a change of perspective, and is a precise structural point.
Means a conceptualised reading of the poem as a whole, judicious short quotes, analysis of language AND structure/form, and more than one interpretation.
Exploratory comparison of methods only (language, structure, form) with judicious terminology. Compare effects, not content.
Top 27.2 answers find a method both poets use (e.g. personification, repetition at the end) and explain how it creates different effects.
Critical, exploratory, conceptualised, judicious references, analysis of methods, perceptive context links.
Considering more than one interpretation, using tentative language (perhaps, could, may), and following an idea through rather than just stating it.
Spend about 40% on the extract and 60% on the wider text; track the idea from beginning to end of the text.
About 50 minutes per essay: 5 min planning, 40 min writing, 5 min checking (AO4 on Macbeth).
About 45 min AIC, 45 min anthology comparison, 35 min Q27.1, 10 min Q27.2.
'Alternatively...', 'A modern audience might...', 'However, it could also suggest...', 'Some readers may see...'.
After every point, ask why the writer wanted the audience to think or feel this. The answer is your writer's-purpose sentence.
Mr Birling, Act 1. He mocks the idea that everyone should look after each other. Shows his selfish capitalism; the Inspector's arrival interrupts this speech.
Mr Birling, Act 1. Dismisses socialist ideas as foolish. Priestley makes the audience reject him through dramatic irony.
Mr Birling to Gerald, Act 1. Hopes the Crofts and Birlings will work together. Shows the engagement is partly a business deal.
Mr Birling, Act 3. He tries to buy his way out of the scandal. Shows he thinks money solves everything; the Inspector says he offers it at the wrong time.
Mr Birling, Act 3, sarcastically to Sheila and Eric. Shows the generational divide and his refusal to learn.
Stage direction for Mrs Birling. Priestley signals her lack of compassion before she speaks.
Mrs Birling, end of Act 2, about the father of Eva's baby. Dramatic irony: she is condemning her own son, Eric.
Mrs Birling, Act 2. Assumes a working-class girl would never refuse stolen money. Shows class prejudice.
Sheila, Act 1, after confessing about Milwards. Shows genuine guilt early on, unlike her father.
Sheila, Act 3, to her parents. She has learnt the Inspector's lesson and is now the moral voice of the family.
Sheila, Act 3, refusing Gerald's ring. Short sentences show new independence; she will not slip back to how things were.
Stage direction for Eric. Suggests unease and hidden secrets (drinking, Eva) beneath the family's polished surface.
Gerald, Act 3, offering the ring back. Shows he wants to return to normal: he has not truly changed.
Gerald on Daisy Renton, Act 2. Focus on looks suggests his help was partly for his own pleasure.
The Inspector, Act 3, telling each of them in turn that they share the blame. Shared, collective responsibility: no single person is to blame, which is Priestley's socialist message.

flashcards.front: Where is An Inspector Calls set?
flashcards.back: Brumley, a fictional industrial city in the North Midlands, in the Birlings' dining room, spring 1912.
The charity Mrs Birling chairs. It refuses Eva help: shows charity used for status and judgement, not compassion.

flashcards.front: Where was the play first performed and why?
flashcards.back: Moscow, 1945 (no London theatre was free). First London performance 1946.
The doorbell rings just as Birling says a man should look after himself. The interruption signals the challenge to his selfish views.
Each act ends on a cliffhanger (Act 1 the Inspector's 'Well?'; Act 2 Eric's entrance; Act 3 the phone call), keeping suspense high.
Birling is repeatedly cut off, first by the doorbell, later by the Inspector. Shows his power and views being silenced.
Gerald leaves for a walk in Act 2 and Eric is absent until the end of Act 2. Exits let tension build and set up dramatic revelations.
Priestley was interested in time theories (e.g. J.W. Dunne). Supports reading the Inspector as a figure from outside normal time.
He voices Priestley's own socialist views: collective responsibility and care for the working class.
Respectable public roles (Lord Mayor, magistrate, charity chair) hide private cruelty, drinking, affairs and theft.
Guilt is a feeling; responsibility means accepting your actions and changing. Sheila and Eric do both; the parents feel neither.
Plan to defeat the 'five giants': Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor, Idleness. Led to the post-1945 welfare state, matching the Inspector's message.

flashcards.front: Ozymandias: "Two vast and trunkless legs of stone"
flashcards.back: The statue's broken remains. 'Vast' shows his ambition; 'trunkless' shows it has been cut down. Power reduced to fragments.

flashcards.front: Ozymandias: "The hand that mocked them, and the heart that fed"
flashcards.back: Sculptor's hand copied and mocked the king's passions; the king's heart fed them. Art outlives power.

flashcards.front: Ozymandias: "Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!"
flashcards.back: Arrogant imperative. Ironic now: the Mighty should despair because their power will fall too.
Short, blunt sentence straight after the boast. Sudden collapse of his claim.

flashcards.front: Ozymandias: "The lone and level sands stretch far away"
flashcards.back: Alliteration and long vowels create emptiness and vast time. Nature outlasts human power.
Turn at line 9, 'And on the pedestal, these words appear': the poem moves from the broken statue to the king's boast and its irony.
In 1817, in a friendly sonnet-writing competition with Horace Smith. Published in 1818.

flashcards.front: Ozymandias: main idea in one line
flashcards.back: Human power and pride are temporary; time, nature and art outlast tyrants.
Owned and controlled, even the Thames. Ironic, as charters also grant rights. Shows no freedom in the city.

flashcards.front: London: "Marks of weakness, marks of woe"
flashcards.back: Repetition and alliteration. Suffering is visible on every face. 'Mark' is repeated across the stanza (I mark / marks).
Soot-blackened, morally stained Church; 'appals' = shocks and covers like a funeral pall. Church ignores child sweeps.

flashcards.front: London: "Runs in blood down Palace walls"
flashcards.back: Soldiers die for the monarchy; blood on the palace blames royalty. Echoes the French Revolution (1789).
Young women forced into prostitution by poverty. Her curse spreads harm to the next generation.
Oxymoron: marriage (new life) joined with death. Society's corruption poisons even love and family.
'In every...' repeated in stanza 2. Builds a relentless list: suffering is universal.
First-person wanderer ('I wander', 'I hear') who observes and reports, like a witness. Present tense makes it feel ongoing.

flashcards.front: My Last Duchess: "That's my last Duchess painted on the wall"
flashcards.back: Opening line. 'My' = possession; 'last' suggests one in a series, and there will be a next one.

flashcards.front: My Last Duchess: "The curtain I have drawn for you"
flashcards.back: Only the Duke reveals the portrait. Now he controls who sees her smile.

flashcards.front: My Last Duchess: "A heart—how shall I say?—too soon made glad"
flashcards.back: Dashes and fake hesitation. He presents her friendliness as a fault: jealousy.

flashcards.front: My Last Duchess: "My gift of a nine-hundred-years-old name"
flashcards.back: Pride in lineage and status. Angry she valued it no more than small kindnesses.
He refuses to lower himself to discuss his feelings with her. Pride over communication.
Final image: Neptune controlling a wild creature. Mirrors the Duke 'taming' his wife; warning for the next.
The Duke means to impress the envoy, but reveals his jealousy and cruelty. Browning lets readers judge him.
The Duke tells the envoy the Count's daughter herself is his 'object', after mentioning the Count's wealth. Ironic: he cares about money and status.

flashcards.front: Storm on the Island: "We are prepared"
flashcards.back: Confident opening statement: collective pride in preparation. Undermined by the end.

flashcards.front: Storm on the Island: "we build our houses squat"
flashcards.back: Low, sturdy houses: practical defence against the weather. Shows the islanders' tough way of life.
Military verb (attack from aircraft). The enemy can't be seen or fought.

flashcards.front: Storm on the Island: "Space is a salvo"
flashcards.back: Metaphor of a burst of gunfire; plosive/sibilant sound. Even empty space attacks.

flashcards.front: Storm on the Island: "bombarded by the empty air"
flashcards.back: Paradox: emptiness attacks. Continues the war semantic field.

flashcards.front: Storm on the Island: "a huge nothing that we fear"
flashcards.back: Final paradox. Fear of an invisible, overwhelming force. Confidence has collapsed.

flashcards.front: Storm on the Island: conversational voice
flashcards.back: Direct address ('You might think', 'you know what I mean') makes the reader part of the community and the fear.

flashcards.front: Storm on the Island: collection and background
flashcards.back: From Death of a Naturalist (1966), Heaney's first major collection. He grew up on a farm in County Derry, Northern Ireland.

flashcards.front: The Prelude: "an act of stealth / And troubled pleasure"
flashcards.back: Stealing the boat brings joy and guilt together. Sets up nature's later 'punishment'.
Simile of grace and pride as the boat moves. The boy's confidence before the volta.

flashcards.front: The Prelude: "Small circles glittering idly in the moon"
flashcards.back: Calm, beautiful light imagery. Peaceful mood that the peak destroys.
Personification: the peak rises like a monster. The volta: awe and terror (the sublime).
The mountain seems to chase him. Nature as a living, punishing force; guilt made physical.

flashcards.front: The Prelude: "There hung a darkness, call it solitude / Or blank desertion"
flashcards.back: After the event his mind feels empty and abandoned. Lasting psychological effect.
Imagery shifts from glittering moonlight and sparkling water to 'black' peak and 'darkness' in his mind. Mirrors his mood.
Romantic idea of awe mixed with terror at nature's vast power. The peak is a clear example.
Rhetorical question ending stanza 2. Confusion and futility; questions the point of the war.

flashcards.front: Exposure: "Like twitching agonies of men among its brambles"
flashcards.back: Simile: the wire looks like dying men. Death is everywhere, even in objects.

flashcards.front: Exposure: "Dawn massing in the east her melancholy army"
flashcards.back: Personification: dawn as an enemy army. Reverses the usual symbol of hope.

flashcards.front: Exposure: "Sudden successive flights of bullets streak the silence"
flashcards.back: Sibilance imitates bullets. Brief action in a poem of waiting.

flashcards.front: Exposure: "on us the doors are closed"
flashcards.back: Imagined trip home: they are shut out. Forgotten and rejected by home.

flashcards.front: Exposure: "For love of God seems dying"
flashcards.back: Double meaning: their love for God, or God's love for them, is dying. Loss of faith.
Final stanza: frozen dead soldiers. Short, blunt metaphor; nature has killed them.
Double meaning: exposure to the cold, and exposing the truth about war to readers at home.
Donalbain, Act 2.3, to Malcolm. Appearance vs reality: friends may be murderers, so the princes flee.

flashcards.front: "Had he not resembled / My father as he slept"
flashcards.back: Lady Macbeth, Act 2.2. She couldn't kill Duncan herself: hint of conscience beneath her ruthlessness.

flashcards.front: "To be thus is nothing, / But to be safely thus"
flashcards.back: Macbeth, Act 3.1 soliloquy. Being king means nothing without security: his paranoia about Banquo.
Banquo, Act 3.1, alone. He suspects Macbeth murdered Duncan, but stays silent.
Macduff, Act 4.3, on hearing his family has been murdered. Raw grief; leads to 'I must also feel it as a man'.

flashcards.front: "Here's the smell of the blood still"
flashcards.back: Lady Macbeth sleepwalking, Act 5.1. Guilt she cannot wash away; contrast with 'A little water clears us'.

flashcards.front: "If chance will have me king, why, chance may crown me"
flashcards.back: Macbeth's aside, Act 1.3. Fate vs free will: he briefly decides to leave it to fate, but later chooses to act.

flashcards.front: "There's no art / To find the mind's construction in the face"
flashcards.back: Duncan, Act 1.4, about the traitor Cawdor. Appearance vs reality; dramatic irony as Macbeth enters.
Lady Macbeth, Act 1.5. Calls on darkness to hide her evil. Light/dark imagery; links her to the supernatural.
Second apparition, Act 4.1. Equivocation: makes Macbeth overconfident because no man 'of woman born' can harm him.
Lady Macbeth, Act 5.1. Reverses her earlier 'what's done is done' (3.2). Guilt is permanent.
Lady Macbeth sleepwalking, Act 5.1. She now fears damnation; the evil she summoned has consumed her.
Stave 1, narrator on Scrooge. Simile: cold and unbreakable; no 'generous fire' has ever been struck from him.

flashcards.front: "Darkness is cheap, and Scrooge liked it"
flashcards.back: Stave 1, narrator. Miserly (saves on candles) and morally dark.

flashcards.front: "a solitary child, neglected by his friends"
flashcards.back: Stave 2, Ghost of Christmas Past at the school. Explains Scrooge's isolation and creates sympathy.
Belle, Stave 2. Money has replaced love in Scrooge's heart: the idol is 'a golden one'.
Bob's toast to Scrooge, Stave 3. Ironic; Mrs Cratchit responds bitterly. Shows Scrooge's impact on the poor.

flashcards.front: "as good a master, and as good a man"
flashcards.back: Stave 5, narrator. Scrooge's full transformation: good to employees and good as a person.
